These attacks can be used to exfiltrate sensitive information from restricted environments, establish command and control channels for malware, bypass network monitoring and data loss prevention systems, or enable unauthorized communication between isolated systems. The covert nature of these channels makes them particularly difficult to detect using traditional security monitoring.
Advanced covert channel attacks may exploit model artifacts such as embedding spaces, latent representations, or internal model states to hide information. Attackers might also use adversarial techniques to encode data in model outputs that appear normal to human observers but contain hidden information extractable through specific decoding methods.
examples:
Research demonstrates emergent steganographic collusion in LLMs ({{ref:mathew-2024-steganographic-collusion}}) where models trained with misspecified reward incentives spontaneously develop hidden encoding schemes in generated text, undetectable by standard oversight.
Studies show remote timing attacks on LLM inference ({{ref:carlini-2024-remote-timing-attacks}}) where efficiency optimizations introduce data-dependent timing that leaks conversation topics and PII through encrypted network traffic.

introduced: Covert Channels in Model Outputs are introduced when AI systems lack proper output monitoring, steganography detection, or behavioral analysis capabilities, allowing attackers to exploit model outputs for hidden information transmission.
exposed: This risk is exposed during model usage when attackers encode hidden information in model outputs, response patterns, or behavioral characteristics, potentially enabling unauthorized data exfiltration or covert communication that bypasses traditional security controls.
mitigated: Mitigation involves implementing comprehensive output validation and sanitization, deploying steganography detection systems, monitoring for anomalous response patterns, analyzing model behavior for covert channels, and applying randomization techniques to disrupt potential information encoding mechanisms.

externalReferences.title: Hidden in Plain Text: Emergence and Mitigation of Steganographic Collusion in LLMs
Remote Timing Attacks on Efficient Language Model Inference

risks.title: Malicious Loader/Deserialization
shortDescription: Unsafe loaders for models and tokenizers that can cause remote code execution or integrity compromise. Malicious Loader/Deserialization poses significant security risks including system compromise and data breaches.
longDescription:
Exploitation of unsafe deserialization processes or malicious model loading mechanisms that can lead to remote code execution, system compromise, or integrity violations when loading AI models, tokenizers, or related artifacts.
Many AI frameworks use serialization formats like pickle, joblib, or custom binary formats to store and load models, weights, tokenizers, and preprocessing pipelines. These formats can contain executable code that runs during the deserialization process. Attackers can craft malicious model files that execute arbitrary code when loaded, potentially compromising the entire system.
This risk extends beyond traditional pickle-based attacks to include malicious model architectures, compromised tokenizer configurations, and poisoned preprocessing pipelines. Even seemingly safe formats can be exploited through buffer overflows, path traversal attacks, or by exploiting vulnerabilities in parsing libraries.
The attack surface is particularly large because model loading often occurs with elevated privileges, and users frequently download models from untrusted sources or model repositories without proper verification. Malicious loaders can also be used to establish persistence, exfiltrate data, or serve as entry points for further attacks on AI infrastructure.
Modern attacks may also target container images, model serving frameworks, or cloud-based model repositories, making the threat landscape even more complex and requiring comprehensive security measures throughout the model lifecycle.
examples:
Research has demonstrated pickle deserialization attacks ({{ref:trailofbits-2021-pickle-exploitation}}) where malicious model files execute arbitrary code during loading.
Security researchers have shown weaponized ML models ({{ref:hiddenlayer-2022-weaponizing-ml-ransomware}}) that can deploy ransomware or establish backdoors when loaded by unsuspecting users.
Studies reveal widespread remote code execution risks in ML model hosting ecosystems ({{ref:siddiq-2026-rce-model-hosting}}) where unsafe deserialization and custom code execution during model loading affect tens of thousands of repositories.

introduced: Malicious Loader/Deserialization risks are introduced when model loading processes use unsafe deserialization methods, lack proper input validation, or fail to verify the integrity and authenticity of model files before loading them into memory.
exposed: This risk is exposed during model loading and initialization phases when malicious code embedded in model files, tokenizers, or related artifacts is executed, potentially compromising the entire system or infrastructure.
mitigated: Mitigation involves using secure serialization formats, implementing strict input validation and sanitization, verifying model integrity through cryptographic signatures, sandboxing model loading processes, and using secure-by-default ML tooling that prevents code execution during deserialization.

externalReferences.title: Never a dill moment: Exploiting machine learning pickle files
Weaponizing ML Models with Ransomware
An Empirical Study on Remote Code Execution in Machine Learning Model Hosting Ecosystems

risks.title: Tool Source Provenance
shortDescription: Use of unvetted or unverified tool registries, MCP server manifests, or tool metadata sources that may provide agents with deceptive tool descriptions, altered schemas, or shadowed tool names.
longDescription:
Agents depend on tool metadata from registries, MCP server manifests, and discovery endpoints to decide which tools to invoke. When these sources are adopted without provenance verification, cryptographic signing, or publisher identity validation, the agent may receive deliberately deceptive tool descriptions or schemas. Three gaps widen this exposure: third-party tools that are discovered or registered without any check of the publisher's identity or provenance, registries or manifests that are added without cryptographic signature verification, and a tool-selection step that trusts a tool's described functionality without independently confirming the tool behaves as claimed.
This risk operates at the tool selection layer, before a prompt is constructed. Unlike {{riskPromptInjection}}, which targets model input processing, {{riskToolSourceProvenance}} targets the trust assumptions in tool discovery. The agent's reasoning core treats tool metadata as authoritative, and unvetted sources exploit that trust.
Attack patterns include Tool Poisoning (malicious logic hidden in tool descriptions), Tool Shadowing and Typosquatting (lookalike tools using similar names or Unicode homoglyphs), and Schema Poisoning (configuration files that alter tool behavior). These were cataloged by Checkmarx in their MCP risk taxonomy (December 2025).
{{riskToolSourceProvenance}} is structurally analogous to {{riskModelSourceTampering}}, which addresses unvetted model artifacts in the supply chain. Both are provenance failures where untrusted sources are consumed without verification. A successful {{riskToolSourceProvenance}} exploit typically manifests as {{riskRogueActions}} when the agent invokes the wrong tool.
examples:
The Checkmarx CxZero MCP Risk Taxonomy ({{ref:checkmarx-2025-mcp-emerging-risks}}) (December 2025) identified Tool Poisoning, Tool Shadowing, and Schema Poisoning as three of the top 11 MCP security risks.
The NeurIPS 2025 paper "Attractive Metadata Attack" ({{ref:mo-2025-attractive-metadata-attack}}) demonstrated that metadata manipulation alone is sufficient to redirect tool selection in agentic systems, achieving 81-95% attack success rates.

introduced: Tool Source Provenance risk is introduced when tool registries, MCP server manifests, or discovery endpoints are adopted without provenance verification or publisher identity validation.
exposed: This risk is exposed during tool discovery and selection when agents consume unvetted tool metadata and make invocation decisions based on unverified descriptions or schemas.
mitigated: Mitigation involves cryptographic signing of tool manifests, publisher identity verification, namespace governance to prevent typosquatting, and least-privilege tool access policies.

externalReferences.title: 11 Emerging AI Security Risks with MCP (Model Context Protocol)
Attractive Metadata Attack: Inducing LLM Agents to Invoke Malicious Tools

risks.title: Prompt/Response Cache Poisoning
shortDescription: Cross-user contamination via shared LLM caches lacking isolation and validation. Prompt/Response Cache Poisoning can lead to information leakage, misinformation propagation, and unauthorized access to cached content.
longDescription:
Malicious manipulation of shared prompt and response caches used by language model systems to optimize performance, resulting in cross-user contamination and potential security breaches.
Many LLM deployments use caching mechanisms to store frequently accessed prompts and their corresponding responses to reduce computational costs and improve response times. When these caches lack proper isolation, validation, or access controls, attackers can exploit them to inject malicious content, extract sensitive information from other users' sessions, or manipulate responses served to subsequent users.
Cache poisoning attacks can occur through several vectors: injecting crafted prompts designed to pollute cache entries, exploiting weak cache key generation that allows cache collisions, or compromising cache storage systems directly. The attack becomes particularly dangerous when cached responses contain sensitive information, personal data, or malicious instructions that get served to unintended users.
This risk is amplified in multi-tenant environments where multiple users or applications share the same caching infrastructure without adequate isolation. Attackers may also exploit cache timing attacks to infer information about cached content or use cache behavior to fingerprint other users' activities.
examples:
Research has shown semantic cache key collision attacks ({{ref:zhang-2026-semantic-cache-collision}}) where crafted prompts can hijack cached LLM responses, serving attacker-controlled content to other users through shared caching mechanisms.
Studies demonstrate privacy risks in KV-cache systems ({{ref:luo-2025-kv-cache-privacy}}) where user inputs can be reconstructed from plaintext cache contents in multi-tenant LLM serving infrastructure.

introduced: Prompt/Response Cache Poisoning is introduced when caching systems lack proper isolation mechanisms, validation of cached content, or secure cache key generation, allowing malicious actors to manipulate shared cache entries.
exposed: This risk is exposed during model serving when poisoned cache entries are retrieved and served to users, potentially delivering malicious content, sensitive information, or manipulated responses from previous interactions.
mitigated: Mitigation involves implementing strong cache isolation per user or tenant, validating cached content integrity, using cryptographically secure cache keys, and applying access controls to prevent unauthorized cache manipulation.

externalReferences.title: From Similarity to Vulnerability: Key Collision Attack on LLM Semantic Caching
Shadow in the Cache: Unveiling and Mitigating Privacy Risks of KV-cache in LLM Inference

risks.title: Retrieval/Vector Store Poisoning
shortDescription: Poisoning retrieval corpora or vector indices to steer RAG outputs. Retrieval/Vector Store Poisoning can compromise the integrity of knowledge retrieval systems and lead to misinformation or malicious content injection.
longDescription:
Malicious modification of retrieval corpora, vector databases, or knowledge bases used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems to influence model outputs in unintended ways.
This attack involves injecting poisoned documents, embeddings, or metadata into vector stores or retrieval systems that are used to provide context to language models. When users query the system, the poisoned content gets retrieved and incorporated into the model's response, potentially spreading misinformation, biased content, or malicious instructions.
Attackers may exploit vulnerabilities in data ingestion pipelines, compromise data sources, or use adversarial techniques to craft documents that rank highly in similarity searches while containing harmful content. The attack can be particularly effective because users often trust retrieved information as factual and authoritative.
Vector store poisoning can also involve manipulating embedding spaces through adversarial examples that appear semantically similar to legitimate queries but retrieve malicious content, or by exploiting weaknesses in similarity metrics used for retrieval ranking.
examples:
Researchers have demonstrated adversarial attacks on retrieval systems ({{ref:zhong-2023-retrieval-corpus-poisoning}}) where malicious documents are crafted to rank highly for specific queries while containing harmful content.
Studies show that poisoning attacks on vector databases ({{ref:long-2024-dense-retrieval-backdoors}}) can successfully manipulate RAG system outputs by injecting adversarial embeddings.

introduced: Retrieval/Vector Store Poisoning is introduced during data ingestion and indexing processes when malicious content is added to knowledge bases, vector stores, or retrieval corpora without proper validation and sanitization.
exposed: This risk is exposed during retrieval and generation phases when poisoned content is retrieved and incorporated into model responses, potentially spreading misinformation or executing malicious instructions.
mitigated: Mitigation involves implementing robust data validation and sanitization during ingestion, maintaining data integrity through cryptographic verification, and filtering both inputs and outputs to detect and prevent malicious content retrieval.

externalReferences.title: Poisoning Retrieval Corpora by Injecting Adversarial Passages
Backdoor Attacks on Dense Retrieval via Public and Unintentional Triggers

risks.title: Agent Delegation Chain Opacity
shortDescription: Multi-hop agent delegation chains become opaque when intermediate agents do not emit structured delegation events, making it impossible to determine which human, agent, or system authorized or performed an action — even when individual authentication steps succeed.
longDescription:
Agentic systems frequently involve multi-hop delegation where one agent acts on behalf of another (or a human) across tools and MCP servers. Agent Delegation Chain Opacity occurs when the delegation chain is cryptographically valid — each hop holds a properly scoped token — but invisible to forensics because intermediate agents do not emit structured delegation events. The root cause is the absence of structured delegation event emission at each hop, not the failure of individual authentication steps.
This risk extends classical identity federation accountability failures to the agentic domain. In traditional systems, delegation chain integrity is a known challenge: Kerberos constrained delegation struggles with tracing initiators through multiple hops, multi-hop OAuth OBO flows lose the original actor claim when intermediate services fail to propagate it, and RFC 8693 Token Exchange is vulnerable to delegation chain splicing where a compromised intermediary can forge chains that never occurred. The AI-specific amplifier is that agentic orchestration creates delegation chains that are longer, more dynamic, and less predictable than classical flows — agents may spawn sub-agents autonomously based on LLM reasoning, the chain topology is not known at design time, and intermediate agents make non-deterministic decisions about whether and how to delegate.
The vulnerability manifests through missing or incomplete delegation metadata at the IAM, orchestration, or MCP layers — for example, omitting the original caller, intermediate agents, or token exchange steps in log records. Even when individual agents authenticate correctly, the provenance of a given action becomes opaque if correlation IDs and delegation context are not preserved in immutable, queryable logs. A system is exposed when an agent action does not carry an immutable delegation chain with correlation IDs, when intermediate agents do not emit structured delegation events that downstream consumers and auditors can independently verify, or when the delegation logs are themselves mutable or readable beyond the set of authorized auditors.
Potential impacts include inability to investigate incidents — the full actor path, from the originating human through each intermediate agent to the tool that acted, cannot be reconstructed after the fact — inability to attribute actions for compliance or forensics, failure to detect broken, shadowed, or otherwise anomalous delegation chains in real time, and inability to perform effective credential revocation for a specific delegation chain. Consequences include accountability failures, regulatory violations, prolonged breach dwell time, and erosion of trust in autonomous agent systems.
This risk is distinct from {{riskRogueActions}}, which addresses what an agent does wrong; Agent Delegation Chain Opacity addresses the inability to determine who authorized the action. {{riskAgenticDelegationConfusedDeputy}} addresses authorization failure at delegation boundaries; this risk addresses visibility failure across the full chain. {{riskCrossTenantCredentialPropagation}} addresses credential propagation across tenant boundaries, which may be a consequence of delegation chain opacity but is a distinct threat surface.
examples: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 demonstrated "agent session smuggling" (2025) ({{ref:unit42-2025-agent-session-smuggling}}) in Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, where a malicious remote agent injects hidden instructions during established cross-agent communication sessions. The smuggled instructions trigger unauthorized tool execution while remaining invisible to end users who only see the final consolidated response — the delegation chain is opaque because no mechanism exposes intermediate agent activity or attributes the unauthorized action to the originating malicious agent.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when delegation chain architecture is configured — specifically when orchestration layers, IAM policies, and MCP server configurations do not require structured delegation event emission at each hop.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when multi-hop agent delegation occurs without correlation ID propagation or structured delegation events. The opacity persists until an incident requires forensic reconstruction of the actor chain, at which point the gap becomes visible.
mitigated: Mitigated by requiring orchestrators to emit signed delegation spans per hop with correlation IDs, actor identifiers, scope deltas, and timestamps, bound to an append-only store. Real-time detection of missing or out-of-order spans shifts the control from post-incident reconstruction to in-flight chain integrity monitoring.

externalReferences.title: When AI Agents Go Rogue: Agent Session Smuggling Attack in A2A Systems

risks.title: Stale Agent Identity Binding
shortDescription: Agent identity credentials persist unchanged after the underlying model artifact is replaced, allowing a substituted model to operate with the original agent's full permissions because no cryptographic binding ties identity to a specific model version.
longDescription:
In agentic systems, agents are assigned persistent identities with associated credentials and OAuth/MCP tokens granting access to tools and resources. Stale Agent Identity Binding occurs when the underlying model (weights, architecture, or inference endpoint) is replaced without invalidating the agent's credentials or identity. The substituted model inherits the original agent's full privileges because agent identity and model artifact exist on separate infrastructure layers with no cryptographic binding between them. The exposure is present wherever an agent identity is not cryptographically bound to a specific signed model artifact or manifest, wherever a model update or swap does not automatically invalidate or re-scope the agent's credentials, and wherever no runtime attestation of the model artifact precedes tool authorization — leaving no point at which a substitution that occurs after credential issuance would be detected.
This risk is the AI/agentic extension of classical stale credential binding failures. In Kubernetes, long-lived service account tokens persist after pods are replaced — a new pod running entirely different code inherits the previous workload's identity and RBAC permissions. In container orchestration, mutable image tags allow the artifact behind a tag to be replaced while the service identity persists unchanged. In VM environments, machine clones inherit the original's domain credentials and certificates. The AI-specific amplifier is that agent identity and model artifact are managed by entirely separate infrastructure layers (IAM vs. model serving) with no standard binding mechanism. A model can be swapped through supply-chain compromise, container replacement, or CI/CD manipulation, and the agent's credentials remain valid because the identity layer has no awareness of the artifact layer.
This risk is distinct from {{riskModelSourceTampering}} and {{riskModelDeploymentTampering}}, which cover the tampering mechanics themselves. Stale Agent Identity Binding covers the identity lifecycle failure that persists after a swap — the agent continues to authenticate with valid credentials regardless of the model behind it. {{riskShadowAndUnknownAgents}} addresses agents that were never registered; this risk addresses registered agents whose identity binding becomes stale after the underlying artifact changes.
Potential impacts include stealthy behavioral changes (data exfiltration, decision manipulation) under legitimate identity, compromise of connected tools and MCP servers, and accountability failures because actions are attributed to the original authorized model. Consequences include loss of integrity, safety incidents, regulatory violations, and systemic distrust in deployed agentic systems.
examples: Zhou's framework on governing dynamic AI agent capabilities (2026) ({{ref:zhou-2026-cryptographic-tool-binding}}) frames this as a capability-context separation problem: an agent's capabilities can change after authorization — through silent escalation, underlying model substitution, or runtime behavioral drift — without any mechanism to detect that the identity credentials still authorizing the agent are now bound to a different capability set. The paper proposes cryptographic binding between agent identity and the specific tool set authorized at issuance as the mitigation.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when agent identities are provisioned without cryptographic binding to the specific model artifact they authorize, or when model serving infrastructure permits artifact replacement without triggering credential re-issuance.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when the underlying model is replaced — through supply-chain compromise, serving infrastructure manipulation, or routine model updates — and the agent continues operating with the original identity and credentials. The stale binding persists through maintenance cycles if re-binding is not part of the update lifecycle.
mitigated: Mitigated by cryptographic binding of agent identity to specific signed model manifests, runtime attestation of the model artifact before authorizing tool access, and automated credential invalidation on any change to the bound model artifact.

externalReferences.title: Governing Dynamic Capabilities: Cryptographic Binding and Reproducibility Verification for AI Agent Tool Use

risks.title: MCP Transport Hijacking
shortDescription: Transport-layer attacks on MCP connections — including man-in-the-middle, session hijacking, DNS rebinding, and replay — intercept or modify agent-to-tool communication because the MCP specification does not mandate transport encryption or mutual authentication.
longDescription:
The Model Context Protocol enables agents to discover and invoke tools by communicating with MCP servers over HTTP or stdio. MCP Transport Hijacking occurs when these connections lack transport-layer protections, allowing attackers to intercept, modify, or replay messages between the agent and the tool server.
This risk extends classical transport-layer attacks to the MCP protocol. TLS stripping, man-in-the-middle interception, and DNS rebinding against locally-running services are well-documented attack patterns. The AI-specific amplifier is that the MCP specification (2025-11-25) does not mandate TLS for Streamable HTTP connections, uses "SHOULD" rather than "MUST" for authentication and localhost binding, and provides zero transport security for the stdio transport. Agents autonomously connect to MCP servers discovered at runtime without human verification of transport security properties. Session identifiers transmitted in HTTP headers are exposed to interception without mandatory TLS.
Attack vectors include man-in-the-middle on unencrypted or weakly configured MCP connections, DNS rebinding against locally-running MCP servers (acknowledged in the MCP specification's own Security Warning), replay of captured JSON-RPC messages, and session hijacking via intercepted session identifiers. Each of these vectors exploits a gap in transport-layer protection: connections that do not enforce mutual TLS, session tokens that are not bound to transport-layer identifiers, sessions that are long-lived or that lack replay protection, and servers that do not validate the Origin header on incoming connections to block DNS rebinding.
This risk is distinct from {{riskInsecureIntegratedComponent}}, which covers vulnerabilities within MCP server implementations (e.g., path traversal). This risk covers the transport channel between agent and server. It is distinct from {{riskOrchestratorRouteHijacking}}, which covers routing and configuration manipulation. It is distinct from {{riskToolRegistryTampering}}, which covers integrity of tool registration and discovery.
Potential impacts include theft of tool schemas and sensitive data flowing between agents and tools, injection of malicious tool responses, unauthorized execution of agent actions, and compromise of the entire agent workflow. The breach may be difficult to detect because the agent identity remains valid while its communication channel is compromised.
examples:
The MCP specification (2025-11-25) ({{ref:mcp-spec-2025-11-25-transports}}) includes a Security Warning acknowledging DNS rebinding as an attack vector against local MCP servers. Authentication and localhost binding are "SHOULD" rather than "MUST" requirements, TLS is not mandated for Streamable HTTP connections, and the stdio transport provides zero transport security. These protocol-level gaps make transport hijacking a design-level concern, not just an implementation oversight.
The MCP specification's backward compatibility section advises that servers wanting to support older clients "continue to host both the SSE and POST endpoints of the old transport, alongside the new MCP endpoint." The deprecated HTTP+SSE transport placed session identifiers in URL parameters, exposing them in server logs, browser history, and proxy logs. Deployments following this backward compatibility guidance inherit the weaker transport's attack surface.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when MCP connections are configured without mandatory TLS, mutual authentication, or origin validation — particularly when MCP servers run locally or in environments where agents connect to third-party endpoints.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when an attacker intercepts, modifies, or replays MCP messages on the transport channel. DNS rebinding attacks target locally-running MCP servers from remote websites.
mitigated: Mitigated by enforcing mutual TLS for all MCP connections, binding session tokens to transport-layer identifiers, validating Origin headers on all incoming connections, restricting local servers to localhost binding, and implementing replay protection with short-lived sessions.

externalReferences.title: Model Context Protocol specification (2025-11-25): Transports

risks.title: Shadow and Unknown Agents
shortDescription: Unregistered agents operate with inherited or valid credentials outside identity lifecycle controls, creating persistent blind spots in agentic systems.
longDescription:
In dynamic agentic environments, agents can be created ad-hoc or spawned through orchestration layers without central registration. Shadow and Unknown Agents describes the risk when these unregistered agents retain or inherit credentials and tokens, allowing them to interact with tools and MCP servers undetected. This breaks the identity lifecycle and creates persistent blind spots in monitoring, attribution, and revocation.
This risk is the AI-specific extension of two classical security challenges: Shadow IT (unauthorized systems operating outside governance processes) and orphaned account management (failure to tombstone decommissioned credentials). The key AI-specific amplifier is that orchestration layers can dynamically spawn credentialed agents without human approval — a capability with no direct classical equivalent.
The vulnerability arises from incomplete provisioning controls, credential reuse across sessions, or weak network isolation. Attack vectors include compromised orchestration components that spawn hidden agents and failure to decommission old agent instances (creating "zombie" agents). Supply-chain injection of backdoored agent templates is a related vector addressed by {{riskToolSourceProvenance}} and {{riskToolRegistryTampering}}; this risk covers the downstream identity lifecycle failure when such agents persist undetected. The exposure is present where agents receive credentials without first registering with a central identity service, where there is no runtime mechanism to detect and block actions from unregistered or decommissioned agents, where credentials are reused across ephemeral agents, and where an orchestration layer that spawns a new agent passes credentials down by inheritance rather than issuing fresh, individually attested ones.
The insider threat dimension is also relevant: a compromised or rogue insider can create shadow agents that persist beyond their own access revocation, analogous to classical insider threats via undocumented service accounts or orphaned API keys.
Potential impacts include stealthy data exfiltration, unauthorized actions across tenants, and long-term attacker persistence. Consequences include accountability gaps (actions cannot be reliably attributed), compliance violations, and increased difficulty in incident response.
{{riskZombieShadowMCPServers}} addresses decommissioned tool server endpoints; this risk addresses unregistered agent identities. Both share the lifecycle management failure mode but differ in the entity type affected.
examples: A Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders (2025) ({{ref:gartner-2025-genai-blind-spots-press-release}}) found that 69% of organizations suspect or have evidence that employees are using prohibited public GenAI. Gartner predicts that by 2030, more than 40% of enterprises will experience security or compliance incidents linked to unauthorized shadow AI.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when orchestration layers or development teams create agents without central registration, or when provisioning controls do not require identity lifecycle enrollment before credential issuance.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when unregistered agents interact with tools, MCP servers, or other agents using inherited or shared credentials. The exposure persists through maintenance cycles when decommissioning processes fail to revoke credentials for retired agents.
mitigated: Mitigated by central agent inventory management requiring registration before credential issuance, cryptographic attestation of agent identity, runtime detection of unregistered agents, and automated credential revocation on lifecycle state changes.

externalReferences.title: Gartner Identifies Critical GenAI Blind Spots That CIOs Must Urgently Address

risks.title: Runaway Agent Tool Loops
shortDescription: Agents enter uncontrolled recursive tool-calling cycles at the orchestration layer, exhausting context windows, compute resources, and API budgets through emergent autonomous behavior or adversarial trigger.
longDescription:
In agentic systems, autonomous agents invoke tools in sequence or recursively based on LLM reasoning. Runaway Agent Tool Loops occur when agents enter uncontrolled tool-calling cycles because termination conditions are absent, broken, or never satisfied. The primary failure mode is emergent: agents that loop because validation functions never return satisfying results, max_turns defaults are not set, or tool responses trigger further reasoning without convergence. No adversary is required.
This risk extends classical infinite loop and fork bomb patterns to the agentic domain. In traditional systems, runaway processes are constrained by watchdog timers, process resource limits (ulimit, cgroups), and OS-level scheduling. The AI-specific amplifier is that LLM-driven agents make non-deterministic decisions about when to stop, and each tool call generates reasoning traces and tool response pairs that accumulate in the context window. The loop degrades the agent's ability to reason about stopping even as it continues — context-window saturation creates a feedback loop where the agent can no longer process enough history to recognize it should terminate.
This risk is distinct from {{riskEconomicDenialOfWallet}}, which addresses adversarial resource exhaustion at the API billing layer through attacks on pricing models and billing mechanisms. Runaway Agent Tool Loops addresses autonomous agent behavior at the MCP orchestration layer, where impacts include context-window exhaustion (task fails silently or incompletely), availability degradation for co-tenants, and safety failures in time-sensitive systems — impacts with no financial dimension. Prompt injection can trigger runaway loops (see {{riskPromptInjection}}), but the underlying vulnerability is the absence of loop bounds at the orchestration layer: deployments that do not enforce per-agent, per-session, or per-tool-call resource budgets and rate limits, that allow recursive or deeply nested tool chains without an automatic bound or a human-approval checkpoint, that rely on MCP servers unable to reject or throttle requests based on cumulative context or cost, and that do not monitor for context-window saturation during tool-calling sequences.
Potential impacts include context-window exhaustion leading to silent task failure, massive unexpected costs, service degradation for other users on shared infrastructure, and safety risks when time-sensitive agent tasks are delayed or never complete. Consequences range from financial damage to availability failures and loss of trust in autonomous agent systems.
examples: The Microsoft AutoGen infinite loop issue (#108) ({{ref:github-autogen-infinite-loops-issue-108}}) documented agents entering infinite tool-calling cycles because the termination condition checked for exact "TERMINATE" text, but agents generated variations that never matched. The loop continued until OpenAI rate limits triggered. No adversary was involved — the failure was emergent from a broken termination function, demonstrating the autonomous failure mode that distinguishes this risk from adversarial cost-spike attacks.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when agent orchestration frameworks are configured without default tool-call limits, context-window budgets, or termination condition validation.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when an agent enters a recursive tool-calling cycle that consumes context window, compute, and API budget without converging on a result or triggering a termination condition.
mitigated: Mitigated by enforcing per-agent, per-session, and per-tool-call resource budgets; setting mandatory max_turns defaults in orchestration frameworks; monitoring for context-window saturation and loop patterns; and implementing circuit breakers that halt agent execution when cumulative resource thresholds are exceeded.

externalReferences.title: Microsoft AutoGen Issue #108: Infinite Loops with GPT-4

risks.title: Agentic Delegation Confused Deputy
shortDescription: A high-privilege agent acts on behalf of a less-privileged caller without validating the caller's authorization at the delegation boundary, allowing the caller to escalate privileges through the deputy's own permissions.
longDescription:
In agentic systems, agents with elevated privileges frequently act on behalf of other agents, users, or external inputs through delegation mechanisms such as OAuth token exchange and MCP tool invocation. The Agentic Delegation Confused Deputy occurs when a high-privilege agent (the deputy) performs an action that the caller could not do directly, because the deputy does not validate the caller's authorization at the delegation boundary. The deputy uses its own permissions without distinguishing the caller's authority from its own.
This risk is a direct extension of the classical confused deputy problem, first identified by Norm Hardy in 1988 when a compiler with file system privileges was tricked into overwriting its billing file by a user who supplied a system path as the output filename. The pattern recurs across computing eras: CSRF exploits the browser as a confused deputy (using session cookies on behalf of a malicious cross-origin caller), and AWS cross-account role assumption ({{ref:aws-iam-confused-deputy}}) without ExternalId validation allows a third-party vendor to be tricked into assuming a victim's IAM role. The AI-specific amplifier is threefold: (1) the deputy's capability set expands dynamically at runtime via MCP server discovery, making the attack surface unpredictable; (2) the deputy autonomously decides which tools to invoke based on LLM reasoning, not static dispatch; (3) multi-hop delegation can chain multiple confused deputies, amplifying the privilege escalation.
Attack vectors include indirect prompt injection via user-submitted data, poisoned MCP tool descriptions, crafted tool responses, and legitimate-looking API calls from less-privileged agents. The trigger mechanism varies (see {{riskPromptInjection}} for injection attacks specifically), but the underlying vulnerability is the same: the deputy does not check the caller's authorization scope before acting, and cannot distinguish that scope from its own when it selects which tools to invoke. The exposure persists wherever a delegation step does not enforce least-privilege narrowing together with an explicit caller-authorization check, wherever confused-deputy protections are applied at only one of the IAM and MCP layers rather than both, and wherever there is no runtime detection of an agent executing an action that exceeds the caller's authorization scope.
This risk is distinct from {{riskRogueActions}}, which covers unintended agent actions broadly (accidental and malicious). The confused deputy specifically addresses the authorization failure at delegation boundaries — the caller could not perform the action directly, but the deputy does it using its own permissions. Rogue actions can occur in single-agent systems; the confused deputy requires asymmetric privilege across a delegation boundary. {{riskAgentDelegationChainOpacity}} addresses the inability to see who authorized an action; this risk addresses the failure to check whether the caller was authorized.
Potential impacts include unauthorized data access across trust boundaries, financial transactions executed on behalf of unauthorized callers, infrastructure modifications, and privilege escalation chains in multi-agent systems. Consequences include accountability failures, regulatory non-compliance, and amplified blast radius when the deputy's permissions span multiple services or tenants.
examples:
In the Supabase/Cursor data exfiltration (2025) ({{ref:generalanalysis-2026-supabase-mcp}}), a developer's Cursor IDE agent connected to Supabase using service_role credentials that bypassed all Row-Level Security. An attacker embedded SQL exfiltration commands in a support ticket. When the agent summarized tickets, it executed the attacker's commands with its elevated permissions, exfiltrating OAuth secrets the ticket author could never access directly — a textbook confused deputy where the agent used its own root-level database access without validating the caller's authorization.
In the Invariant Labs WhatsApp MCP exploit (2025) ({{ref:invariantlabs-2025-whatsapp-mcp-exploited}}), a malicious MCP server poisoned its tool descriptions with hidden instructions targeting a co-installed WhatsApp MCP server. The agent — which had legitimate WhatsApp send authority — exfiltrated chat history to an attacker-controlled number. The malicious server had no WhatsApp access of its own; it exploited the agent as a confused deputy to launder its requests through the agent's cross-server authority.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when agent delegation boundaries are configured without caller authorization validation — specifically when high-privilege agents accept delegation requests without verifying whether the caller's authority matches the requested action's privilege level.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when a less-privileged caller (another agent, external input, or low-privilege user) submits a request that the high-privilege deputy fulfills using its own permissions. The deputy cannot distinguish the caller's authorization scope from its own.
mitigated: Mitigated by enforcing caller authorization validation at every delegation boundary, scoping the deputy's effective permissions to the intersection of its own permissions and the caller's authorization, and applying least-privilege narrowing at each delegation hop.

externalReferences.title: AWS IAM User Guide: The confused deputy problem
Supabase MCP can leak your entire SQL database
WhatsApp MCP Exploited: Exfiltrating your message history via MCP

risks.title: Cross-Tenant Credential Propagation
shortDescription: Shared or insufficiently tenant-scoped agent credentials allow a compromise in one tenant to propagate access across tenant boundaries through the identity layer.
longDescription:
Multi-tenant agentic platforms frequently share infrastructure components across tenants for efficiency — base models, credential pools, MCP tool server endpoints, and OAuth token caches. Cross-Tenant Credential Propagation occurs when agent identities or credentials are not strictly scoped to individual tenants, allowing a compromise in one tenant to authenticate to another tenant's resources through the shared identity layer.
This risk extends what the Cloud Security Alliance identifies as "Insufficient Identity, Credential, and Access Management" — a top cloud threat — to the agentic domain. Multi-tenant SaaS systems have long struggled with shared service accounts, wildcard TLS certificates, shared OAuth client credentials, and connection pool credentials that cross tenant boundaries. CWE-653 (Insufficient Compartmentalization) captures the general pattern of failing to isolate security domains. The AI-specific amplifier is that agentic platforms additionally share model serving endpoints, MCP tool registries, and OAuth token pools across tenants, and the dynamic nature of agent delegation means a compromised credential can propagate through delegation chains across tenant boundaries — agents autonomously use credentials without human verification at each hop.
The vulnerability arises from insufficient tenant scoping at the agent identity layer: shared OAuth client credentials, MCP tokens that are valid across tenants, or agent identity pools that serve multiple organizations. A compromise in one tenant — through credential theft, infrastructure exploitation, or insider access — yields credentials that work across tenant boundaries because nothing restricts their scope to the originating tenant. The exposure is present wherever agent identities are not strictly scoped to a single tenant, wherever credential pools, OAuth token caches, and MCP server endpoints are shared rather than isolated per tenant, and wherever tenant-boundary validation is not enforced at every MCP hop and delegation step — any of which lets a compromise confined to one tenant reach another tenant's resources.
This risk is distinct from {{riskAcceleratorAndSystemSideChannels}}, which covers hardware-layer cross-tenant leakage (timing, cache, speculative execution). It is also distinct from {{riskPromptResponseCachePoisoning}}, which covers cross-user contamination via shared LLM caches. This risk specifically addresses the identity and credential layer — shared or unscoped credentials that allow authentication across tenant boundaries.
Potential impacts include widespread data breaches spanning multiple tenants, unauthorized cross-tenant actions, intellectual property theft, and complete breakdown of multi-tenancy guarantees. Consequences include major compliance violations (GDPR, SOC 2), loss of customer trust, and systemic risk across the shared platform.
examples:
The Asana MCP cross-tenant data exposure (2025) ({{ref:bleepingcomputer-2025-asana-mcp-data-exposure}}) demonstrated this pattern directly in the agentic domain: a logic flaw in Asana's MCP server feature exposed data from one organization's instance to other organizations' MCP users for approximately 1,000 customers, because tenant context was not maintained across MCP sessions.
Wiz researchers discovered the BingBang vulnerability (2023) ({{ref:wiz-2023-bingbang-aad-misconfiguration}}) affecting approximately 25% of Azure AD multi-tenant application registrations, which accepted valid OAuth tokens from any Azure tenant without checking the tenant ID claim. A token issued for an attacker's tenant was accepted by apps belonging to other tenants, including Microsoft's internal Bing management applications — a cross-tenant credential propagation through the identity layer where the credential itself was valid across tenant boundaries.
In the UNC6395/Salesloft Drift breach (2025) ({{ref:valencesecurity-2025-salesforce-oauth-breach}}), a threat actor compromised Salesloft's infrastructure and stole per-customer OAuth tokens that Drift stored for approximately 700 Salesforce organizations. Each bearer token granted direct Salesforce API access bypassing MFA — a single compromise of a multi-tenant intermediary's centralized credential store yielded cross-tenant access through the identity layer.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when agent identities, credential pools, or MCP server endpoints are configured to serve multiple tenants without strict tenant-scoped isolation at the identity layer.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when a compromise in one tenant (credential theft, infrastructure exploitation, or insider access) yields credentials that authenticate to other tenants' resources because the credentials are not tenant-scoped.
mitigated: Mitigated by issuing strictly tenant-scoped agent credentials with no cross-tenant validity, enforcing tenant boundary validation at every MCP hop and delegation step, and isolating credential pools, token caches, and MCP endpoints per tenant.

externalReferences.title: Asana warns MCP AI feature exposed customer data to other orgs
Salesforce OAuth Token Breach: What Every Security Team Must Know
BingBang: AAD misconfiguration led to Bing.com results manipulation and account takeover

risks.title: Zombie / Shadow MCP Servers
shortDescription: Decommissioned or unregistered MCP servers remain accessible and respond to agent tool calls, allowing attackers to intercept or redirect legitimate requests.
longDescription:
MCP servers expose tools to agents and are frequently created, scaled, or retired during operations. Zombie / Shadow MCP Servers occur when decommissioned servers are not fully removed from service discovery, DNS, load balancers, or tool registries, leaving stale endpoints that remain responsive to agent connections. An attacker who claims the abandoned endpoint receives all tool calls that agents route to it.
This risk is the agentic extension of dangling DNS and subdomain takeover — a well-documented vulnerability pattern ({{ref:owasp-wstg-4-2-10-subdomain-takeover}}) where orphaned DNS records to decommissioned cloud services allow attackers to claim abandoned resources and intercept traffic. The AI-specific amplifier is that agents autonomously discover and invoke tool servers without human verification at each call. In classical systems, a developer would notice a stale API endpoint returning unexpected responses; in agentic systems, the agent silently processes the zombie server's responses as legitimate tool output, potentially poisoning reasoning chains that influence downstream actions.
Transport security alone does not close this gap: an attacker who controls DNS for a stale endpoint can obtain a valid ACME-issued certificate, and mTLS will authenticate them as a "valid" server. Transport security works as specified — the missing layer is provenance binding to the registered principal. This is why the risk requires a registry-bound provenance control ({{controlComponentIdentityProvenance}}) in addition to transport security and inventory management.
The vulnerability stems from incomplete lifecycle management: tool server entries persist in registries, DNS, or agent configurations after the legitimate server is decommissioned. Dynamic discovery mechanisms that do not require runtime attestation or liveness verification exacerbate the risk — agents trust registry presence as proof of legitimacy. The exposure is present where an MCP server can become discoverable without registering under cryptographic attestation, where decommissioning does not guarantee complete removal from every discovery mechanism (registry, DNS, load balancer, and agent configuration alike), where agents do not re-verify a tool server's liveness and identity at invocation time rather than trusting the discovery-time record, and where nothing automatically detects and blocks calls routed to decommissioned or unverified endpoints.
This risk is distinct from {{riskToolSourceProvenance}}, which addresses adopting unvetted tool sources — zombie servers were previously vetted and legitimate. It is distinct from {{riskToolRegistryTampering}}, which addresses active modification of registry entries — zombie servers involve stale entries that were never cleaned up. It is distinct from {{riskInsecureIntegratedComponent}}, which addresses vulnerabilities in running tool implementations — zombie servers involve the absence of a legitimate tool at an endpoint now controlled by an attacker. {{riskShadowAndUnknownAgents}} addresses unregistered agent identities; this risk addresses decommissioned tool server endpoints.
Potential impacts include stealthy interception of tool calls, injection of malicious schemas or responses, data exfiltration from agent interactions, and persistent attacker access long after official decommissioning. Consequences include undetected breaches, compliance failures, and erosion of trust in the agentic infrastructure.
examples:
Dangling DNS and subdomain takeover is a well-documented vulnerability pattern (OWASP) ({{ref:owasp-wstg-4-2-10-subdomain-takeover}}) where orphaned DNS CNAME records to decommissioned cloud services allow attackers to claim the abandoned resource and intercept all traffic. The MCP equivalent: a tool registry entry persists after server decommissioning, and an attacker claims the stale endpoint URL — agents route tool calls to the attacker automatically because they trust registry presence without runtime liveness verification.
ACME certificate authorities (e.g., Let's Encrypt) automate issuance of domain-validated certificates based solely on control of the DNS record at issuance time. An attacker who claims a decommissioned subdomain can obtain a valid ACME certificate within minutes, and mTLS between agent and the reclaimed endpoint will succeed. Transport security is not broken in this scenario — it is working exactly as specified. The missing control is runtime attestation that the authenticated key holder is the currently registered, non-revoked principal for the role, not merely the holder of a key bound to the domain.

introduced: Introduced during deployment when MCP servers are provisioned and registered in tool registries, DNS, or agent configurations.
exposed: Exposed at runtime when decommissioned servers are not fully removed from all discovery mechanisms. Agents continue calling stale endpoints because registry presence implies legitimacy. The exposure persists through maintenance cycles when decommissioning processes are incomplete.
mitigated: Mitigated by requiring cryptographic attestation and runtime liveness verification for all MCP server endpoints, automating removal from all discovery mechanisms on decommission, and monitoring for agent calls to unresponsive or unverified endpoints.

externalReferences.title: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide 4.2.10: Test for Subdomain Takeover

controls.title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies for Model Training
description: Use technologies that minimize, de-identify, or restrict use of PII data in training or evaluating models, including differential privacy, secure aggregation protocols, federated learning, data anonymization, and synthetic data generation.

controls.title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies for Inference
description: Use technologies that minimize, de-identify, or restrict use of PII data during model deployment and inference, including secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, inference log de-identification, on-device processing, and privacy-preserving query mechanisms.

controls.title: Training Data Management
description: Ensure that all data used to train and evaluate models is authorized for the intended purposes.

controls.title: Training Data Sanitization
description: Detect and remove or remediate poisoned or sensitive data in training and evaluation.

controls.title: User Data Management
description: Store, process, and use all user data (e.g. prompts and logs) from AI applications in compliance with user consent.

controls.title: Model and Data Inventory Management
description: Ensure that all data, code, models, and transformation tools used in AI applications are inventoried and tracked.

controls.title: Model and Data Access Controls
description: Minimize internal access to models, weights, datasets, etc. in storage and in production use.

controls.title: Model and Data Integrity Management
description:
Ensure that all data, models, and code used to produce AI models are verifiably integrity-protected during development and deployment.
Implement repository trust policies, cryptographic signatures, attestation frameworks, and offline verification capabilities to ensure integrity and authenticity of models and artifacts.

controls.title: Model and Data Execution Integrity
description:
Ensure that the code and model results from training and development are of known provenance and lineage and not modified from known-good sources in unexpected ways at inference time.
Examples include:
Validating expected code and model signatures / hashes at inference-time.
Limiting and immutably recording all modifications to runtime AI system components via oversight processes.
Other integrity controls appropriate to the deployment context.

controls.title: Secure-by-Default ML Tooling
description: Use secure-by-default frameworks, libraries, software systems, and hardware components for AI development or deployment to protect confidentiality and integrity of AI assets and outputs.

controls.title: Input Validation and Sanitization
description: Block or restrict adversarial queries to AI models.

controls.title: Output Validation and Sanitization
description: Block, nullify, or sanitize insecure output from AI models before passing it to applications, extensions or users.

controls.title: Adversarial Training and Testing
description: Use techniques to make AI models robust to adversarial inputs (i.e. prompts) in the context of their use in applications.

controls.title: Application Access and Resource Management
description:
Ensure comprehensive access governance through:
Identity and authorization controls that restrict resources to authorized users and endpoints for authorized actions.
Resource governance controls including usage quotas, rate limiting, cost monitoring, and anomaly detection to prevent resource exhaustion and economic denial of wallet attacks.

controls.title: User Transparency and Controls
description: Inform users of relevant AI risks with disclosures, and provide transparency and control experiences for use of their data in AI applications.

controls.title: Agent User Control
description: Ensure user approval for any actions performed by agents/plugins that alter user data or act on the user's behalf.

controls.title: Agent Permissions
description:
Use least-privilege principle as the upper bound on agentic system permissions to minimize the number of tools that an agent is permitted to interact with and the actions it is allowed to take. An agentic system's use of privileges should be contextual and dynamic, adapting to the specific user query and trusted contextual information. This design also applies to agents that have access to user information. For example, an agent asked to fill out a form or answer questions should share only contextually appropriate information and can be designed to dynamically minimize exposed data using reference monitors.
At delegation boundaries, an agent acting on behalf of a caller must verify the caller's authority for the requested action — not rely on the agent's own (often broader) permissions. Each delegation hop should narrow the agent's effective authority to the intersection of its own permissions and the caller's authorization, preventing the agent from being used as a confused deputy to execute actions the caller could not perform directly.

controls.title: Red Teaming
description: Drive security and privacy improvements through self-driven adversarial attacks on AI infrastructure and products

controls.title: Vulnerability Management
description: Proactively and continually test and monitor production infrastructure and products for security and privacy regressions

controls.title: Threat Detection
description: Detect and alert on internal or external attacks on AI assets, infrastructure, and products

controls.title: Incident Response Management
description: Manage response to AI security and privacy incidents

controls.title: User Policies and Education
description: Publish easy to understand AI security and privacy policies and education for users.

controls.title: Internal Policies and Education
description: Publish comprehensive AI security and privacy policies and education for your employees.

controls.title: Product Governance
description: Validate that all AI models and products meet the established security and privacy requirements.

controls.title: Risk Governance
description: Inventory, measure, and monitor residual risk to AI in your organization.

controls.title: Agent Observability
description: Ensure an agent's actions, tool use, and reasoning are transparent and auditable through logging, allowing for debugging, security oversight, and user insights into agent activity.

controls.title: Isolated and Confidential Computing
description:
Use technologies that minimize the risk of 3rd-party access to critical resources via hardware isolation invariants and/or physically isolated computing systems.
Examples include including CPU and TPU-based confidential computing technologies (TEEs, secure enclaves), system isolation, secure scheduling, and side-channel monitoring to prevent cross-tenant information leakage.

controls.title: Retrieval and Vector System Integrity Management
description: Implement provenance tracking, cryptographic signing, deduplication, embedding anomaly detection, and index integrity checks to protect retrieval systems and vector databases from poisoning attacks.

controls.title: Orchestrator and Route Integrity
description: Implement signed route manifests, configuration integrity verification, and response provenance tracking to prevent routing manipulation and ensure request routing to authorized models.

controls.title: Agent Inventory Management
description:
Ensure that all agents operating in the system are registered in a central inventory before credential issuance, with lifecycle state tracking (active, suspended, decommissioned) and automated detection of unregistered agents. This control addresses agent identity governance — knowing what agents are authorized to exist — as distinct from agent observability, which addresses what agents do.
This control extends the inventory management concept from {{controlModelAndDataInventoryManagement}} to dynamic, running agent entities. Where model/data inventory tracks static artifacts through build and deployment pipelines, agent inventory tracks entities with operational lifecycle states in a live system. Enforcement includes credential revocation on lifecycle state change and blocking of unregistered agent actions. The same inventory discipline extends to MCP tool server endpoints, providing the lifecycle authority on which runtime provenance and observability controls depend.

controls.title: Agent Integrity Management
description:
Ensure that each running agent's identity and configuration are cryptographically bound to its registered inventory entry and verifiable at runtime. This includes credential binding to individual agent identities (not shared pools), attestation of agent configuration against a registered baseline, and automated revocation propagation on decommission or underlying model swap.
This control extends the integrity management concept from {{controlModelAndDataIntegrityManagement}} to agent identity. Where model/data integrity verifies that artifact content (weights, code) has not been tampered with, agent integrity verifies that a running agent's identity credentials match its registered entry. A model can pass artifact integrity checks while the agent wrapping it has drifted from its registered configuration or had its credential bindings compromised.

controls.title: Agent Credential Isolation
description:
Ensure that credentials issued to agents are scoped to individual tenants and cannot propagate across tenant boundaries at any point in an orchestration or delegation chain. This control addresses the credential issuance and propagation properties of agents — answering "are this agent's credentials structurally isolated to its tenant?" — as distinct from agent integrity (which attests that an agent matches its registered identity) and agent permissions (which governs the action scope of tool calls).
Implementation requires: per-tenant credential issuance with no shared credential pools across tenant boundaries; short-lived, tenant-scoped tokens for agent-to-tool authentication, with lifetimes bounded to the duration of a single task or session; tenant boundary validation at every MCP protocol hop and delegation step, so that a credential issued in tenant A cannot be forwarded to or reused in tenant B's context; and credential rotation and revocation scoped to tenant context, ensuring that decommissioning an agent in one tenant does not leave credentials valid in another.

controls.title: Inter-Component Transport Security
description:
Enforce authenticated, encrypted, and integrity-protected communication channels for all inter-component connections in AI systems, including agent-to-tool, model serving, orchestration, and application API channels.
Implement the following transport-layer controls across all component communication paths:
TLS/mTLS enforcement: Require TLS 1.2 minimum (TLS 1.3 preferred) for all inter-component connections. Require mutual TLS (mTLS) for machine-to-machine paths — agent-to-tool server, orchestrator-to-model serving endpoint, and application-to-serving API — so that both parties authenticate before any payload is exchanged. Locally-exposed tool server endpoints (e.g., MCP servers on localhost) are in scope and must not be treated as implicitly trusted.
Mutual authentication: Each component must present a valid certificate or credential verified against an expected identity before the connection is accepted. This applies to machine-to-machine paths, not user-facing authentication (covered by application access controls).
Session token binding: Bind session tokens and API credentials to transport-layer identifiers (e.g., TLS channel binding per RFC 5929) so that a token captured from one TLS session cannot be replayed on a different channel.
Replay protection: Apply nonce, timestamp, or sequence number mechanisms to tool invocation requests and inter-component messages carrying side-effecting instructions, preventing captured messages from being reinjected.
Origin validation: Validate the origin of requests to locally-exposed endpoints against an allowlist of expected callers, preventing DNS rebinding attacks.
Certificate lifecycle management: Issue individual certificates per component identity rather than shared wildcards. Automate certificate rotation before expiry. Revoke certificates immediately on component decommission or credential compromise.
This control addresses the transport layer — how component messages are protected in transit. It is distinct from {{controlOrchestratorAndRouteIntegrity}} (which governs where traffic is routed), {{controlSecureByDefaultMLTooling}} (which governs tooling selection and configuration), and {{controlIsolatedConfidentialComputing}} (which governs hardware-level compute isolation). Those controls assume secure channels; this control establishes them.

controls.title: Component Identity Provenance
description:
Ensure that when one component invokes another, the calling component can verify the callee is the currently registered, non-revoked principal for that role — not merely the holder of a key for a domain or network address. This control closes the gap that transport security leaves open: TLS and mTLS prove key possession for an endpoint, but do not attest that the endpoint is the legitimate principal a registry system of record says it should be.
Implementation requires: a binding between a component's runtime identity and an authoritative registry entry, such that revocation in the registry is observable to callers within a bounded time window; verification of that binding at invocation time, not solely at channel establishment; and audit telemetry that records the provenance assertion used so post-hoc detection of calls against revoked or expired principals is possible.
This control is mechanism-agnostic. Implementers may use SPIFFE/SVIDs, capability tokens, signed registration receipts, mTLS with a private CA whose issuance is gated on registry state, short-lived JWTs from a registration authority, hardware-attested identities, or other approaches that satisfy the intent. The control specifies the question that must be answered at invocation time — "is this the registered principal?" — not the cryptographic protocol used to answer it.
This control is distinct from {{controlInterComponentTransportSecurity}}, which secures the channel, and from {{controlAgentInventoryManagement}}, which maintains the registry of authorized principals. Inventory is the lifecycle authority; provenance is the runtime attestation that surfaces inventory state to callers; transport is the channel over which both ride.

controls.title: Agent Execution Bounds
description:
Enforce per-agent, per-session, and per-tool-call execution limits at the orchestration layer to prevent runaway tool-calling cycles. This control addresses the enforcement of loop bounds, context-window budgets, and circuit breakers within agent reasoning and tool invocation sequences — as distinct from API-layer rate limiting (which operates at the external request boundary) and agent observability (which detects loops but does not halt them).
Implementation requires: mandatory max_turns defaults for all agent-to-tool execution sequences, with no framework permitting unbounded execution by default; per-agent and per-session tool-call budgets that are enforced by the orchestration layer before each tool invocation; context-window budget tracking that halts agent execution before context saturation degrades reasoning quality; and circuit breakers that terminate agent execution when cumulative resource thresholds (compute, tokens, wall-clock time) are exceeded. Loop detection at the orchestration layer should identify repeated tool-call patterns and trigger early termination.

personas.title: Model Provider
description:
Actors that develop, train, evaluate, and tune AI/ML models (foundation models, specialized models, or domain-adapted models). This includes those that develop models from scratch or significantly modify existing models for distribution. This also includes model aggregators, model marketplaces, and those licensing models.
Actors that also operate runtime environments serving model predictions are additionally covered by AI Model Serving.
responsibilities: Model artifact integrity and availability for distribution
identificationQuestions: Are you training or fine-tuning AI/ML models for use by others, including classical ML, statistical, optimization, and rule-based models?
Do you modify, extend, or wrap existing models (e.g., distillation, quantization, adaptation, or adding guardrails) for use by others as a distributable model artifact?
Do you evaluate, benchmark, or perform quality assurance on AI/ML models as part of training, adaptation, or distribution decisions?
Are you making models available for others to download, license, or integrate?
Do you host or curate a catalog of AI/ML models provided by third parties?
Do you issue or manage licenses governing how AI/ML models may be used?

personas.title: Data Provider
description: Actors that supply training data, evaluation datasets, or inference data to model providers or application developers. This includes data aggregators, data marketplaces, and those licensing datasets.
identificationQuestions: Do you collect, curate, or prepare data for use by others in training, evaluating, or operating AI/ML systems?
Do you supply datasets or data feeds to model providers or application developers, including labeled datasets, synthetic data, or benchmark corpora?
Do you label or annotate data (e.g., classification tags, bounding boxes, or preference judgments) so others can train or evaluate AI/ML systems?
Do you document or verify data provenance, lineage, licensing, or usage restrictions for datasets that others rely on?
Do you operate a catalog, marketplace, repository, or delivery service through which others can discover or obtain AI-relevant datasets, rather than AI models or software artifacts?

Do you determine whether specific datasets may be shared or used for AI purposes based on privacy, consent, contractual, or regulatory requirements, as the data owner or supplier rather than as an enterprise-wide governance or compliance function?

personas.title: AI Platform Provider
description: Actors that provide infrastructure, compute resources, APIs, and platform services for AI model hosting, training, or inference. This includes internal infrastructure teams, cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP), MLOps platforms, and platform-level API gateway services (e.g., load balancing, API authentication, and request throttling layers).
responsibilities: Infrastructure support, capacity, security, and availability
Infrastructure support for model hosting and serving
identificationQuestions: Do you provision or manage compute resources (e.g., GPU clusters, cloud instances, or on-premises hardware) used for AI model training, fine-tuning, or inference?
Do you operate or maintain networking, storage, or data infrastructure that supports AI workloads?
Do you provide platform services for the AI lifecycle (e.g., MLOps tooling, experiment tracking, or model hosting environments)?
Do you manage API gateway services for AI systems, including load balancing, authentication, or request throttling?
Do you enforce multi-tenant isolation, access controls, or security policies at the infrastructure layer for AI workloads?
Do you provide the infrastructure environment in which AI models run, rather than managing the model serving logic itself?

personas.title: AI Model Serving
description: The entity responsible for provisioning, managing, and securing the runtime environment that serves AI and ML model predictions at scale. This persona covers all model types — including classical ML, statistical, optimization, and generative AI models — focusing on the secure execution of predictions, ensuring runtime integrity, confidentiality, and availability of data and outputs. It separates its duties from model training, tuning, or registry storage (Model Provider) and physical infrastructure management (AI Platform Provider), focusing on the secure orchestration and delivery of the model serving application layer.
responsibilities: Manage and secure model serving API endpoints and enforce application access policies
Perform runtime input validation and sanitization to prevent injection attacks and data poisoning
Execute models within isolated or confidential computing environments to protect runtime data
Enforce granular model and data access controls during loading and execution phases
Verify model and data integrity at load-time and runtime to prevent execution of tampered artifacts
Secure orchestration and routing of serving requests across distributed model instances
Monitor, validate, and sanitize model outputs to prevent data leakage and ensure safety
Implement runtime privacy-enhancing technologies to protect sensitive input data
Provide transparency mechanisms regarding model serving parameters and data usage
Facilitate red teaming and adversarial simulation to validate model serving security
identificationQuestions:
Do you operate or manage the runtime service that serves AI/ML model predictions to applications, users, or downstream systems?
Do you expose or secure model inference endpoints at the model serving application layer (rather than the infrastructure or platform gateway), including request handling, authentication, authorization, or rate limiting?
Are you responsible for loading, dispatching to, or load-balancing across deployed model versions during inference?
Do you validate or sanitize inference inputs at the model serving layer before they reach a model, including prompts, feature payloads, or API requests?
Do you monitor, filter, or enforce controls on model outputs before they are returned to callers or users?
Do you verify deployed model artifacts, runtime configuration, or serving routes before or during inference?

personas.title: Agentic Platform and Framework Providers
description:
Actors that provide the development environments, software frameworks, and orchestration runtimes required to implement agentic reasoning, planning, and tool execution.
Examples include agentic frameworks and libraries (e.g., LangChain, Semantic Kernel), agent-native development environments (e.g., Cursor, GitHub Copilot Workspace), and managed agent orchestration platforms (e.g., Vertex AI Agent Builder, OpenAI Assistants API).
identificationQuestions:
Do you build or maintain software that orchestrates which tools an AI model invokes (e.g., tool-calling frameworks, agent orchestrators, or planning engines)?
Do you manage the state or history of multi-turn agentic workflows (e.g., conversation history, execution state, or tool results)?
Do you provide, as a reusable framework or platform rather than a single application, integration layers that connect large language models to external APIs or services (e.g., tool integrations, plugins, or MCP servers)?
Do you build or maintain libraries or SDKs that abstract LLM tool-calling (e.g., tool definition, schema generation, or output parsing)?
Do you define the agent architecture for AI systems (e.g., reasoning loops, planning workflows, or reflection patterns)?
Do you provide runtime guardrails or safety boundaries for agentic tool execution (e.g., sandboxed execution, permission boundaries, or pre-execution policy enforcement)?

personas.title: Application Developer
description: Actors that integrate AI models (via APIs or embedded models) into applications, products, or services. They may consume models without modifying them, or perform light customization (prompt engineering, RAG, etc.).
identificationQuestions:
Do you build or maintain applications, products, or services that embed AI/ML capabilities for end users or downstream systems?
Do you integrate AI/ML models into applications or services (e.g., via APIs, embedded models, or prompt-engineered workflows)?
Do you define how user inputs, business logic, or application context are passed to AI models and how model outputs are used, within a specific application rather than a reusable framework?
Do you implement application-layer controls around AI features for your application's end users, such as authentication, authorization, input validation, output filtering, or user-facing safeguards?
Do you customize AI features (e.g., prompt design, output handling, or application-specific guardrails) for a specific application use case, consuming an existing model rather than producing one for others?
Do you deliver AI-powered functionality directly to end users or downstream systems as a finished product or service?

personas.title: AI System Governance
description: Actors responsible for defining security control objectives, measuring implementations, and enforcing compliance for AI systems across the AI system lifecycle. This includes AI risk officers, compliance teams, and governance boards.
identificationQuestions:
Do you define security, compliance, or risk management requirements that AI systems in your organization must satisfy?
Do you assess whether AI controls are implemented effectively across teams or systems you do not directly operate, including through audits, control testing, metrics reviews, or compliance checks?
Do you approve, gate, or oversee the use of AI systems based on policy, legal, regulatory, or enterprise risk assessments?
Do you maintain processes for AI incidents, exceptions, or risk acceptances (e.g., escalation procedures, documentation requirements, or corrective-action tracking) at an organizational or program level?
