archetypes.title: Chat agent with tools
summary: A hosted conversational agent where a human is in the loop for every turn: chat is the core input, tools execute mid-conversation on the user's behalf, and consequential actions are proposed in the thread before they run. The human-present counterpart of the single agent workflow, and the shape most domain copilots take.
description:
The defining property is that the human reads every reply before the next action. That one fact reorganises the control set: in-thread approval is the primary gate — an action is proposed in the conversation, in words the user can read, before it executes — where the single agent workflow, acting with nobody present, has to lean on compensating transactions instead. The gate is only as good as the proposal text: an approval rendered as "OK to proceed?" approves nothing in particular.
Authority is on-behalf-of. The tools act as the conversing user, on a grant scoped to the session, not as a workload identity with standing powers — the reachable set is what this user may touch, decided per call. Sessions end and the grant ends with them; an agent tier that accumulates authority across conversations has quietly become the single agent workflow without its controls.
The conversation itself is the persistence surface. Context accumulates across turns — retrievals, tool results, uploaded files — and everything in it stands beside the system instruction on the next model call. One poisoned tool result steers every later action in the session, which is why memory is scoped to the conversation and why returned content is classified on the way back in.
Every model and tool call leaves through the AI gateway on brokered credentials, the same crossing every agent architecture in this catalogue draws. The chat surface changes who is watching, not how the calls leave.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: the same conversational surface with tools behind it. The assistant's bright line — one mutating tool changes the entire control set — lands here first: the retrieval-time controls stay, and the action controls arrive with the human still present to gate them.
Against the single agent workflow: the same loop with the human kept in the turns. In-thread approval replaces the compensating transaction as the primary control; remove the human from the turns and you are in that architecture, and should be reading its page.
Against the realtime voice agent: the same conversational, acting shape over text — which means there is time to deliberate. Filtering, in-thread approval and reconsideration are exactly the controls the audio medium removes.

exemplars.name: Domain support copilots
exemplars.note: Customer-facing chat agents that look up accounts, draft remedies and execute them — refunds, changes, escalations — with the customer or an agent confirming each consequential step in the thread.

exemplars.name: Internal operations copilots
exemplars.note: Chat surfaces over internal systems — tickets, deployments, HR and finance requests — where employees converse and approve, and the tools act on the systems of record.

exemplars.name: Chat-framework deployments
exemplars.note: The agent-SDK and chat-UI starter shape: a hosted loop, a tool list, and a streaming chat front end. Structurally this architecture from the first commit, whatever it grows into.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: Present for every turn, and the approval gate for the actions that matter. Also the author of untrusted input — the conversation is model input written by the party the actions will benefit.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The chat surface and its session machinery. The identity established here is the authority every tool call downstream acts on.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published chat surface — web, app or embedded widget.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Who is conversing, bound to the session before the loop runs — the identity the tools act as.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: Plans within a turn, proposes actions in the thread, and carries the conversation's accumulated context into every model call. Runs under its own workload identity but acts on the user's grant.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Reads the turn and the history, calls the model, proposes the next reply or action.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the turn, the conversation memory and the tool results into one prompt. Everything merged stands beside the system instruction.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: The conversation's accumulated context and the retrieval index behind it. Scoped to the session and the user — cross-conversation memory would let one user's text steer another's actions.

items.label: Conversation state
items.note: Every turn, retrieval and tool result so far — read back on each call as context.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Grounding content retrieved into the thread, with the permissions of the asking user.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The one crossing every model and tool call leaves through. The agent tier holds no standing credentials; the gateway brokers them per call, meters spend and writes the audit trail as a tap on the crossing.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived, user-scoped credentials injected per call; the loop holds no standing keys.

items.label: Rate & budget limits
items.note: Caps token spend per session and per user, before a long conversation becomes a bill.

items.label: Audit tap
items.note: Every call recorded as a side effect of the crossing, not a favour asked of the agent.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Returns the reply and the proposed tool calls — content the thread renders and the human reads.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The action surface: MCP servers, plain APIs and connectors, and A2A peer agents — every call carrying the conversing user's grant, not the service's authority.

items.label: MCP servers
items.note: Tool providers with declared scopes — admitted, never discovered.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Business systems the conversation drives on the user's scoped grant.

items.label: A2A peer agents
items.note: Cross-org delegation over the A2A protocol. A peer's output enters the thread as input.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The systems the conversation actually changes — where an approved action becomes a real one, and where the content that returns was authored by somebody else.

items.label: Org data
items.note: The systems of record the approved actions land on.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Mail sent, tickets moved and calendar entries written on the user's behalf, mid-conversation.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Third-party services, and the untrusted content they return into the thread.

items.label: Vectorstore
items.note: The retrieval index behind grounded answers — content written by many hands, read back into the thread as context.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Identity, admission, evaluation, audit and the stop — each outside the loop it governs. The in-thread approval is a control the user operates; this column is the set the operator does.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: The user's identity and the agent's workload identity, issued and kept distinct.

items.label: Agent & tool registry
items.note: Which tools may be offered to the conversation. Admission, not discovery.

items.label: Evaluation gates
items.note: Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or tool change.

items.label: Audit sink
items.note: Append-only, off the agent's write path — the thread is not the audit trail.

items.label: Kill switch
items.note: Ends the sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

edges.label: conversation
edges.note: Turn in, reply back — and the in-thread approval prompt when an action is consequential. The human reads every reply before the next action runs.
The turn arrives with the user's identity attached; the reply and any action proposal return on the same path.
The conversation so far reads back as context on every call, and each turn's results are written forward — the session's persistence surface.

edges.label: model & tool calls
edges.note: Every call out of the loop crosses here on a brokered credential scoped to the conversing user. The agent holds no standing keys of its own.
Inference on the brokered credential. The completion proposes the reply and the tool calls — content the human will read, and unauthenticated input all the same.
Approved actions leave with the user's narrowed grant; tool results return into the thread as context.
Actions land on real systems; whatever comes back — records, pages, API responses — is untrusted content entering the conversation.

edges.label: admission
edges.note: Tools exist in the conversation only if the registry admitted them.

edges.label: evaluation
edges.note: Model and prompt changes pass an evaluation gate before they serve conversations.

risks.note: The conversation is model input authored by the party the actions benefit, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction.
Records, pages and API responses return into the thread — content somebody else authored, standing beside the user's words on the next call.
Conversation memory carries a poisoned turn forward: one bad retrieval steers every later action in the session.
The completion proposes the tool calls, and it is unauthenticated content.
An action the human approved without reading is not an overseen action. Approval fatigue is this architecture's version of no gate at all.
The agent acts for the user with the service's reach. Keeping every tool call on the user's grant, not the workload's, is what closes the gap.
The session accumulates everything retrieved on earlier turns; a late question can surface records the current topic never needed.
Per-token inference behind a public chat surface makes unbounded conversation a spend problem.

capabilities.note: In-thread approval before consequential actions, with the proposal specific enough to be worth reading — the architecture's primary control.
A delegated grant scoped to the session and the user, not a standing power the service holds.
Every tool call bounded by what the conversing user may touch, decided per call.
A distinct workload identity for the agent tier, kept separate from the user grants it carries.
Brokered, per-call, user-scoped credentials; the loop holds no standing keys.
Conversation-scoped memory with hard boundaries — no cross-session reads, ever.
Returned content is classified before it re-enters the thread as context.
Named destinations only — the same allowlist that bounds actions is the last boundary for a steered session trying to send context somewhere it should not go.
The thread renders model output — sanitise markup and links before display, because a rendered image URL can carry the conversation to an attacker without a single click.
Redaction on what a session may accumulate, because the thread outlives the turn that needed it.
Session and per-user ceilings at the edge, before token spend and action volume are committed.
Every proposal, approval and action recorded off the agent's write path — the thread is not the audit trail.
A stop that ends live sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

scenarios.title: A turn that ends in an action

steps.note: The user asks for something consequential, in their own words.
The turn enters the loop with the user's identity attached.
The conversation so far loads as context.
The context leaves the loop on a brokered, user-scoped credential.
The model proposes a reply and a tool call.
The proposal renders in the thread — specific enough to be worth reading — and the user approves.
The approved action leaves with the user's grant, not the service's.
The action lands on the system of record, attributable to the session that approved it.

scenarios.title: A tool result steers the next turn

steps.note: A routine lookup runs mid-conversation.
The fetch reaches a record somebody else authored.
An embedded instruction returns with the content.
It persists into conversation state like any other result.
Every later call this session reads it beside the system instruction — the approval gate is now the control.

scenarios.title: The session outlives the topic

steps.note: An innocuous late question, many turns into the conversation.
Context assembly reads back everything earlier turns retrieved.
Records the current question never needed travel with it.
The reply can surface any of it — session-scoped memory and DLP on accumulation are what bound the answer.

archetypes.title: Remote MCP server you publish
summary: A tool server operated as a service for other people's agents: an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models. The scopes, the tenancy and the tool descriptions are all your design decisions — and the descriptions execute as instruction inside somebody else's model.
description:
The inversion is what makes this its own architecture. Every other cloud archetype here calls tools; this one is the tool. The caller is an autonomous agent acting for a user, the arguments were produced by a model, and the tool descriptions this server publishes become instructions inside that model's context. A poorly worded description causes misuse; a deliberately worded one is an attack on the caller. Publishing a server means treating changes to descriptions and error messages with the seriousness of an API contract change.
Authorization is the second inversion. Standard OAuth answers "may this client act for this user", and here that is necessary and not sufficient: the client is an agent that may have been steered by content it read elsewhere. Scopes therefore need to be narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is bounded, and consequential operations need confirmation semantics the protocol can express, rather than relying on the client to prompt its user. In an enterprise deployment the identity work is federated rather than invented: the user signs in at the IdP the organisation already governs, an identity assertion is exchanged for an audience-bound token, and admin policy and revocation stay where the organisation already enforces them. Client registration is pre-arranged or metadata-document based — the self-service dynamic registration of the early protocol is deprecated.
The deployment shape is deliberately conventional: a service edge in front terminating hostile machine traffic, one stateless application behind it, data and upstream systems behind that. The protocol is stateless by design — there are no sessions to bind, only server-minted state handles whose possession proves nothing — so the service scales horizontally like any web tier, and every request re-verifies authorization from the token. The ordinary multi-tenant disciplines apply with unusual force: every read and write checks both that the scope permits the operation and that the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record; rate limits are sized for machine callers that retry, loop and parallelise; and results are bounded in size, because an oversized result is both a cost problem for the caller and a way to crowd their context window. There is no model anywhere in this service — every distinctive control follows from the client being one.
The one rule with no exceptions is at the back: the caller's token never travels upstream. A handler that reaches another system does so as its own OAuth client, on a credential a secrets manager issued to this service — passing the inbound token onward is the confused deputy the protocol documents by name, and it turns one compromised agent into a multi-service problem.
distinguishedBy:
Against a third-party MCP server you consume: opposite side of the same boundary. There the scopes are someone else's design and the work is admission and observation; here the scopes, the tenancy and the descriptions are all design decisions.
Against an AI-augmented API backend: that one has AI inside it and a conventional client. This one has no AI inside it at all and a model as the client. The security work is entirely about the caller's nature.

exemplars.name: Product MCP servers
exemplars.note: SaaS vendors publishing remote tool servers for their own products so customer agents can act without a bespoke integration.

exemplars.name: Internal MCP servers
exemplars.note: The same pattern inside one organisation, exposing internal systems to internal agents. Same architecture, and the temptation to skip the authorization work is much stronger.

exemplars.name: Gateway-fronted fleets
exemplars.note: Organisations publishing many servers behind one API-management or MCP gateway tier, with identity, metering and audit centralised at the edge. The protocol's routing headers were designed for exactly this mediation.

blocks.title: Delegating user
blocks.note: The person the calling agent acts for, and the source of the authorization. Not present at call time, which is why consequential operations cannot rely on them being asked.

blocks.title: Calling agent
blocks.note: Someone else's agent, with arguments composed by a model that may have read hostile content. A non-human caller that is neither a person nor a bot to block.

blocks.title: Enterprise IdP
blocks.note: The identity provider the consuming organisation already governs. Users sign in here, and an identity assertion is exchanged for an audience-bound token — so admin policy, workforce lifecycle and revocation stay in the one place the organisation already enforces them, instead of being reinvented per server.

items.label: SSO & policy
items.note: The sign-in and the admin policy every delegated grant traces back to.

items.label: Token exchange
items.note: The identity assertion swapped for a token bound to this server's authorization server — the enterprise-managed authorization profile, standardised so it works the same across servers.

blocks.title: Authorization server
blocks.note: Issues scoped, expiring, audience-restricted tokens to named clients. The one place a compromised agent's access can be withdrawn without redeploying anything.

items.label: Token issuance
items.note: Short-lived and audience-restricted — a token other resource servers accept turns one compromised agent into a multi-service problem.

items.label: Client registration
items.note: Pre-registered clients or client-ID metadata documents. The early protocol's self-service dynamic registration is deprecated — anonymous clients were the cost.

items.label: Consent records
items.note: Which user authorised which client for which scopes, and when.

blocks.title: Service edge
blocks.note: The front door that terminates hostile machine traffic before the application sees it — an API gateway or MCP gateway tier. The protocol's routing headers exist so this tier can route, meter and rate-limit per tool without parsing request bodies.

items.label: WAF & DDoS
items.note: The commodity protections, in front because the callers are machines at machine rates.

items.label: Rate limits & quotas
items.note: Per-client and per-tenant, sized for callers that retry, loop and parallelise. Limits tuned for human clients are not limits here.

items.label: Header routing
items.note: Method and tool names ride request headers so the gateway can route and meter without reading bodies — mediation the current protocol was redesigned for.

blocks.title: MCP service
blocks.note: The application a team actually deploys: transport, tool router and handler code in one stateless service. Every request arrives self-contained and is re-authorized from the token — there is no session to inherit trust from.

items.label: Protocol endpoint
items.note: Streamable HTTP on a single POST endpoint, Origin validated, stateless by protocol design — which is what lets the tier scale horizontally.

items.label: State handles
items.note: Server-minted names for cross-call state, bound to the token's subject and re-authorized on every request. Possession of a handle is not authentication.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Execute with the request's brokered identity, never a standing service account.

items.label: Input validation
items.note: Arguments arrive model-generated, so validation assumes plausible nonsense — and a handler that re-resolves the tenant from an argument is trusting a model to name it.

blocks.title: Tool definitions
blocks.note: Names, descriptions and schemas — not documentation, but text the calling model treats as instruction. Changing them is changing somebody else's prompt.

items.label: Tool descriptions
items.note: Versioned, reviewed artifacts, because they execute inside another organisation's model.

items.label: Input schemas
items.note: The contract model-generated arguments are validated against.

items.label: Confirmation flags
items.note: Operations marked as requiring the caller to confirm with its user. The server cannot enforce it; declaring it is the only lever it has.

blocks.title: Tenant data
blocks.note: Per-tenant records the tools reach. Isolation here is the claim consuming organisations cannot verify and will ask about in assurance.

items.label: Tenant records
items.note: Every read and write checks the tenant on the token against the tenant on the record.

items.label: Tenant isolation
items.note: A discipline across every handler, not one component's job.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The systems the tools actually wrap — most published servers are a thin governed surface over existing APIs. Reached on the server's own credential, issued by a secrets manager, to named destinations only. The caller's token stops at the service.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: The internal and partner APIs the handlers call as this service, never as the caller.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Vendor systems reached on standing service credentials the secrets manager scopes and rotates.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Scope design, description review, registry listing, audit and revocation — the controls that decide a hijacked agent's blast radius long before any call arrives.

items.label: Scope catalogue
items.note: What each scope permits. Coarse scopes are the difference between a hijacked agent doing one thing and doing everything the user could.

items.label: Registry listing
items.note: The server published to the registry or private subregistry clients are allowed to admit from, versions pinned — so consumers can detect a definition that quietly changed after approval.

items.label: Description review
items.note: Tool text reviewed as a security artifact, because it executes in a caller's context. A benign-looking copy edit can change how thousands of agents behave.

items.label: Call audit
items.note: Which client, for which user, called what with which arguments and what came back — with trace context propagated, because the protocol now carries it. Also the only way to answer a customer asking what their agent did here.

items.label: Revocation & kill
items.note: Withdraw a client's tokens or disable a tool without redeploying the service.

edges.label: SSO & consent
edges.note: The user signs in where the organisation already governs identity, and consents to a named client with named scopes. The last point at which a human decides anything in this architecture — every subsequent call happens without them.

edges.label: token exchange
edges.note: The IdP's identity assertion is exchanged for a token audience-bound to this server. Central policy and revocation ride this edge — disable the user at the IdP and the delegation chain dies with them.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: Model-composed arguments in; bounded results back into the caller's context window. The identity check cannot establish whether the agent was steered by content it read elsewhere.

edges.label: routed call
edges.note: Routed and metered on the protocol's method and tool-name headers, throttled before the application spends anything on it.

edges.label: token validation
edges.note: Every request is validated against the issued token — client, user, scopes, audience, expiry — before it reaches a handler. The service re-verifies even when the edge pre-checks, because audience validation is this server's own obligation.

edges.label: scoped read / write
edges.note: Two checks on every operation: the scope permits it, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record. Skipping the second is how cross-tenant access happens in practice.

edges.label: server's own credential
edges.note: The rule with no exceptions: the caller's token never travels upstream. Handlers call out as this service, on secrets-managed credentials, to named destinations only — egress anywhere else is an exfiltration path, not a feature.

edges.label: schema into caller's context
edges.note: Tool text crossing into another organisation's model, where it executes as instruction. No authentication applies to what a description means.

edges.label: scope definitions
edges.note: The scope catalogue is where a hijacked agent's blast radius is actually decided — long before any call arrives.

edges.label: description review
edges.note: Because the text runs in someone else's model, editing it is closer to shipping an API change than to updating documentation.

risks.note: This server is on the causing side. Its descriptions, errors and results all land in a caller's context, so its output hygiene is somebody else's input security.
Tool text treated as editable copy rather than a versioned artifact — a quiet edit changes how every consuming agent behaves.
The token proves a user consented; it cannot prove the agent still represents their intent. Scope design is the whole of the answer.
Long-lived or unrevocable tokens keep a decommissioned or compromised client alive. Expiry and revocation are the only levers after issuance.

The stateless protocol renamed the threat, not the stakes: a state handle that is guessable, or honoured without re-checking the token it was minted for, hands one caller another's context and tenant.
Machine callers retry, loop and parallelise. Limits tuned for human clients are not limits here — and they belong in front of the application, not inside it.
Arguments are model-generated plausible nonsense, and the user is not present to be asked. Confirmation semantics are declared, not enforced, by this side.
Every read and write needs the tenant on the token checked against the tenant on the record. It is a discipline across all handlers, not one component's job.
Passing the caller's token upstream is the confused deputy the protocol forbids by name — it converts one compromised agent into access at every system that accepts the token.
The read path carries the volume. A coarse scope plus a broad query returns everything the user could see, to an agent that may have been steered.
Results enter the caller's context as content. An oversized or manipulative result is a denial-of-service against a model rather than a server.
A server nobody listed, versioned or watches is still reachable and still trusted by every client that once admitted it. Registry listing and pinning are how consumers notice a change — or a corpse.

capabilities.note: Bind consent to a named client and named scopes at the IdP the organisation already governs — the delegated grant every later call traces back to, revocable where the workforce already is.
Named clients with short-lived, audience-restricted tokens and working revocation. The calling agent is a non-human identity you did not create but must manage.
Design scopes narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is one operation, not everything the user could do.
Per-client and per-tenant limits sized for machine callers, with idempotency keys because agents retry — enforced at the edge on the protocol's routing headers.
TLS, Origin validation, and state handles bound to the authenticated subject with authorization re-verified per request — possession of a handle proves nothing.
Enforce both checks on every operation: scope permits it, and token tenant matches record tenant — on reads as well as writes.
Upstream credentials issued by a secrets manager to this service, scoped and rotated — never embedded in configuration, and never the caller's token.
Handlers reach named upstreams and nothing else. Unbounded egress from a tool server is the exfiltration path a steered agent is looking for.
Treat definitions as versioned security artifacts: schema-pinned, change-controlled, and published with provenance callers can check.
Adversarially review descriptions and error text before release — the question is what a model will do with the words, not what a human reads into them.
Declare confirmation semantics on consequential tools so the caller must confirm with its user. Declaring it is the only lever this side of the boundary has.
Bound result size and structure before it leaves — what returns becomes part of another organisation's prompt.
Record client, user, tool, arguments and result per call, with trace context — the trail that answers a customer asking what their agent did here.

scenarios.title: A user authorises a client

steps.note: Consent happens at the IdP the organisation already governs. The last human decision in the flow.
The identity assertion is exchanged for a token audience-bound to this server.
The agent calls in with its scoped token; the user is no longer present.
Routed and metered at the edge before the application spends anything.
Client, user, scopes, audience and expiry are validated per request.
Scope check plus tenant-match check, on this and every subsequent operation.

scenarios.title: A hijacked agent calls in

steps.note: The agent was steered by content it read elsewhere. Its token is valid, and the rate limits constrain the mechanics, not the intent.
Every identity check passes; argument validation assumes plausible nonsense.
The tenant check bounds reach to the one tenant; the scope bounds it to named operations.
The blast radius was decided by scope design long before this call arrived.

scenarios.title: A handler reaches upstream

steps.note: The tool call arrives on the caller's audience-bound token.
The handler runs with the request's brokered identity.
The caller's token stops here. The handler calls upstream as this service, on a secrets-managed credential, to a named destination — nothing else is reachable.

scenarios.title: A description edit ships

steps.note: The edit is reviewed as an interface change — text a model will act on, not copy.
The new wording lands in every consuming agent's context on their next session.

deviations.subject: The service is drawn as one application block, not protocol stages
deviations.reason: Transport, router and handlers deploy as one stateless service, so they are one block with items — the thing a team ships and scales. Tool definitions stay separate because they are a different artifact class: versioned content with a review pipeline, whose distinctive edge runs into the caller's context rather than through the service.

deviations.subject: An enterprise IdP is drawn even though the protocol does not require one
deviations.reason: The target state federates identity to the provider the organisation already governs — the standardised enterprise-managed authorization profile — because per-server identity silos are how revocation gets missed. A consumer-facing server without an enterprise IdP collapses this edge into the authorization server and keeps everything else.

deviations.subject: Sessions are gone because the protocol removed them
deviations.reason: The current protocol revision deleted sessions and the initialize handshake; cross-call state is explicit server-minted handles carried as arguments. The old session-hijacking risk is drawn as state-handle hijacking on the service instead.

archetypes.title: Self-hosted open-weights inference
summary: An open-weights model served on infrastructure the organisation operates — the same inference runtime as the endpoint local model runtime, with an AI gateway in front of it and a governance plane behind it. Weights land in storage from a public hub or the organisation's own fine-tuning pipeline, and the whole model-provider role moves inside the boundary.
description:
The trade is explicit: a data-disclosure risk goes away and a supply-chain, availability and safety risk arrives. There is no provider applying content policy, no provider absorbing a traffic spike, and no provider patching the serving stack. Every control a managed API supplies by default is now a component this organisation runs or does without — which is why the gateway and the governance plane are the blocks that separate this architecture from the same software installed by one person on a workstation.
The supply chain is the distinctive risk. Weights are large artifacts that arrive in storage from a public hub or from the organisation's own fine-tuning pipeline, and several distribution formats execute code on load. The control is scanning and format policy in the promotion gate, before an artifact reaches the runtime — a blocking gate, not a report — and digest verification at load, so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly.
Multi-tenancy inside the runtime has no equivalent elsewhere in this catalogue. Continuous batching mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators, the KV cache holds their context, and prefix caching across tenants is a performance feature that is also a disclosure path. Whether cache entries may be shared across tenants is a serving configuration flag with data-protection consequences, and it rarely reaches a review.
Availability is a security property here in a way it is not with a managed API. Capacity is finite and expensive, admission control at the gateway is what stops one caller becoming everyone else's outage, and quotas are a control rather than a billing feature.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint local model runtime: identical software, entirely different operational position. There it was installed by one person and has no inventory entry; here it has a gateway in front, a promotion pipeline, an identity and someone on call.
Against consuming a managed model API: this architecture replaces one boundary crossing with a whole subsystem. The guardrails, abuse monitoring, capacity management and patching the provider was doing are now blocks on this diagram.

exemplars.name: Serving runtimes on Kubernetes
exemplars.note: Open-source inference servers with continuous batching and paged attention, scheduled onto GPU node pools with an inference-aware gateway in front.

exemplars.name: On-premises inference for data residency
exemplars.note: The same stack in a datacentre because the data cannot leave. The most common non-cost reason organisations take on this architecture.

blocks.title: Consuming applications
blocks.note: Internal applications and agents sharing one cluster. Their isolation from each other is a property of the serving configuration, not of the network between them.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The governed front door in front of finite capacity — the same gateway block every hosted architecture in this catalogue routes through. With no provider applying content policy, the guardrail checks enforced here are a service the organisation runs itself or does without.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Workload identity per calling tenant — the thing quotas and cache-isolation decisions key off.

items.label: Rate & budget limits
items.note: Per-tenant ceilings on finite capacity. What stops one caller becoming everyone's outage.

items.label: Audit tap
items.note: Every request and completion recorded at the one crossing every caller shares.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: The same runtime the endpoint architecture draws — loading weights, batching requests, serving completions — operated here as a shared service across tenants on shared accelerators. The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and its distributed control plane assumes a trusted network: job APIs and inter-node channels ship unauthenticated by design, so network isolation is a control, not a hardening step.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution — and where the registry digest is verified.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

items.label: Continuous batching
items.note: Mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators. Efficiency and co-tenancy are the same mechanism.

items.label: KV & prefix cache
items.note: Tenants' live context, held to avoid recomputing it. Sharing prefixes across tenants is a performance feature and a disclosure path in the same flag.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Versioned weight artifacts with provenance and a promotion state — expensive to reproduce, trivial to copy. Nothing serves that was not promoted, provided the load path verifies the digest.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts whose format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution.

blocks.title: Model sources
blocks.note: Where the weights come from: a public hub, where publisher identity says nothing about what the artifact does on load — or the organisation's own fine-tuning pipeline, which is its own architecture in this catalogue.

items.label: Public model hub
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

items.label: Self-trained model
items.note: A checkpoint from the organisation's fine-tuning and model pipeline, promoted like any other artifact.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: The controls a managed provider would have supplied, now operated in-house: artifact scanning, per-version evaluation, and posture over serving configuration.

items.label: Artifact scanning
items.note: Format and content inspection as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, before the runtime opens the file.

items.label: Evaluation & red teaming
items.note: Per model version, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested.

items.label: Posture & inventory
items.note: Which versions serve where, at what configuration — including whether cross-tenant cache sharing is on.

edges.label: inference request
edges.note: The tenant on the token is what quotas and cache-isolation decisions key off. A request that arrives without one gets whatever the default tenant can do.
Admitted requests scheduled into the batch; completions back through the guardrail checks. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted when self-hosting.

edges.label: fetch / load
edges.note: Promoted artifacts load into the runtime, digest-verified against the promotion record. Without that verification the gate can be bypassed by writing to storage directly.

edges.label: weights in
edges.note: Fetched from the hub or produced by the organisation's own training pipeline. Provenance establishes who made the artifact and nothing about what it does on load.

edges.label: scan & promotion gate
edges.note: Scanning and evaluation gate promotion — blocking, not advisory. A scan that runs after deployment has documented an incident.

edges.label: posture & drift
edges.note: Posture watches serving configuration for drift, including the cache-sharing flags. A posture tool that can read the cache has joined the data path it was meant to observe.

risks.note: Publisher identity is the only assurance the hub offers, and it says nothing about the artifact's behaviour.
Several weight formats execute code on load. Format policy on this edge is the only place that fact can be addressed once for everything downstream.
The stored artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy, which makes storage access control an asset-protection question.
A load path that skips digest verification turns the promotion gate into a suggestion.
The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and no provider is patching it on anyone's behalf.

The gateway is third-party code holding every tenant's brokered credentials — a compromised release of the gateway itself is the whole credential portfolio, a supply chain incident class with recent precedent.
Batching puts several tenants' requests in one forward pass; isolation is a property of several configuration choices at once.
Shared accelerators are a physical substrate common to every tenant, below every namespace boundary.

Cross-tenant prefix sharing puts one tenant's context where another's request can reach it, and it looks like a cache hit rather than an incident — a hit is measurable from outside as latency, and published attacks reconstruct other tenants' prompts from that timing alone.
A poisoned cache entry serves every later request that matches it.
Capacity is finite and there is no provider to absorb a spike. Admission control here is an availability control, not a billing feature.
With no provider applying output policy, an unguarded return leg hands raw completions to every caller.

capabilities.note: Format and content scanning as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, before any artifact reaches the runtime.
Safety and adversarial evaluation per model version — a new checkpoint is a new model with new behaviour.
One governed front door for every caller: routing, admission and policy at a single crossing.
Workload identity per calling tenant, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.
Per-tenant quotas on finite capacity, enforced at admission rather than discovered at saturation.
Content and injection classification on both legs, because no provider is applying policy for you.
Reviewed serving configuration — batching, cache sharing, tenancy flags — treated as security settings, not tuning knobs.
Tenant-scoped cache keys, so a prefix hit can never cross a tenant boundary.
Hardware-backed isolation for the highest-sensitivity tenants where shared accelerators are not acceptable.
Track and patch the serving stack's CVE stream on your own schedule, because nobody upstream will.
Encryption, access control and integrity digests on weights at rest, matched by verification at load.
Continuous posture over which versions serve where and at what configuration, catching drift before an incident does.

scenarios.title: A new checkpoint is promoted

steps.note: The artifact arrives — fetched from the hub or produced by the training pipeline — with provenance recorded.
Scanning and per-version evaluation gate the promotion. Blocking, or it is not a gate.
The promoted artifact loads into the runtime, digest-verified against the promotion record.

scenarios.title: A tenant calls the endpoint

steps.note: The workload identity on the request decides its quota and its cache scope.
The admitted request is scheduled into a batch alongside other tenants' traffic; tenant-scoped cache keys are what keep the prefix lookup safe.
The completion returns through the guardrail's output leg, not around it.

scenarios.title: A spike hits finite capacity

steps.note: Admission control decides who waits. There is no provider to absorb the spike.
Within-quota traffic is scheduled; everything else is shed at the front door rather than at the accelerator.

deviations.subject: No separate GPU or cache blocks are drawn
deviations.reason: The accelerators, the batch and the KV cache are internals of the inference runtime — the same block the endpoint architecture draws — so they appear as items inside it rather than as blocks, and the multi-tenancy risks pin to the runtime and its serving path.

deviations.subject: The model registry is folded into Storage and the promotion gate
deviations.reason: Registry semantics — versioning, provenance, promotion state — live in the storage block and the governance plane's gate over it; drawing a separate registry service duplicated the storage block it fronted.

vLLM security guide — API-key limits, unauthenticated auxiliary endpoints and trusted-network assumptions
Selective KV-cache sharing — cross-tenant prompt reconstruction from cache-timing side channels

CISA and NSA — deploying AI systems securely

archetypes.title: Fine-tuning and model registry pipeline
summary: A build system whose artifact is a model. Curated data goes in, a tuned checkpoint comes out, and everything that is true of a compiler and its supply chain is true here — except that the output cannot be diffed and the defects cannot be found by reading it.
description:
Treating this as a build pipeline is the whole of the correct framing. It has source inputs, a build environment, dependencies, an artifact, a registry and a promotion path, and it deserves the controls a software pipeline gets: reproducibility, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks is inspection: a compiled binary can be decompiled and diffed; a tuned checkpoint cannot be read for backdoors in any practical sense. Input control and evaluation are the substitutes for code review — what went into the training set and how the result behaves are the only two things anyone can actually examine.
Poisoning is therefore the primary risk and it is durable. A poisoned example influences every inference the model ever makes, survives redeployment, and is not removable without retraining — and the dose is small: published results show a near-constant few hundred poisoned documents backdoor models regardless of scale, so poisoning needs a foothold, not a percentage. A targeted poisoning that only activates on a trigger phrase is invisible to accuracy metrics and to any evaluation that does not know what to look for — which is why curation is the last place a bad example can be removed rather than baked in, and why lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset is what makes a discovered poisoning scopeable at all.
Training data is also a disclosure surface in a way inference data is not. Memorised examples can be extracted from the model afterwards, so restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was. The two access questions to settle early: who may promote a checkpoint to production, and who may read the corpus. Both default to a broad platform-team role, and both are higher-privilege than they look — which is why promotion is a separated human decision and the signing key lives outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.
distinguishedBy:
Against the batch pipeline: same build-system trust properties, different artifact. That produces data; this produces a model. The data can be corrected in place; the model cannot.
Against self-hosted inference: that consumes artifacts, this produces them. They meet at the registry, and the promotion gate between them is where both archetypes' supply-chain controls concentrate.

exemplars.name: Managed fine-tuning services
exemplars.note: Provider-hosted tuning against a customer dataset, producing a private checkpoint served from the same platform. Availability varies sharply by provider and by year.

exemplars.name: Self-operated tuning on accelerator fleets
exemplars.note: Adapter or full fine-tuning on the organisation's own hardware, with a registry and promotion pipeline built alongside.

exemplars.name: Adapter and preference tuning
exemplars.note: Lightweight tuning producing an adapter rather than a full checkpoint. Smaller artifact, same supply-chain questions, and an additional one about who may load an adapter at serve time.

blocks.title: Labelling workforce
blocks.note: Human or model-generated labels and preferences, frequently from an outsourced workforce. A supply chain with a direct path into model behaviour and almost no scrutiny.

blocks.title: Training content origins
blocks.note: Scraped corpora, purchased datasets, user-generated content and internal records. Each carries a different provenance claim and most carry none.

items.label: Scraped & purchased sets
items.note: Authored by parties the pipeline never authenticates.

items.label: Internal records
items.note: Often restricted-access data about to be baked into a widely served artifact.

blocks.title: Curation & filtering
blocks.note: Deduplication, quality filtering and removal of sensitive or improperly sourced content. The last point at which a poisoned example can be removed rather than baked in.

items.label: Quality & safety filters
items.note: After training, a bad example is in the weights and cannot be taken out.

items.label: Sensitive-content removal
items.note: What stays in can later be extracted from the model by anyone who can query it.

items.label: Provenance capture
items.note: Per-example source and licence, recorded now because it cannot be reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Training corpus
blocks.note: The assembled, versioned dataset. Read access is higher-privilege than it looks — it is the union of everything the organisation decided a model should learn.

items.label: Dataset versions
items.note: Immutable and versioned, so a run can be tied to exactly what it saw.

blocks.title: Base model & deps
blocks.note: The starting checkpoint and the training frameworks, pulled from outside. Everything the base model already contains is inherited — tuning adds behaviour and does not subtract it.

items.label: Base checkpoint
items.note: A backdoor in the base survives tuning and every benchmark that does not know its trigger.

items.label: Frameworks & dependencies
items.note: An ordinary software supply chain executing with access to the corpus and the artifact.

blocks.title: Training job
blocks.note: The build. Reproducibility — same data, same code, same seed, same artifact — is what makes an incident investigable at all.

items.label: Tuning run
items.note: Scoped to the dataset approved for this run, so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs.

items.label: Reproducibility record
items.note: Data version, code version, seed and base model, captured during the run.

items.label: Write-once output
items.note: Candidate-only writes, so a job cannot overwrite an already-promoted artifact. The signing key lives outside this environment for the same reason.

blocks.title: Evaluation & red teaming
blocks.note: Capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation testing — the substitute for reading an artifact nobody can read. Blocking, because a report on an unreadable artifact changes nothing on its own.

items.label: Capability & safety evals
items.note: A targeted poisoning passes every benchmark that does not know its trigger. The safety half is not optional either way: fine-tuning on entirely benign data measurably erodes the base model's alignment, so the post-tune safety evaluation is re-establishing a property the tuning itself degraded.

items.label: Backdoor probing
items.note: Adversarial search for triggers and behavioural anomalies against the previous version.

items.label: Memorisation testing
items.note: Extraction and membership-inference testing before promotion — the only way to learn the artifact remembers its training data before someone else does.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: Versioned artifacts with lineage back to the exact dataset and code that produced them, and a promotion gate to production that nothing bypasses. The registry platform is itself attack surface — the common self-hosted trackers ship without authentication, and their registry APIs have been exploited in the wild.

items.label: Candidate checkpoints
items.note: Unpromoted, unsigned, and served to nobody.

items.label: Lineage metadata
items.note: Which examples, which code, which base model, which run — recorded, not reconstructed.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signature applied at promotion and verified at load, which is what makes the gate meaningful. The signing format is standardised now — model signing has production tooling and major catalogues sign with it.

blocks.title: Serving & consumers
blocks.note: The inference platforms that pull promoted models. This archetype ends at the registry; the promotion gate is the seam between producing the artifact and serving it.

items.label: Inference platforms
items.note: Verify the signature at load — a registry bypass shows up here or never.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Lineage, promotion authority and signing — the record of what produced what, and the separated decisions about what may ship.

items.label: Data & model lineage
items.note: The only route to scoping the damage when a dataset turns out to have been poisoned or improperly sourced months later.

items.label: Promotion authority
items.note: Separation of duties: whoever runs training cannot promote unilaterally. The default configuration usually grants both to the same role.

items.label: Artifact signing
items.note: Keys held outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output. Verification happens at load, in whichever platform serves it.

edges.label: raw content
edges.note: Curation is the only place a poisoned or improperly sourced example can still be removed. After training it is in the weights.

edges.label: labels & preferences
edges.note: Frequently an outsourced workforce with a direct influence on model behaviour and very little scrutiny relative to that influence.

edges.label: curated dataset
edges.note: Corpus writes decide what the model will learn. The write path deserves the review a production deploy gets.

edges.label: approved training data
edges.note: Scoped to the dataset version approved for this run, so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs.

edges.label: base checkpoint & dependencies
edges.note: Everything already in the base model is inherited, and the frameworks execute with access to the corpus and the artifact.

edges.label: candidate checkpoint
edges.note: Write-once and candidate-only — a job cannot overwrite a promoted artifact, and cannot sign anything.

edges.label: evaluation gate
edges.note: Blocking, before promotion: capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation results are the substitute for code review on an artifact nobody can read.

edges.label: promoted model
edges.note: Pulled only after promotion, with the signature verified at load. Deliberately the only path from training to traffic.

edges.label: signing & promotion
edges.note: A separated human promotion decision, a signature applied outside the build, and lineage recorded during the run rather than reconstructed later.

risks.note: A poisoned example that survives curation influences every inference the model ever makes, and is not removable without retraining.
Labels and preference data steer behaviour directly, and the workforce producing them gets almost no scrutiny relative to that influence.
A licensing or privacy defect discovered after training is a retraining decision, not a deletion. Irreversibility starts at the training job.
Corpus read access is the union of everything a model should learn, and it defaults to a broad platform-team role.
A tampered base checkpoint or dependency is inherited whole — tuning adds behaviour and does not subtract it.
Training frameworks and their transitive dependencies execute with access to the corpus and the artifact — an ordinary supply chain in an unusually valuable position.
The checkpoint may have memorised its inputs, turning a restricted dataset into an artifact with broad access. There is no runtime control for this path.
A targeted poisoning activates only on its trigger and passes every benchmark that does not know it — the gate is necessary and insufficient alone.
The registry holds the crown-jewel artifacts. Read access to checkpoints is model theft with none of the serving-side telemetry.
Whoever runs training should not be able to promote unilaterally. The default configuration usually grants both to the same role.

capabilities.note: Record per-example source and licence at ingestion — provenance cannot be reconstructed later, and it is the only route to scoping a poisoning.
Filter poisoned, sensitive and improperly sourced content here — the last point where removal is deletion rather than retraining.
Make evaluation a blocking gate on promotion: capability, safety and regression against the previous version, with results recorded per candidate.
Probe candidates adversarially for backdoors and trigger behaviour — the tests that assume the training data was hostile.
Run extraction and membership-inference tests before promotion, because a model that memorised its corpus has widened that data's audience permanently.
Encrypt checkpoints at rest, restrict reads, and sign at promotion so serving can verify the artifact it loads.
Gate corpus reads and writes separately, and scope each training job to its approved dataset version.
Promotion is a human decision by someone who did not run the training — separation of duties on the highest-privilege action in the pipeline.

Scan base checkpoints and loaders before use — serialised model formats are a code execution vector, not just data. Scanners have documented bypasses, so format policy that refuses executable formats outright is the stronger half of the gate.
Maintain the lineage record — dataset version, code, base model, run — for every artifact in the registry, recorded during the run.
Promote gradually behind traffic splitting, with the signature verified at load and a rollback target retained.
Hold signing keys outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.

scenarios.title: A tuning run ships a model

steps.note: Raw content arrives with mixed and mostly absent provenance claims.
What survives filtering becomes a versioned, provenance-stamped dataset.
The job reads exactly the approved dataset version, nothing wider.
The base checkpoint and frameworks come in — everything they contain is inherited.
The candidate lands write-once, unsigned, served to nobody.
Capability, backdoor and memorisation testing gate the candidate.
A separated human promotes; the signature is applied outside the build.
Serving pulls the promoted artifact and verifies the signature at load.

scenarios.title: A poisoning is discovered months later

steps.note: Lineage maps the poisoned examples to every model version that learned from them.
Affected versions are rolled back to the last clean checkpoint.
The poisoned examples are removed and the dataset re-versioned.
Retraining is the only removal — the weights cannot be edited.

scenarios.title: A backdoored base model arrives

steps.note: The trigger behaviour rides in with the checkpoint; scanning and provenance are the only upstream checks.
The candidate carries the backdoor intact — tuning did not remove it.
A gate that does not know the trigger passes it, which is why base-model provenance matters before this point.
