archetypes.title: Coding and desktop agents
summary: A vendor-built agent application driven by a person who is present — a terminal CLI, an IDE extension, or a desktop GUI, all the same engine in a different shell. The harness and its tool surface ship inside the vendor's application: file and edit tools, a shell, MCP servers, installed skills, and optionally computer use, with sandboxed execution for the tools that need containing. The shell changes the review surface, not the security architecture. Remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory are now opt-in features of the same engine — owner-bound and admin-toggleable, which is what still separates this from the personal autonomous agent.
description:
The defining property is the human in the loop and the fact that the loop is scoped to a task. The person starts it, watches it, and is the approval gate for the actions that matter. That is the default posture rather than a guarantee: every product now ships opt-in unattended modes — scheduled automations, event triggers, sessions steered from a phone over an outbound relay — each bound to the owner's account and switchable off from the vendor control plane. Most of this archetype's security posture rests on that gate being real rather than nominal — and approval fatigue is the failure mode that makes everything else matter. A gate that fires on every file write trains the user to accept, so the architectures that hold up narrow what needs approving: sandboxed tools, permissions scoped in advance on the harness-to-tools path, and default-deny egress, so the prompts that do fire are rare enough to read.
Everything the agent reads is untrusted input with the same standing as the user's instruction: source files, dependency manifests, issue text, documents, mail — and screenshots, where an injection can be a picture of text. The tool plane is admitted by configuration that often arrives with the content itself: a project dotfile that ships in the clone can register tool servers the user never chose, and the disclosed vulnerability pattern in this archetype is overwhelmingly about that file. The same convergence produced a memory layer: agent-written notes and rules files merged into every later session — the persistent instruction channel the personal agent used to own alone, now on by default in several of the products. Computer use is the sharpest tool the application can switch on — the agent acts through the GUI and inherits every application already signed in, through an interface built on the assumption that a human is driving.
The application boundary is the vendor's: tool capabilities and connectors are built into the CLI or GUI and configured there, and the only governance this archetype has is the published surface of the vendor's control plane — managed settings, a tool-server allowlist, audit export. In a managed deployment they are the difference between a governed tool and a shadow one; in the default install none of them are on, and the same binary runs with no policy, no audit and no inventory entry.
The open-source harnesses that run the same loop without a vendor are their own architecture in this catalogue — same engine, different custody: pasted keys, community supply chains, and no control plane. This page is the vendored pattern, where the vendor column is the partial governance the archetype has.
distinguishedBy:
Against the open-source coding agents: the same engine and the same human-present default, but here the vendor column exists — expiring session credentials instead of pasted keys, a signed distribution channel instead of community registries, an owner-bound relay instead of a bearer-secret serve port, and a managed-settings tier an administrator can actually switch on.
Against the personal autonomous agent: the capabilities have converged — this one now takes remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory too — so what separates the archetypes is defaults, identity and custody. Here each of those is opt-in, addressable only by the owner's vendor account over an outbound relay that opens no inbound port, and switchable off from an admin console. The personal harness listens as its resting state, on raw platform identities an unbounded sender set can use, holds long-lived keys the user pasted in — and has no console anyone can switch anything off from.
Against a vendor-managed runtime in the cloud: the same engine run by the vendor on their infrastructure gets an isolated filesystem, default-deny egress and a clean teardown. Here it runs on a machine that also holds the user's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions, and sandboxed tools are the only thing separating them from the agent's shell.

exemplars.name: Terminal CLIs
exemplars.note: The engine in a shell against a working directory — Claude Code and Codex in their CLI form — with a permission model for file writes and command execution and project-scoped tool servers.

exemplars.name: IDE extensions and agent-first IDEs
exemplars.note: The same engine in an editor: the VS Code extensions are the identical loop with an inline review surface, and Cursor is an IDE built around one. The tool-server configuration lives in a repository dotfile — the specific location that has repeatedly proven to be a code-execution path when written or swapped between approval and use.

exemplars.name: Desktop assistant apps
exemplars.note: Claude Desktop and the ChatGPT desktop app: chat over local files and standing connectors with the vendor's coding engine embedded underneath, plus an opt-in computer-use mode that drives the graphical interface behind OS screen-recording and input grants.

exemplars.name: Managed enterprise deployments
exemplars.note: The same product with centrally managed settings, an allowlist of permitted tool servers and exported audit. The architecture is unchanged; the vendor control plane being switched on is the difference.

blocks.title: User
blocks.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate — a developer at a CLI or anyone at the desktop app. The archetype's posture depends on that staying true, which is why every other control exists to keep the prompts rare enough to read.

blocks.title: Repos, docs & screen
blocks.note: Everything the agent reads: repository content arriving in the clone, documents and mail the user points it at, and screenshots. Contributed to by people who are not the user, and read into context as though it were instruction.

items.label: Code & project docs
items.note: A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to.

items.label: Tool config dotfile
items.note: The tool-server declaration that ships with the code. The single most attacked artifact in this archetype.

items.label: Docs & screenshots
items.note: Documents authored by anyone, and screenshot text as pixels — an injection can be a picture of an instruction, with no provenance at all.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The loop behind the terminal, editor or chat window, running as the user. Remote steering arrives over an outbound relay — no inbound port — and only the owner's vendor account can address it. Who may address the loop, not whether it can be reached, is what now separates it from a personal agent harness.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides the next edit, command or screen action from the task and everything it has read so far.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the instruction, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The steering surfaces away from the machine: the phone, the browser, the chat thread. Everything they send reaches the harness through the vendor's relay on the owner's account — which makes this box, not the machine, the place remote-control policy is enforced: trusted-device enrolment, fresh sign-in requirements, and the admin toggle that turns the path off.

items.label: Phone & web apps
items.note: The owner's own surfaces, signed into the same vendor account as the harness.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: The @-mention surfaces — and the widest admission decision here, because whoever the channel admits can raise a session of their own.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: The cross-session layer the products converged on: notes the agent writes itself and rules files merged into every later prompt. Read back as instruction on the next task — the personal agent's persistence primitive, now on by default in several vendor products and present as rules files in all of them.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Agent-written notes loaded at the start of every session. Context, not enforced configuration — and prose the next task treats as instruction.

items.label: Rules & instructions
items.note: The AGENTS.md-class files, user-level and repo-committed — the repo-committed ones are authored by whoever last committed.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The application's action surface, running as the user on a machine that also holds their SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. Admission is configuration — which may have arrived with the clone.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write across the working tree and the user's documents. Scope is a setting, not a boundary.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution with the user's full authority when it runs outside the sandbox.

items.label: Local & remote MCP
items.note: Local child processes with the user's privileges, and remote servers on an authorised grant — both admitted by configuration, and both feeding tool descriptions into context as model input.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions and helpers the engine loads — project- or user-installed, executing with the agent's authority.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: The opt-in mode that drives the GUI through OS grants. The tool that cannot be enumerated: the reachable action set is everything a person at the desk could do.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Where builds, tests, shell commands and driven desktops run when isolation is on — a container or VM whose own configuration the agent must not be able to reach. The control that turns "approve every command" into "approve the ones that leave the box".

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The vendor's application backend and the published surfaces of its control plane — managed settings, connector brokering, audit export, and the relay behind the remote and scheduled features. The partial governance this archetype has, operated by the vendor rather than the organisation. Everything behind the published interfaces is the vendor's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Centrally enforced permissions and a tool-server allowlist the user cannot override. Off by default; the difference between a governed deployment and a shadow one.

items.label: Connector broker
items.note: Holds the OAuth grants into the user's services and exercises them on the agent's behalf.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Exported prompts, tool calls and approvals. In an unmanaged install there is no record at all.

items.label: Remote & scheduled sessions
items.note: The relay that lets a phone or chat mention steer the local loop, and the scheduler that runs it with nobody watching. Outbound-only and bound to the owner's account — and the admin console can turn both off.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API behind the vendor's service. The completion it returns drives file writes, commands and screen actions.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The published interface. Receives code, documents and screenshots; returns the plan.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the tool plane reaches over the network: registries, the web, and the SaaS accounts behind standing connector grants — and where fetched content comes back in as context indistinguishable from the user's instruction.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: Dependencies and their metadata, authored by strangers and read into context.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context, and the exfiltration path out.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Mail, calendar and workspace accounts reached through standing OAuth grants — authorised once, scoped to a service rather than a task, and outliving the conversation.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Cloud documents pulled into context through a grant the user forgot they gave.

edges.label: task / approval
edges.note: The user states the task and answers the approval prompts. Whoever is at the machine is the user, as far as the agent is concerned.
The loop writes what it learns and reads it back as instruction on the next task — the same edge the personal agent has always had, now drawn here too.

edges.label: read into context
edges.note: Repository content, documents and screenshots are read into context as instruction, and the tool-server declaration arrives in the same clone. A contributor is not the user, and nothing authenticates the difference.

edges.label: app session
edges.note: The application session on a vendor-issued, session-scoped credential that expires on its own. Code, documents and screenshots leave for inference; the completion that comes back is unauthenticated content, and it drives the tool calls.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person, not at the keyboard: the instruction is written on a phone, in a browser, or in a chat thread instead of the terminal.

edges.label: remote steering
edges.note: Instructions from away arrive through the vendor relay: the local harness polls outbound, no inbound port opens, and only the owner's account can address it. The trade is that the session's admission decision now lives with the vendor's identity system — and with whatever a chat channel admits.

edges.label: model inference
edges.note: The vendor's service calls the model provider's inference API — the same consistent block every architecture uses for model inference.

edges.label: tool calls
edges.note: Tool calls out with whatever scope the permission model granted; file contents, screen content and tool results back into context. The permission gate on this path is the archetype's standard control.
Remote tool calls, package fetches and connector reads out; descriptions, dependencies, mail and page content back in as model input. Also the path an exfiltration attempt takes.

risks.note: Source files, manifests, issue text, documents and screenshots are unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the user's instruction — and screenshot text carries no provenance at all.
Configuration admits the whole tool plane and can arrive with the clone. Injecting into it, swapping it after approval and auto-registration are the disclosed paths.
Memory files and rules are prose a later session treats as instruction. An injection that writes here outlives the task that carried it — including rules committed by whoever last touched the repo.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives file writes, shell commands and clicks.
Code, documents and screenshots leave for inference — usually more than the user pictured sharing.
A gate that fires on every action trains the user to accept, and an accepted prompt is not oversight.
A binary a user can fetch without asking anyone. Unmanaged, it has no policy, no audit and no inventory entry — and that is the common case.
On the computer-use path the driven applications carry whatever authority is already signed in, and cannot tell an agent from the person the session belongs to.
Local MCP servers are third-party code running as the user, in the same trust zone as everything else.
The machine also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions, and outside the sandbox nothing separates them from the agent's shell on the way out.

The remote channel is only as good as the account and device binding behind it — a stale login or an unenrolled device steering a machine full of credentials is an account-compromise blast radius, not a UX feature.
A remote server's grant is explicit and revocable, but says nothing about whether its tool descriptions are honest — and they are model input.

capabilities.note: The standard permission gate between harness and tools: per-tool grants scoped to the working tree and the task — and, on the desktop, OS grants narrowed to folders and the contained display — instead of the user's full authority.
Make sandboxed tools the default path for commands and computer use — an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and accounts, so the approval gate only fires for actions that leave the box.
Non-overridable approval on consequential actions, kept rare by the surrounding controls so each prompt is actually read.
Treat memory and rules as untrusted input on read; review what the agent writes, and treat a repo-committed rules change like a code change.
Provenance and behavioural review before a server is admitted; pin versions so an update is a decision.
Keep the user's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profile outside the agent's reachable filesystem and environment.
Trusted-device enrolment and the admin toggle decide which surfaces may steer at all — enforced at the relay, outside the machine being steered.
A managed allowlist of tool servers, enforced from the vendor control plane outside the configuration file it governs — never auto-registration from a cloned repo.
Turn on session audit export — prompts, tool calls and approvals — so an incident is reconstructable.
Redact what code, document and screen content may leave for inference, because the inputs are the user's private files.
Default-deny outbound with an allowlist — the last boundary between a content-borne injection and an attacker's collection endpoint.
Review and narrow the standing connector grants; expire the ones no task has used.
Treat repository and document content as untrusted on read; it cannot be authenticated, only bounded.
Find the installs that never enrolled, because this archetype spreads one user at a time.

scenarios.title: The user asks for a change

steps.note: The task is stated by a human who will stay for the whole session.
The session rides a vendor-issued credential; context leaves for the model.
The vendor's service calls inference; the completion becomes the next action.
Edits and commands execute with whatever scope the permission model granted.
The diff comes back to the person who asked, who approves what matters.

scenarios.title: A clone brings its own tool servers

steps.note: The tool configuration dotfile arrives with the code, authored by whoever last committed.
Declared servers launch as the user — unless a managed allowlist enforced from the vendor control plane says otherwise.
A declared remote server is reached, and its tool descriptions enter context as model input.

scenarios.title: A poisoned document phones home

steps.note: A hidden instruction in a source file, document or screenshot is read into context.
The instruction shapes the completion, which the loop treats as the plan.
The plan becomes a file write, a command or a screen action, inside whatever scope the tools hold — contained if it runs in the sandboxed tools, signed-in everywhere if not.
The exfiltration attempt has to cross the egress allowlist — the last control standing.

scenarios.title: A phone steers the session

steps.note: The person steps away from the machine; the instruction is written on a phone or in a chat thread.
The vendor relay authenticates the owner's account — and the trusted-device policy fires here or nowhere.
The local harness picks it up on its outbound poll — no port opened, nothing for a scanner to find.
Execution is local, with the machine's full context — the person just is not at the keyboard.
Results stream back through the relay; approvals can be answered from the phone.

deviations.subject: The desktop assistant is folded into this architecture rather than drawn separately
deviations.reason: The desktop apps embed the same engine the CLIs run, pointed at a broader audience; what varied between the two drawings was the GUI shell, the connector emphasis and the computer-use toggle — all items on this diagram, not different architectures.

deviations.subject: The application boundary is drawn as a containment frame, not a block
deviations.reason: The harness and tool services ship inside the vendor's CLI or GUI; the React Flow view draws that as a labelled frame around both, because the application is a boundary things live in, not a service things call.

deviations.subject: The OS permission layer is a control on the harness-to-tools path, not a block
deviations.reason: One-time OS consent dialogs gate file access, screen recording and input control, but they are a permission-scoping control on tool calls, not a service in the data path — so they live with the permission-scoping capability on that edge.

deviations.subject: Connector traffic is drawn from Tool services, not the vendor
deviations.reason: The OAuth grants live with the vendor's connector broker, so the bytes flow through the vendor. The drawing keeps the standard Tool services to Downstream services reading and names the broker on the vendor block, because the reader's question is what the agent can reach, not which datacentre the call transits.

archetypes.title: Local model runtime
summary: An open-weights model served on the user's own machine, listening on a local port so other local processes can call it. Chosen to keep data off a vendor's infrastructure, which succeeds — and moves every control the vendor was providing onto the device.
description:
The reason people run this is sound: prompts and documents never leave the machine, there is no per-token cost, and it works offline. The architectural consequence is that the guardrails, rate limiting, abuse monitoring and content policy a hosted API applies on the way in and out are simply absent, and nothing replaces them by default. Guardrails here are a control the device owner deploys on the request path, not a component the runtime ships — in the common install nothing sits on that path, and raw model output goes straight back to the caller.
The runtime is a local network service. It binds a port, speaks an HTTP API, and historically ships without authentication because the assumed caller is a process on the same machine. That assumption fails in two directions: any local process — including a browser tab, through a permissive CORS policy — can call it, and a runtime bound to a routable interface rather than loopback is reachable from the network. Who may bind the port and who may call it are the admission decisions of this architecture, and by default nobody makes them.
The supply chain is the axis specific to this archetype. Weights are large binaries fetched from public hubs, and several serialization formats execute code on load — the format matters more than the source, because a safe-by-construction tensor format from an unknown publisher beats a pickle-based one from a known publisher. Safe-by-construction has limits of its own: the formats that cannot execute on load are still opened by fast-moving native parsers whose memory bugs are a code-execution class of their own, and one popular format embeds chat templates that execute at inference time, past every static scan. The scan has to sit in front of the fetch, because the runtime is usually the thing doing the fetching.
There is no governance column, and that absence is the finding: no model inventory, no weight scanning pipeline, no policy on binding or sources exists anywhere in the default deployment. This runtime is installed by one person in an afternoon and appears in no inventory — every control named on this page presumes someone first learns it exists.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference in a datacentre: identical software, entirely different operational reality. There the runtime has a network policy, an identity, a scanner in the pipeline and someone on call. Here its port is protected by the assumption that nothing else on the machine is hostile.
Against the other endpoint archetypes: this one is not an agent. It has no loop, no tools and no autonomy — it is a dependency the others consume. It earns its own architecture because its risks are supply chain and local exposure rather than agency.

exemplars.name: Local inference servers
exemplars.note: Desktop applications and daemons that download open-weights models and expose an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API on a loopback port for other local software to call.

exemplars.name: OS and vendor-provided local runtimes
exemplars.note: Platform-level local inference offered as a system service, with a managed model catalogue. Narrower supply chain, same local-service exposure.

exemplars.name: Public model hubs
exemplars.note: Where the weights come from. Publisher identity is verifiable to varying degrees; what the artifact does on load is a property of its format, not its publisher.

blocks.title: Unexpected callers
blocks.note: Anything on the machine that can open a socket — including a browser tab, where the runtime allows cross-origin requests. Not the caller the API was designed for, and nothing tells them apart.

blocks.title: Local applications
blocks.note: The intended consumers: editors, agents and tools on the same machine, calling the local API instead of a hosted one — and often built expecting a hosted API's safety floor.

blocks.title: Local HTTP API
blocks.note: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on a local port, unauthenticated by design in the flagship runtimes — the vendors point at VPNs and reverse proxies rather than shipping auth. Which interface it binds and who may call it are this architecture's admission decisions, and exposure scans keep finding the runtimes that made neither.

items.label: Completion endpoint
items.note: The published local interface every consumer on the machine shares.

items.label: Interface binding
items.note: Loopback is an assumption, not a policy. Bound to a routable interface, the runtime is reachable from the network.

items.label: Cross-origin policy
items.note: A permissive CORS policy lets any web page the user visits drive local inference.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: Loads weights, batches requests, serves completions. Also the process that fetches the weights, which is why the supply-chain control has to sit in front of the fetch. Whatever safety behaviour exists is whatever the weights carry.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution — and where a malformed file in a "safe" format exercises the native parser, a different bug class with the same outcome.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts whose format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution — a more useful question than who published them.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Readable by any process with the user's privileges, and swappable by the same.

blocks.title: Public model hub
blocks.note: Distribution for open weights. Publisher identity ranges from verified to arbitrary, and neither transport security nor a signature says anything about what the artifact does when the runtime opens it.

items.label: Open-weights catalogue
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

edges.label: completion request
edges.note: Local software calls the local API the way it would a hosted one — usually assuming a safety floor that is not there.

edges.label: unauthenticated request
edges.note: The same endpoint, reached by callers nobody intended: a browser tab through CORS, or the network if the binding is routable. Locality is standing in for authorization.
Prompts in, raw completions back. Input and output classification is a control deployed on this path — in the common install it is a straight pipe.

edges.label: fetch / load
edges.note: The runtime fetches artifacts to disk and loads them at start. For several formats the load is an execution event, which makes this the supply chain's last step.

edges.label: weight download
edges.note: Transport is authenticated and the publisher may be verifiable. Neither says what the artifact does when opened.

risks.note: Pickle-class formats execute code on load. The risk is a property of the artifact format, not of the publisher.
Publisher identity at publish time, nothing at load time — and a hub account is a takeover target.
Any local process can saturate the runtime; a browser tab can do it from a web page.
The artifacts sit on disk with the user's file permissions — readable by anything running as the user.
Installed by one person in an afternoon, in no inventory. Responding to a bad model release presumes someone knows this runtime exists.
The serving stack itself is fast-moving native code with its own CVE history, running unsandboxed — and patched over an auto-update channel that is part of the attack surface.
Where this block is absent — the common case — raw model output goes straight to callers built expecting a hosted API's floor.
With no provider-side safety layer, whatever refusal behaviour the weights carry is the whole of the defence, and it is removable by fine-tune.

capabilities.note: Format and content inspection in front of the fetch — a scan that runs after the runtime opens the file has documented an incident, not prevented one.
Authenticate local callers rather than treating locality as authorization; a browser tab is local too.
Deploy the input and output classification a hosted API would have applied — nothing supplies it here by default.
Bound what any single caller can consume, because the callers share one unmetered port.
A device-enforced policy on whether local inference may run at all, from which sources, and bound to loopback only.
Restrictive file permissions and integrity checks on the artifacts, so a swap is detectable.
Which models, at which versions, from which sources, on which machines — the precondition for every response.
Find the runtimes nobody registered, derived from the machine rather than self-reported.
Evaluate what the weights actually do before serving them to other software — there is no provider evaluation to inherit.

scenarios.title: An application asks for a completion

steps.note: A local tool calls the OpenAI-compatible endpoint as if it were hosted.
The request crosses whatever classification the owner deployed — often none — and the model serves the completion with whatever behaviour the weights carry.
The response returns with no provider floor under it.

scenarios.title: A poisoned checkpoint

steps.note: A well-reviewed model name, a compromised artifact — the download verifies transport, not behaviour.
The runtime opens the file. In a pickle-class format the load is the execution event; in a safe format, a malformed header exercises the parser instead — either way, with the user's privileges.

scenarios.title: A browser tab finds the port

steps.note: A visited web page calls the local endpoint through a permissive cross-origin policy.
Nothing distinguishes this caller from the intended ones. The page now drives local inference — for free, and invisibly to the user.

deviations.subject: Guardrails are a control on the request path, not a block
deviations.reason: Input and output classification is something the device owner deploys, not a component of the runtime — so it is pinned as a numbered control on the API-to-runtime path rather than drawn as a service that does not exist in the common install.

archetypes.title: Open-source coding & desktop agents
summary: The same engine as the vendored coding agents without the vendor: an open-source harness a developer installs from a community registry and runs with their own keys. The interaction model is identical; what is missing is every control the vendor column supplied — session credentials, managed settings, audit export, an owner-bound remote relay — and nothing replaces them by default.
description:
Architecturally this is the vendored coding agent with the vendor service column deleted. The harness, the tool surface, the memory layer and the untrusted-content ingress are the same drawing; the differences are custody and supply chain. Credentials are pasted, long-lived keys that sit in plaintext configuration in most of the harnesses; governance is files on the same disk the agent can edit; and the binary itself arrives through community package registries and marketplaces — the category's landmark incident is a compromised harness release published with stolen publisher tokens.
The target state routes every model and remote call through an AI gateway the organisation operates — the credential broker that vaults the key the user would otherwise paste, the egress allowlist, the audit tap. The common state has nothing at that crossing: the harness calls the provider directly and the only record is the provider's bill. The gateway is drawn because this catalogue draws architectures as they should be built; the deviation records the distance.
Remote control exists here too, with a weaker admission model than the vendor products. The harnesses ship server modes — a listening port on the machine, localhost by default, with auth ranging from a mandatory shared secret down to none at all — plus official mobile clients over relay tunnels, and a fast-growing ecosystem of chat bridges that put messaging-platform identity in front of the loop. None of it binds admission to an owner account the way the vendor relays do, which is why the remote surface here is drawn with the same seriousness as the personal agent's channels.
There is no governance plane, and that absence is the finding: no managed settings tier, no session audit export, no admin toggle for the remote surface. Where enterprise controls exist for this category they are bolt-on — managed configuration paths and enterprise policy services a team must adopt deliberately — and the sanctioned posture is something the organisation publishes, not something the software ships.
distinguishedBy:
Against the vendored coding agents: the same loop, the same tool surface, the same human-present default. What changes is custody — pasted keys instead of expiring session credentials, community registries instead of signed vendor channels, bearer secrets and platform identity instead of an owner-bound relay — and the absence of any control plane an administrator could switch on.
Against the personal autonomous agent: this one is still invoked by a present developer and scoped to a workspace, with no heartbeat and no ambient senders. But the drift is real and one-directional — server modes, chat bridges, scheduled recipes — and a deployed OSS harness that listens on channels and runs unattended has become the personal agent and should be read on that page.

exemplars.name: Terminal harnesses
exemplars.note: The opencode/Crush class: TUIs over a client/server core, with headless serve modes and web surfaces. The most popular open-source agents, and the clearest expression of the pattern.

exemplars.name: IDE-extension harnesses
exemplars.note: The Cline family and its forks: marketplace-distributed extensions plus emerging standalone cores. The distribution channel is the marketplace — which is also the attack surface the category's worst incident used.

exemplars.name: Desktop and mobile-remote harnesses
exemplars.note: Goose-class agents with desktop apps, server binaries, scheduled recipes, and an official mobile client over a relay tunnel — the furthest drift toward the personal agent's shape, and the category's strongest remote-admission model.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The steering surfaces away from the machine — real in this category, with a weaker admission story than the vendor products: a serve port with optional or absent auth, a relay tunnel, or a chat bridge admitting whoever the platform admits. No owner account binds any of it; the controls are a mandatory secret, pinned transport, and an allowlist the operator maintains.

items.label: Phone & web apps
items.note: Web UIs served by the harness itself, and mobile clients reaching it over relay tunnels.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: Community bridges put messaging platforms in front of the loop — admission becomes platform identity, exactly the personal agent's model.

blocks.title: User
blocks.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate — the same posture as the vendored products, enforced by nothing but the harness's own permission prompts.

blocks.title: Repos, docs & screen
blocks.note: Everything the agent reads: repository content, documents, screenshots. Contributed to by people who are not the user, and read into context as though it were instruction.

items.label: Code & project docs
items.note: A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to.

items.label: Tool config dotfile
items.note: The tool-server declaration that ships with the code — and in this category, the rules and configuration files are the governance surface too.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The loop behind the terminal or editor, running as the user. The same engine as the vendored products — several of these harnesses began as forks or reimplementations of them — addressable remotely wherever its server mode is on.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides the next edit or command from the task and everything it has read so far.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the instruction, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: Local API server
items.note: The serve mode: a listening port, localhost by default, auth ranging from a mandatory shared secret to none. The remote surface, and the exposure scans' target.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: The converged cross-session layer: rules files and agent-written memory read back as instruction on the next task — repo-committed rules are authored by whoever last committed.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Agent-written notes and memory banks, loaded into later sessions as context.

items.label: Rules & instructions
items.note: The AGENTS.md-class files — user-level and repo-committed, portable across harnesses.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The action surface, running as the user on a machine that also holds their SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. Admission is configuration files on the same disk the agent can edit.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write across the working tree and the user's documents.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution with the user's full authority — the category default is bare-host.

items.label: Local & remote MCP
items.note: Local child processes with the user's privileges, and remote servers on standing grants.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions and helpers, increasingly shared across harnesses' skill directories.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Largely absent in this category — the vendor harnesses ship kernel sandboxes, the community ones mostly punt. The item is the target state.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The organisation-operated crossing that replaces the missing vendor column: the vault for the key the user would otherwise paste, deny-by-default egress, and the only audit trail this architecture can have. Target state — the common install calls the provider directly and leaves no record but the bill.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived provider credentials injected per call; the harness holds no key at rest.

items.label: Egress allowlist
items.note: Deny by default; providers, registries and remote tool servers each named explicitly.

items.label: Audit tap
items.note: Every crossing recorded as a side effect — nothing else in this architecture writes a log.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API, called on whatever credential the crossing supplies — or a local runtime standing in for it, which is this catalogue's local model runtime architecture.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The published interface. The completion it returns drives file writes and commands.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror of approved harnesses, extensions and skills — this architecture's supply chain includes the agent itself, and the community channels it ships through have already carried a compromised release. The private mirror moves the review; the risk stays until it happens.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: Harness releases, extensions and skills — reviewed, pinned and mirrored before installation.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the tool plane reaches over the network — and where fetched content comes back in as context indistinguishable from the user's instruction.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: Dependencies and their metadata, authored by strangers and read into context.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context, and the exfiltration path out.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Accounts reached through standing grants that outlive the conversation.

edges.label: task / approval
edges.note: The user states the task and answers the approval prompts — the same gate as the vendored products, with no managed tier able to make any of it non-overridable.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person, not at the keyboard — or, through a chat bridge, not necessarily the same person.

edges.label: serve port / relay / bridge
edges.note: Three shapes, one crossing: a direct connection to the harness's listening port, a relay tunnel the harness dials out to, or a chat bridge forwarding platform messages. Admission is a bearer secret at best — never an owner-bound account.

edges.label: read into context
edges.note: Repository content, documents and screenshots are read into context as instruction — and in this category the configuration that governs the agent ships the same way.
The loop writes what it learns and reads it back as instruction on the next task.

edges.label: model & remote calls
edges.note: The target-state crossing: brokered credentials, named destinations, a recorded call. The common state skips it entirely — a pasted key and a direct connection.

edges.label: model inference
edges.note: Inference on a brokered credential; the completion that returns is unauthenticated content.

edges.label: tool calls
edges.note: Tool calls out with whatever scope the harness's permission model granted; file contents and command output back into context.
Remote tool calls, package fetches and connector reads out; content authored by strangers back in as model input.

edges.label: installs & updates
edges.note: The install path for the harness, its extensions and its skills. In the common state this is a public marketplace on publisher self-attestation; the mirror is the target.

risks.note: Source files, manifests and documents are unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the user's instruction.
Memory files and rules are prose a later session treats as instruction — including rules committed by whoever last touched the repo.

A serve port with optional auth, a guessable bearer secret, or an over-broad chat allowlist hands the loop — and the machine behind it — to whoever finds it. The exposure-scan history of the neighbouring personal-agent category is the precedent.
The credential story: the key the gateway is meant to vault sits, in the common state, in plaintext configuration on disk — readable by the agent, its tools, and any repository script they run.
A binary anyone can install from a package manager, in no inventory, with no vendor tenancy to enumerate. Discovery is entirely the organisation's problem.
Configuration admits the whole tool plane, arrives with the clone, and is writable by the agent itself — governance and attack surface in the same files.
Local MCP servers and skills are third-party code running as the user.
The harness, its extensions and its skills all arrive through community channels on publisher self-attestation — and a compromised release of the harness itself has already shipped once.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives file writes and shell commands.
The approval gate is the harness's own prompt, with no managed tier behind it — one --yolo flag from being no gate at all.

capabilities.note: Vault the provider keys behind the gateway's broker — keychain-backed where the harness supports it, never plaintext in a dotfile a repository script can read.
Deny-by-default egress at the crossing: providers, registries and remote tool servers each named — the control the missing vendor column will never supply.
Spend ceilings at the crossing, because the only native meter is the provider's invoice.
The remote surface is admitted deliberately or not at all: mandatory shared secret, pinned transport, named allowlist — and off by default on any managed machine.
The standard permission gate between harness and tools — per-tool grants scoped to the working tree, configured outside the repository the agent works on.
The category ships bare-host by default: sanction the harnesses that support sandboxed execution, and treat its absence as a finding in harness selection.
Keep SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profiles outside the agent's reachable filesystem and environment.
Treat memory and rules as untrusted input on read; a repo-committed rules change is a code change.
Treat repository and document content as untrusted on read; it cannot be authenticated, only bounded.
Pin harness, extension and skill versions against the mirror; an update is a decision, because the update channel is the category's proven attack path.
Keep the approval gate real: dangerous-command detection on, auto-approve flags banned on managed machines, prompts rare enough to read.
Find the installs nobody registered — package-manager and process telemetry, not self-reporting.

scenarios.title: The user asks for a change

steps.note: The task is stated by a human who stays for the session.
The turn's model call crosses on a brokered credential — or, in the common state, does not cross here at all.
The completion returns and is treated as the plan.
Edits and commands execute with whatever scope the harness's permission model granted.
The diff comes back to the person who asked.

scenarios.title: A phone reaches the serve port

steps.note: The instruction is written on a phone, a web UI, or a chat thread.
Admission is whatever the deployment configured — a shared secret, a tunnel, a platform allowlist. Nothing checks that the sender is the owner.
Execution is local, with the machine's full context and the user's credentials around it.

scenarios.title: The harness updates itself

steps.note: A new release of the harness or one of its extensions is pulled — the supply chain's proven path.
The update loads into the process with everything the agent has — a compromised release is code execution as the user.

deviations.subject: No governance plane is drawn
deviations.reason: The category has none: no managed settings tier, no session audit export, no admin toggle. Where enterprise control exists it is bolt-on and adopted per team. The empty space beside this drawing is the finding, exactly as it is for the personal agent.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway is drawn although the common install lacks it
deviations.reason: This catalogue draws target states. The gateway is the organisation's replacement for the missing vendor column — key vault, egress policy, audit — and the common state, a pasted key calling the provider directly, is recorded here rather than drawn as a second model path.

deviations.subject: The package registry is drawn as this architecture's supply chain, not just the tools'
deviations.reason: The registry delivers the harness itself, its extensions and its skills. The category's landmark incident was a compromised harness release on a community channel, so the install edge carries the provenance risk and the pinning control.

archetypes.title: Personal autonomous agent
summary: An always-on daemon on a personal device that takes ambient messages from anyone who can reach its channels, runs an unattended agent loop with the user's own credentials, and keeps what it learns in files it will read back as instruction. Assembled by the user from a harness, wired-up tools and pasted-in keys — there is no vendor application wrapping it.
description:
The harness is a long-lived process, not an invocation. It owns the channel bridges, the agent loop, a heartbeat that fires with nobody watching, and a memory directory the next turn treats as context. Nothing about it is scoped to a task: it starts when the machine starts and ends when the user kills it.
Three default postures make this a distinct architecture rather than a variation on a coding assistant — each now exists as an opt-in feature over there, and is the resting state here. It listens — whoever can reach a bridge can address the agent, and the bridge is the authorization decision. It runs unattended — the heartbeat starts the loop with no human seeing the plan before the tools execute. And it remembers in a medium it re-reads as instruction — one successful injection written into memory survives restarts and re-executes on the schedule.
The target state wraps the harness whole. A microVM-class sandbox contains the daemon, its memory and a deliberately local tool surface — files, shell and skills, with their own kernel, filesystem, packages and network — and remote reach is pushed outside the boundary. The AI gateway is the general-purpose exit: deny-by-default egress for all outbound traffic, credentials injected at the crossing so the sandbox itself holds no secrets, and the audit tap. Remote MCP servers and external APIs sit behind the gateway as their own tool surface, and only they touch downstream services. Two other openings exist: a read-only pull from a private, organisation-maintained package registry, and the owner's workspace folders, shared into the sandbox explicitly and nothing else. The boundary is also what the approval prompts traded away — shipped sandboxes run the agent approval-free inside, on the position that isolation, egress policy and credential injection replace per-command consent. Products now ship exactly this wrap for the popular harnesses; the drawing is that pattern, vendor-neutral.
What the drawing still does not contain is a governance plane. No agent identity distinct from the user, no policy engine consulted per tool call, no audit sink beyond the gateway's tap, no kill switch beyond killing the process. The sandbox bounds the blast radius; it does not govern the agent.
distinguishedBy:
Against the coding and desktop agents: the capabilities have converged — those now take remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory too — so what separates the archetypes is defaults, identity and custody. There, each of those is opt-in, reaches the machine as an outbound relay only the owner's vendor account can address, and can be switched off from an admin console. Here, listening is the resting state, the sender set is whoever the messaging platform admits, the keys are long-lived and pasted in, and the whole thing is pieced together by the user with no console anyone can switch anything off from. The exposure scans still tell the story: personal gateways bind ports and get found by the tens of thousands; a vendor agent's remote channel opens no inbound port at all.
Against a cloud agent service: the same loop hosted by a provider gets an identity, a policy boundary, an audit trail and an administrator by default. Moving this architecture off the endpoint changes almost nothing about the loop and almost everything about the governance.

exemplars.name: OpenClaw
exemplars.note: The reference implementation of the pattern: a gateway daemon owning all state, channel bridges for a dozen messaging platforms, an embedded agent runtime, Markdown memory with a scheduled heartbeat, in-process skills from a public registry, and paired device nodes.

exemplars.name: Hermes Agent
exemplars.note: An independent implementation with a candid threat model, which states plainly that its deny rules guard against an honest-but-wrong agent rather than an adversarial one. Its self-improvement feature — the agent writing its own skills — is this archetype's persistence vector made into a product decision.

exemplars.name: Homegrown harnesses
exemplars.note: The long tail: a script, a messaging webhook, an API key in a dotfile, and cron. Structurally identical and considerably more common than either named project.

blocks.title: Unsolicited senders
blocks.note: Anyone who can reach a connected channel. On a public messaging network that is an unbounded set, and the message body is model input.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The owner's own surfaces: the messaging apps they address the agent through, and the gateway's control UI. Identity here is whatever the messaging platform asserts — the same channels everyone else uses, with no second factor — and the control UI is a real attacked surface, not an admin convenience.

items.label: Messaging apps
items.note: The owner instructs the agent over the same platforms unsolicited senders use.

items.label: Control UI
items.note: The gateway's own dashboard — the surface whose token-exfiltration flaw powered the exposed-instance scans.

blocks.title: Owner
blocks.note: The person the agent acts for, addressing it over the same channels as everyone else.

blocks.title: Channel bridges
blocks.note: One adapter per messaging platform, each implementing its own sender check. The count of channels is the count of independent authorization surfaces — disclosed bypasses in this archetype cluster in newly added bridges.

items.label: Channel adapters
items.note: Per-platform inbound and outbound message handling.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The local tool surface inside the sandbox — files, shell and skills only. No computer use and no MCP in here: remote transports live behind the gateway, and the device's GUI is out of the loop's reach by construction.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write on the sandbox's own filesystem and the mounted workspace folders — never the rest of the host.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution inside the sandbox. Package installs pull read-only from the private registry — the shell's one path off the machine.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Prose plus executable code loaded into the daemon's own process. A skill has whatever the agent has.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: One long-lived process that owns every piece of state: the loop that plans, calls tools and reads results back as context. Historically bound to all interfaces, which is how exposure scans found instances by the tens of thousands.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans, calls tools, reads the results back as context. Nobody reviews the plan.

items.label: Heartbeat
items.note: A periodic tick that starts the loop with no human present and re-reads the memory files. The mechanism that converts a one-time injection into a recurring one.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the message, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Cross-session plain-text files plus the embedded search over them. Written by the agent, read back as instruction on every subsequent turn including the unattended ones. This is the persistence primitive. It lives on the sandbox's own filesystem — surviving restarts, removed with the sandbox — so quarantine and memory wipe are the same operation.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Prose the next turn treats as instruction.

items.label: Search index
items.note: Retrieval over everything the agent has ever kept.

blocks.title: Owner workspace
blocks.note: The host folders the owner chooses to share into the sandbox — mounted at their real paths, and the only part of the host filesystem that exists in there. Direct mode mounts them read-write, so an edit is on the host the moment it is made; clone mode mounts them read-only and the agent works on a private copy whose changes return by git. The enterprise posture is clone mode.

items.label: Shared folders
items.note: Explicitly listed paths only. The home directory, keychains and dotfiles are not hidden from the agent — they are simply not there.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror of approved packages and skills — reachable read-only from the sandbox's install path, and nothing else. The common state is an open community marketplace where admission is publisher self-attestation; the provenance risk stays pinned here because a private mirror moves the review, it does not remove it.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: Reviewed, pinned and mirrored by the organisation before the agent can fetch them.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The egress proxy at the sandbox boundary, and the general-purpose exit. Deny-by-default for all outbound traffic, credentials injected into request headers at the crossing so the sandbox holds no secrets, and the audit tap on everything that leaves.

items.label: Egress allowlist
items.note: All outbound traffic denied by default, not just the web; models, tools, channels and registries each named explicitly.

items.label: Credential injection
items.note: Secrets stay in the host's keychain and are injected into headers at the proxy — inside the boundary the agent sees only placeholder values, so there is no key to read, log or exfiltrate.

items.label: Audit tap
items.note: Every crossing recorded as a side effect — the only audit trail this architecture has.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API, reached only through the gateway on an injected credential. Everything behind the published interface is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The published interface. The completion it returns drives the tool calls.

blocks.title: Remote tool services
blocks.note: The remote transports, kept outside the sandbox: MCP servers and external APIs the allowlist names. The sandbox reaches them only through the gateway, and only they touch downstream services.

items.label: Remote MCP
items.note: Remote servers on standing grants, admitted by configuration — their tool descriptions enter context as model input.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: External service calls on the agent's behalf, made with injected credentials.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the remote tools reach with the user's credentials — and where fetched content comes back in as context indistinguishable from the user's own words.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: The user's own mail, calendar and service accounts, reached with the user's own sessions.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context.

items.label: Paired devices
items.note: Companion devices exposing camera, screen and remote execution. The grant is to the harness — so it is also a grant to anything that has compromised the harness.

edges.label: unsolicited message
edges.note: Any party who can reach a channel can address the agent. The bridge is the admission decision.

edges.label: instruction / reply
edges.note: The owner writes on their own surfaces — the messaging apps, or the gateway's control UI. Everything after this crossing rides platform identity.
The bridge decides the sender is the owner from the messaging platform's own identifier — as strong as the platform makes it, with no second factor.
Normalised messages in; rendered replies out, to wherever the agent addresses them.
Local tool calls out, results back into context — files, shell and skills, all inside the sandbox.
The loop writes what it learns and reads it back as instruction on every later turn — including the unattended ones.

edges.label: model & egress calls
edges.note: Every call out of the sandbox crosses the boundary here, on a credential the gateway injects and against per-tool permissions checked at the crossing. The completion that comes back is unauthenticated content that drives tool calls.
Inference on an injected credential — reachable because the allowlist names it, and logged at the crossing.

edges.label: remote MCP & APIs
edges.note: The only route to remote transports. Admission is the allowlist; every call is logged and carries an injected, scoped credential.
Actions land on real accounts through the remote tools; whatever comes back re-enters the loop as context.

edges.label: read-only pull
edges.note: The install path: shell package pulls reach the private registry and nothing else, with no write permission in either direction.

edges.label: workspace mount
edges.note: The third opening. In direct mode a written file is a host file immediately — including files the host executes implicitly, like git hooks, CI configuration and IDE task definitions. Clone mode turns the crossing into a git fetch the owner performs.

risks.note: The message body is model input, from an unbounded set of senders.
Memory is prose the next turn treats as instruction. One injection that writes here survives restarts and re-executes on the heartbeat.
Fetched content re-enters the loop as context indistinguishable from the user's words.
Nothing registers the agent with anyone. Organisations discover these by scanning for them.
The heartbeat restarts the loop unattended; nothing bounds what a bad turn spends.
In the common deployment, credentials sit at rest inside the same blast radius as the code that reads them; the target state moves them behind the gateway's injection.
In the common state admission is publisher self-attestation, for artifacts that are prose plus code. The private mirror moves the review; the risk stays until it happens.
Bridges and skills are third-party code in one process.
The configuration admitting remote servers is agent-writable in most deployments, which makes tool registration a self-service operation for an attacker with code execution.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives the tool calls.
Unattended triggering, unscoped authority and no approval gate compound here.
Direct-mode edits land on the host as they happen. A modified git hook or CI file executes outside the boundary the sandbox was supposed to hold.
Replies go wherever the agent addresses them — not necessarily back to the sender who prompted the turn.

capabilities.note: Classify inbound content before it reaches the loop; treat every message as untrusted.
One sender-admission decision enforced for every bridge, not re-implemented per channel.
Credentials injected at the boundary, short-lived and scoped; nothing inside the sandbox holds a key at rest.
Treat memory as untrusted input on read; scope and review what gets written.
Per-tool grants on the local surface instead of the daemon's full authority.
Tool permissions evaluated at the boundary against the agent's identity — what this agent may call, per destination, decided outside the loop it governs.
Share named folders only, and prefer the read-only clone mode — the mount list is a permission grant on the host filesystem.

Wrap the harness whole — daemon, memory and local tools in one microVM-class boundary with its own kernel, filesystem and network, not a per-command box. This boundary is what makes approval-free unattended operation defensible at all.
Provenance and behavioural review before a remote server is admitted; pin what the allowlist names.
Deny-by-default egress at the boundary — models, tools, channels and registries each named — enforced outside the loop it contains.
The install path is scoped to one destination and read-only — no write permission, so a compromised loop can pull approved packages and nothing else.
A human approval gate on consequential actions, because no one saw the plan.
A stop that is not "find the process and kill it" — and that survives the heartbeat.

scenarios.title: A stranger messages the agent

steps.note: The message arrives from an unbounded set of senders. The allowlist is the gate.
The body enters the loop as model input.
The turn's model call crosses the boundary on an injected credential.
The model plans; the completion comes back and is treated as the plan.
Local tool calls execute inside the sandbox — no human sees the plan first.
Anything remote has to be on the allowlist, and crosses on an injected credential.
Actions land on real accounts; anything fetched re-enters as context.
The reply goes wherever the agent addresses it — not necessarily the surface that prompted the turn.

scenarios.title: The heartbeat fires with nobody watching

steps.note: The tick re-reads memory — including anything an attacker wrote there last week.
The unattended turn's calls cross the boundary like any other.
Recalled prose becomes the instruction for this turn.
The loop acts, unattended, inside the sandbox.
Edits reach the shared folders — in direct mode, that is the host, immediately.
A one-time injection has become a recurring implant — bounded now by the allowlist.

scenarios.title: A skill is installed

steps.note: The install is a shell command inside the sandbox.
The pull is read-only, and only the private registry is reachable.
The package was reviewed and mirrored first — but it still loads into the daemon's process with everything the agent has.

deviations.subject: The sandbox boundary is drawn as containment, not as a block
deviations.reason: The wrap-the-whole-harness product is a boundary around the daemon, its memory and its local tools, with the AI gateway as the general-purpose exit and a read-only registry pull as the only other opening. The React Flow view draws that frame literally; the SVG view shows the same blocks and edges without the enclosure.

deviations.subject: Remote transports are drawn as their own block outside the sandbox
deviations.reason: Remote MCP and external APIs are reachable only through the gateway, so they are drawn behind it as "Remote tool services" — the same transports the cloud architectures call Tool services — while the in-sandbox Tool services block keeps only the local surface: files, shell and skills. The shipped products document the caveat this drawing encodes: a local stdio MCP server runs on the host with host permissions, outside the boundary, which is why the target state admits remote transports only behind the gateway.

deviations.subject: The workspace mount is drawn as a third opening
deviations.reason: Shipped sandboxes share the owner's chosen folders into the microVM, read-write by default. That crossing is real attack surface — a direct-mode edit to a file the host executes implicitly leaves the boundary without ever touching the gateway — so the drawing refuses the fiction of a two-opening sandbox.

deviations.subject: The registry pull is drawn from Tool services, not the harness
deviations.reason: Installs happen through shell commands, so the drawing runs the read-only pull from the tool surface that executes them; the grant belongs to the agent either way.

deviations.subject: No governance plane is drawn
deviations.reason: This archetype has none — no agent identity, no policy engine, no audit sink, no registry, no kill switch. The sandbox products have begun selling one — centrally managed policies over a fleet's network, filesystem and tool access — but that plane governs the sandbox, not the agent, and the archetype as assembled still has nothing. The other architectures in this catalogue draw a governance column; the empty space where it would be is this diagram's finding, and inventing one would misrepresent the pattern.
