archetypes.title: Enterprise AI chat with connectors
summary: A general-purpose assistant subscription for the workforce, where each user connects their own data sources and uploads their own files. The grant model is per user and per connector, which makes the organisation's total exposure a sum nobody computes.
description:
The contrast with a tenant-wide assistant is entirely in who consents. There, an administrator grants the vendor the corpus once. Here, each user authorises their own connectors — a repository, a drive, a ticket system — and the organisation's data path to the vendor is the union of thousands of individual decisions, each made in a modal dialog. Any single grant is usually appropriate; what nobody has is the aggregate, which makes the archetype's core problem visibility rather than permission.
File upload is the parallel path and often the larger one. A user pasting a document into a chat window has moved data across the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record beyond what inspection catches. Every control that watches connectors misses this entirely, which is why in-browser and network inspection carry more weight here than the vendor's own administrative surface does.
The remaining structural question is the boundary between the enterprise tenant and the consumer product. The same vendor typically offers both, the consumer one has different retention and training terms, and the difference between being in your tenant and being signed into a personal account is a session cookie. Tenant restriction enforced at the edge is what makes the enterprise agreement — retention limits, training opt-out, audit export — apply to the traffic at all.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide assistant: administrator-granted and corpus-wide there, user-granted and connector-by-connector here. That single difference relocates the control set from permissions governance to discovery and aggregate visibility.
Against shadow AI: this is the sanctioned version of the same traffic. The sanctioned tenant is where you want the traffic to go, and most of the work in this archetype is making sure it does.

exemplars.name: Enterprise assistant subscriptions
exemplars.note: Workforce-wide licences for a general assistant, with administrative controls over retention, training and which connectors may be enabled.

exemplars.name: Per-user connector catalogues
exemplars.note: Marketplaces of source connectors each user authorises for themselves, typically over OAuth, with the vendor holding the resulting grant.

blocks.title: Employee
blocks.note: Authorises their own connectors and uploads their own files. Every grant reasonable, the aggregate visible to nobody.

blocks.title: Chat surface & uploads
blocks.note: The browser tab or desktop client — the last point where the prompt, the attachment and the tenant it is going to are all visible to something the organisation operates.

items.label: Browser / client
items.note: The vendor's interface on your device. Which tenant a session lands in is decided by a cookie, and visible here.

items.label: File upload
items.note: The path no connector governance sees. A pasted document crosses with no grant, no scope and no record other than what inspection catches.

blocks.title: Identity & secure edge
blocks.note: Tenant assertion and inline inspection — the block doing most of the real work in this archetype, because the vendor's admin console cannot see traffic that never reached the managed tenant.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Establishes the user and, critically, which tenant they are in. Tenant restriction here is what stops the consumer product being an alternative.

items.label: Secure service edge
items.note: Inline inspection of prompts and uploads, and the enforcement point for which tenants and services are reachable.

blocks.title: Consumer product
blocks.note: The same vendor's unmanaged offering, reachable from the same browser with a personal login. Different retention terms, no administrative visibility, one cookie away.

items.label: Personal accounts
items.note: Authenticated to the provider and anonymous to the organisation. None of the enterprise terms apply to anything sent here.

blocks.title: Vendor chat service
blocks.note: Inference, conversation storage and the connector broker are all behind the published surfaces — only the interfaces you integrate with are drawn.

items.label: Managed tenant API
items.note: Where enterprise terms apply — retention, training opt-out, audit export. Everything the agreement promises depends on traffic arriving here.

items.label: Connector broker
items.note: Holds the OAuth grants users issued and calls their systems on their behalf — now including custom remote MCP servers where an owner admits them. The grants persist after the conversation, the project and the employee.

items.label: Agent modes
items.note: The assistants are agents now: multi-step work across connectors, scheduled tasks, code execution and computer use, running on the vendor's infrastructure. Write actions are admin-gated per app and per action — where an administrator gated them.

items.label: Tenant configuration
items.note: Retention, training opt-out, connector allowlist, history export. Set once and rarely revisited against a product that ships new connectors.

blocks.title: User-connected systems
blocks.note: Repositories, drives and trackers, each authorised by an individual. Their union is the organisation's actual data path to the vendor — and retrieval is only as safe as the source permissions, because an assistant makes pre-existing oversharing instantly discoverable.

items.label: Repos, drives & trackers
items.note: Reached as the user who consented — correct as access control, invisible to anyone trying to see the total.

items.label: Content authored elsewhere
items.note: Tickets and documents written by people outside the conversation, entering it as context through a grant one employee made.

blocks.title: Tenant governance
blocks.note: Tenant configuration you author, plus the discovery and inspection you run independently of the vendor — the half that covers uploads and the consumer tenant, which no vendor export ever will.

items.label: Tenant policy
items.note: Retention, training opt-out, which connectors are permitted. Re-review whenever the vendor ships a connector — the default for new ones is rarely off.

items.label: Connector inventory
items.note: Which sources are connected, by how many people, holding what classification — the aggregate no individual grant decision produces.

items.label: Shadow use discovery
items.note: Finding traffic to the consumer product and competing tools, independent of the vendor. Usually surfaces more data movement than the sanctioned tenant does.

items.label: Audit & detection
items.note: Vendor export plus first-party network and browser telemetry — the second part covers what the first cannot see.

edges.label: prompt & attachment
edges.note: Prompts and pasted files go in; responses render back into the browser as unauthenticated content.
The prompt and the upload are inspected here or nowhere. Connector governance does not see uploads, and the vendor's console sees them only after they have arrived.

edges.label: to the corporate tenant
edges.note: Authenticated into the managed tenant, where retention and training terms apply. Everything the enterprise agreement promises depends on the traffic arriving here.

edges.label: blocked or logged
edges.note: Where tenant restriction is absent this crossing simply succeeds, and none of the enterprise terms apply to anything that goes through it.

edges.label: connector retrieval / actions
edges.note: The broker calls each system as the user who consented, on a standing OAuth grant scoped to a whole system rather than a task — retrieved content enters the conversation as context, and in the agent modes the same grants carry write actions back out: mail sent, files changed, tickets moved, mid-conversation.

edges.label: configure / enumerate / export
edges.note: Tenant policy goes down; grant enumeration and audit export come back — all of it dependent on the vendor exposing per-user grants and events to an administrator.

risks.note: A pasted document crosses the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record. Every control that watches connectors misses this path entirely.
The consumer version of the same product is one login away and carries none of the enterprise terms.
Consumer retention and training terms apply to whatever lands here, with no administrative visibility of the account even existing.
Thousands of individually appropriate consents whose union nobody computed — the organisation's data path assembled one modal dialog at a time.

Content authored elsewhere arrives through connectors as conversation context — and the documented incident class is zero-click: a crafted mail or document steers the assistant into exfiltrating over rendered links, images, or the vendor's own service-side fetches, with the user never clicking anything.

The agent modes act through the same standing grants retrieval uses. A steered assistant with a write-capable connector is an actor, not a search box — and the approval semantics live in the vendor's UI, not yours.
The broker's OAuth grants outlive the conversation, the project and the employee who issued them.
What the vendor retains, retrieves and trains on per conversation is governed by configuration and contract, not by anything observable.
Responses are unauthenticated content rendered into a browser.

capabilities.note: Inline inspection plus tenant restriction — the control doing most of the real work, because it covers both connectors' blind spots: uploads and the consumer product.
Assert which tenant each user may reach and who is licensed; tenant restriction here is what makes the enterprise terms apply.
Inspect prompts and uploads in flight — the only record the upload path will ever produce.
In-browser visibility of which tenant a session is in and what is being pasted — the vantage the vendor cannot offer.
Block or log the consumer tenant at the edge; without enforcement the crossing simply succeeds.
Find the personal-account and competitor traffic that never touches the managed tenant — it is usually the larger flow.
Own tenant configuration as living policy — retention, training opt-out, connector allowlist — re-reviewed every time the vendor ships a connector.
Treat standing OAuth grants as non-human identities — inventoried, expiring, and revoked when the employee or project goes.
Admin-gate the write-capable connectors and agent modes, and require per-action confirmation on writes — the vendor ships the toggles; leaving them at default is the decision not to use them.
Govern by classification which systems may be connected at all, so individual consent cannot outrun policy.
Fuse the vendor's export with first-party edge and browser telemetry — only the combination covers uploads and the consumer tenant.
Treat connector-retrieved content as untrusted input in policy and user guidance — the vendor's guardrails are the only inline control.
Know what sensitive data sits in the systems users are connecting, before the grants aggregate it.

scenarios.title: A prompt with an attachment

steps.note: A document is pasted into the chat — no connector, no grant, no record yet.
Inspection happens here or nowhere.
The traffic lands in the managed tenant, where retention and training terms actually apply.
The response returns and is rendered as unauthenticated content.

scenarios.title: One cookie away

steps.note: The same browser, but a personal login to the same vendor's consumer product.
The session looks almost identical; only tenant-aware inspection can tell the difference.
With tenant restriction, this is blocked or logged. Without it, corporate data leaves under consumer retention and training terms, invisibly.

scenarios.title: A connector grant outlives its project

steps.note: The broker keeps retrieving on a standing OAuth grant issued for a project that ended a year ago.
Grant enumeration surfaces the aggregate — which systems, how many people, what classification — and stale grants are revoked.

archetypes.title: UI/low-code managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor platform where non-engineers assemble agents from prompts, connectors and triggers. The agents are real, the authors are not engineers, and there is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data.
description:
The builder is a self-service surface, and that is both the product and the problem. A business user can create an agent, grant it connectors, give it a trigger and publish it to colleagues without any of the checkpoints a software delivery pipeline would impose — no pull request, no staged rollout, no security sign-off unless the platform enforces one. The result is a population problem rather than an instance problem: individual agents are simple; the risk is four hundred of them, each with connector grants, each authored by someone who has left, and no way to list which reach customer data.
Credential inheritance is the specific technical trap. A low-code agent typically runs on connections authorised by its author, so a published agent lends its author's access to every colleague who uses it. A user who could not read a table directly can often read it through an agent someone else built, and neither party intended that. Whether the platform supports per-invoker authorisation rather than author-credential execution is the single question worth asking during evaluation.
The authoring surface is also an injection surface: instructions, knowledge sources and connector descriptions are assembled by someone who is not thinking about untrusted input, and a shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to. Because no sandbox or runtime enforcement can be inserted into a vendor's execution, every control drawn here is a population control — inventory, publication gating, connector policy, and audit that can retire what nobody uses.
distinguishedBy:
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: same hosting model, different author. There engineers define agents in code and the delivery pipeline still applies; here the builder UI replaces that pipeline with a publish button, and the unit of concern moves from the definition of one agent to the governance of a population.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: same intent — a paved road for many builders — with the paving done by a vendor. You inherit their guardrails and their environment model, and you cannot add a deployment gate they did not build.

exemplars.name: Suite-embedded agent builders
exemplars.note: Low-code agent authoring bundled with a productivity or CRM suite, available to any licensed user by default unless an administrator turns it off.

exemplars.name: Standalone agent-building platforms
exemplars.note: Vendor platforms whose product is the builder itself, with connector marketplaces and publication to internal or external audiences.

blocks.title: Citizen builder
blocks.note: Authors the instructions, attaches the connectors, and publishes. Not operating under code review, and frequently no longer at the company by the time the agent matters.

blocks.title: Agent consumers
blocks.note: Colleagues — and sometimes customers — using an agent built by someone else. Rarely aware of whose credentials it runs on.

blocks.title: Identity & entitlements
blocks.note: Authenticates builders and consumers, and restricts who may build at all — the bluntest and often most effective population control. Whether the consumer's identity, rather than the author's, reaches the connector is the archetype's decisive question.

items.label: User authentication
items.note: Builders and consumers both arrive here. Building typically requires no elevated role — the same permission as opening a document.

items.label: Invoker credentials
items.note: Per-invoker authorisation preserves the access model the organisation already has; author-credential execution bypasses it by publishing.

items.label: Agent identities
items.note: The platforms now mint a directory principal per agent — the hook that lets conditional access, DLP and revocation attach to one agent instead of the whole population.

blocks.title: Attached knowledge
blocks.note: Folders, sites and documents attached to an agent as grounding. Often writable by more people than the agent's audience, which turns a shared drive into an instruction channel.

items.label: Grounding sources
items.note: Whoever can write to the attached folder writes instructions the agent will follow for every one of its users.

blocks.title: Agent builder platform
blocks.note: Authoring, hosting and execution are all the vendor's — only the published surfaces are drawn, and no deployment gate can be added that the vendor did not build.

items.label: Authoring surface
items.note: Prompt, connectors, triggers, publication — every one a security decision made by someone who was not asked to make one.

items.label: Agent runtime
items.note: Where the population of agents executes. One diagram stands for hundreds of near-identical instances — and on several platforms agents discover and call each other by default, so one steered agent borrows a teammate's stronger connectors.

items.label: Connector framework
items.note: The vendor's integration layer. Its authorisation model — author or invoker credentials — decides whether publishing an agent is also a privilege grant.

blocks.title: Connected systems
blocks.note: Whatever the connectors reach. The union across all published agents is the platform's real data footprint, and no single agent's author can see it.

items.label: Business data
items.note: Tables, files and records reached by agents nobody reviewed.

items.label: Mail & action paths
items.note: Connectors that send and write. A source of confidential data plus a path to send mail is the pairing worth banning outright.

blocks.title: Maker governance
blocks.note: Population management — who may build, what may be published, what is connected, and what can be revoked at once. Every control here is per-population, because reviewing individual agents does not scale to self-service creation. The vendors now sell this column as a product too — fleet-level agent control planes — which changes the work from building it to configuring it.

items.label: Agent inventory
items.note: Every agent, its author, its connectors, its audience and its last use. The one control that makes the population tractable.

items.label: Publication gate
items.note: Review before an agent reaches an audience beyond its author — the nearest available thing to code review, if the platform offers it and it is turned on.

items.label: Connector policy
items.note: Which connectors may be combined and which environments allow publication. Blocking a pairing scales where reviewing agents does not — and check the enforcement default: some platforms enforce centrally out of the box, others ship policy soft-enabled, where makers never feel it.

items.label: Usage audit
items.note: Which agents ran, for whom, reaching what — the basis for retiring the ones nobody uses.

edges.label: authors & publishes
edges.note: Building an agent typically requires no elevated role. The permission to create something that acts on company data is the same permission as opening a document.

edges.label: uses a published agent
edges.note: The consumer authenticates to the platform. Whether that identity continues to the connector, or is replaced by the author's, decides whether the access model holds.
Authoring sessions and agent invocations both flow here — authenticated, but nothing about authentication says anyone reviewed what was built.

edges.label: grounding content
edges.note: Attached knowledge enters agent context as instruction. The write permissions on the source folder are the only gate, and they were never designed as one.

edges.label: connector read / write
edges.note: The archetype's decisive crossing. Author-delegated grants lend the author's access to every user; invoker-delegated grants preserve the access model the organisation already has.

edges.label: inventory / gate / run history
edges.note: Admission, publication review and connector policy go down; enumeration and run history come back. All of it is platform-reported — adequate here, because there is no way to build an agent off-platform.

risks.note: An agent running on its author's credentials lends that access to every colleague who invokes it — publishing becomes a privilege grant nobody intended.
Agents with write connectors act on production data with no review between authoring and effect.

Creation is self-service and retirement is nobody's job. The population grows by default, and organisations discover it by counting — including the sharing modes that publish an agent to anyone with the link, on the vendor's own domain, where exposure research keeps finding them by the thousands.
Each connector grant is defensible alone; the union across hundreds of agents authored by people who never met is nobody's decision and nobody's picture.
A shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to — an instruction channel wearing a grounding label.
Grounding sources are attacker-writable at the fidelity of ordinary file permissions, and poisoned content persists across every future invocation.
Grants authorised by a departed author keep executing for everyone still using the agent.
Agents and their connector grants outlive their projects and their authors; only inventory and usage audit notice.

capabilities.note: Build the inventory first — every agent, author, connector set, audience and last use. Every other population control depends on it.
Restrict who may build, and demand per-invoker authorisation so a published agent cannot lend its author's access.
Author connector policy — which connectors may combine, which environments may publish. Banning a pairing scales where per-agent review cannot.
Turn on the publication gate so review stands between an author and an audience — the nearest available thing to code review.
Treat every connection an agent holds as a managed non-human identity — owned, scoped, expiring, and revocable as a class.
Govern what connectors may reach by classification, so the platform's aggregate footprint is a decision rather than an accident.
Treat grounding sources as untrusted input; restrict attachable locations to ones with governed write access.
Run maker governance as a programme — environments, licensing, lifecycle and ownership transfer when authors leave.
Find the sensitive data inside connector reach before four hundred agents do.
Keep run history per agent and per consumer — the basis for retiring what nobody uses and investigating what someone did.
Assess the platform vendor's execution, isolation and guardrail claims — none of them are testable from your side.

scenarios.title: An afternoon's agent reaches production data

steps.note: A business user signs in with the same role they use to open documents.
Prompt written, connectors attached on the author's own grants, trigger set, published to the team.
The publication gate reviews it — if the platform offers one and an administrator turned it on.
A colleague invokes the shared agent.
The connector executes on the author's credentials — the consumer just read a table they were never entitled to.

scenarios.title: A shared drive becomes an instruction channel

steps.note: Someone writes a document with embedded instructions into the folder an agent uses as grounding.
The injected instruction exercises the agent's connectors — reading what it can reach, sending what it can send.
Retrieved data flows back into the agent's response, for every user who asks.

scenarios.title: The author leaves

steps.note: Inventory shows agents whose author has departed — still published, still triggered, still holding grants.
Author-delegated connections keep executing until ownership is transferred or the grants are revoked as a class.

archetypes.title: API/SDK managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor's API-driven hosted agent service: the loop, the memory, the sandbox and the tool gateway supplied as published, separately billed products, driven through an SDK or API rather than a builder UI. The customer owns the front end, the agent definitions, the tools admitted, the identities and the audit export. The governance plane arrives built in, and the trade is that it is configured rather than designed.
description:
Every provider converged on the same decomposition: a runtime, a memory service, a tool gateway, an identity service, a code interpreter and browser, observability, evaluation and policy. That convergence is itself the finding — the governance plane most self-built agent architectures never get is exactly what these services sell. The provider blocks on this diagram are drawn because they are documented, separately addressable products, not inferred internals; the loop's execution behind them remains genuinely uninspectable.
The consequential choice is between the managed harness and the code escape hatch. Every provider offers both: a declarative agent whose loop they run, and a bring-your-own-code runtime where they supply the sandbox and the identity but the loop is the customer's. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams routinely start with the first, hit a limitation, move to the second, and do not notice which controls stopped applying.
Managed memory is the component most likely to be switched on without a decision. Its scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence, and cross-user scope means one user's content can shape another's turn.
The genuine advantage is agent identity: first-class, revocable principals distinct from the service and from the user, supplied as a service. Using them properly — rather than collapsing everything onto one service principal — is most of what separates a well-governed deployment from a poorly governed one on the same platform. The costs are portability and opacity: the policy language moves to no other provider, and debugging a misbehaviour means reading traces rather than code.
distinguishedBy:
Against building the agent tier: the same components with the provider supplying them. The work moves from designing an identity model, a policy engine and a sandbox to configuring three, and from having to build observability to having to export it.
Against the UI/low-code managed agent runtime: same hosting model, different author. Here engineers define agents in code against an SDK or API, and the software-delivery pipeline — review, versioning, staged rollout — still applies to the definition even though the loop is the vendor's. The low-code sibling replaces that pipeline with a builder UI and a publish button, which moves the risk from the definition to the population.

exemplars.name: Frontier-lab managed agent APIs
exemplars.note: Agent runtimes operated by the model vendor and driven entirely through an API — a hosted loop with a managed sandbox, invoked by the customer's code, with sessions and memory as API resources.

exemplars.name: Hosted background coding agents
exemplars.note: Vendor-run remote agents that take a task and a repository grant and work unattended in the vendor's environment, reporting back as pull requests or session transcripts.

exemplars.name: Hyperscaler agent runtimes
exemplars.note: Managed agent services decomposed into runtime, memory, gateway, identity, sandbox, observability, evaluation and policy, billed per component and driven through SDKs.

exemplars.name: Managed harness with a code escape hatch
exemplars.note: A declarative agent the provider runs, alongside a bring-your-own-code runtime for cases the declarative form cannot express. The pair is now standard across providers.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: Whose identity should reach the tool call, rather than being replaced by the agent's along the way.

blocks.title: Agent definition & code
blocks.note: The deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do — instructions, tool configuration, or the customer's own loop code. Treating it with less rigour than application code is common and unwarranted.

items.label: Declarative definition
items.note: Instructions and tool bindings the provider's harness runs, inheriting platform guardrails automatically.

items.label: Custom loop code
items.note: The escape hatch. It inherits only the controls it explicitly calls.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The customer's surface, where the user's identity is established — and where output handling still belongs, because only the application knows where the text will land.

items.label: App & API surface
items.note: The published entry point users and systems call.

items.label: User identity
items.note: Established here and carried into the runtime, or the agent acts as itself for everyone.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The hosted loop, invoked and configured through published interfaces; the execution itself is not inspectable. Provider code in the path, released on the provider's schedule, with the customer's agent inside it.

items.label: Runtime API
items.note: Where agents are invoked and sessions managed — the published surface over an unreadable loop.

items.label: Declarative harness
items.note: The provider runs the loop and applies guardrails automatically.

items.label: Custom-code runtime
items.note: The customer's loop in the provider's container — sandbox and identity supplied, guardrails only on request.

blocks.title: Managed memory
blocks.note: A documented, separately billed memory service whose scope — session, user or cross-user — is selected by configuration. Cross-user scope means one user's content reaches another's turn, and it is a flag rather than a design review.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: What the agent keeps between turns and reads back as context.

items.label: Scope configuration
items.note: The whole control, in one flag.

blocks.title: Managed sandbox
blocks.note: Code interpreter and hosted browser, isolated by the provider. Among the strongest reasons to choose a managed runtime over building the tier — and the isolation guarantee is a vendor claim the customer cannot test. The direction of travel is hybrid: providers now offer sandboxes and even runtime compute that live in the customer's own perimeter, trading the untestable claim for operational ownership.

items.label: Code interpreter
items.note: Generated code runs here, not in the application's process.

items.label: Hosted browser
items.note: Web content is fetched and rendered inside the provider's isolation.

blocks.title: Managed tool gateway
blocks.note: The provider's brokered path to tools and MCP servers, with scoping and logging supplied. Reached automatically by a declarative agent and only on request by custom code — the asymmetry deployments most often lose coverage to.

items.label: Scoped tool brokering
items.note: Per-tool grants under the agent's own identity, not a service-wide credential — with user tokens held in the platform's vault and exchanged on the user's behalf, never pasted into configuration.

items.label: MCP & connectors
items.note: The tool population the customer admits — the part of the tool plane the customer owns.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The records the agent acts on under grants the customer issues, and the external content it reads — which comes back as context nothing has authenticated.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Reached under grants issued to the platform, ideally per tool and per agent.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Documents and pages the agent reads; the platform's guardrails see it, nothing vouches for it.

blocks.title: Customer governance
blocks.note: The controls the customer owns on a platform the provider operates: agent identities, tool and agent admission, policy and guardrail configuration, evaluation gates, and the audit export that keeps the trail out of the provider's console alone.

items.label: Agent identities
items.note: A first-class, revocable principal per agent — supplied by the platform and frequently collapsed back into one shared principal by teams who do not use it.

items.label: Agent & tool admission
items.note: Which definitions may deploy and which tools may be offered. Admission, not discovery.

items.label: Policy & guardrail config
items.note: Authored by the customer, enforced by the provider inside a loop the customer cannot see. Where enforcement sits is the evaluation question: the strongest platforms enforce default-deny policy and guardrails at the tool gateway, outside agent code, with floor settings a builder cannot lower — on others the guardrails are code the builder must remember to call.

items.label: Evaluation gates
items.note: An agent definition that has not faced adversarial input should not reach a production alias.

items.label: Audit export
items.note: Traces exported out of the provider's console, so they can be correlated with everything else.

edges.label: request / response
edges.note: The user's identity is established here and must be carried the rest of the way, or per-user authorization silently becomes a service-wide grant.

edges.label: invoke agent
edges.note: Two identities on one call — the application's and the user it acts for. Dropping the second is the confused-deputy failure this architecture makes easy to avoid and easy to commit.

edges.label: deploy
edges.note: An agent definition is a deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do. It deserves the same review, gating and provenance as application code.

edges.label: session & memory
edges.note: The scope flag on this edge is the whole control. Cross-user scope is a supported configuration whose consequence is one user's content shaping another's turn.

edges.label: code & browsing
edges.note: Generated code and web rendering go to provider-operated isolation rather than anywhere nearer the data.
Automatic for a declarative agent, opt-in for custom code. The controls on this edge are the ones the escape hatch silently drops.

edges.label: tool calls / content
edges.note: Actions land on customer systems under per-tool grants; whatever is read comes back as context indistinguishable from instruction.

edges.label: identity & admission
edges.note: Per-agent principals and the admitted tool list are applied here — where the managed identity earns its place, and where one shared principal undoes it.

edges.label: scope configuration
edges.note: Memory scope is decided here as a reviewed policy choice, not left as a default.

risks.note: Three identities are in play — the application's, the user's and the agent's — and the failure is collapsing them into one.
A managed runtime makes agents cheap to create, so the population grows faster than the inventory.
The runtime, its memory, its gateway and its sandbox are the provider's code in the path, released on the provider's schedule.
The loop is not inspectable; traces are the only window, and they only exist where the platform emits them.
Cross-user memory scope puts one user's content in another user's turn, selected by a configuration flag.
Content read through tools re-enters the loop as context; the platform's guardrails see it, nothing authenticates it.
Consequential writes on customer systems from a loop nobody watches, bounded only by the grants and policy the customer configured.
Revocable per-agent principals only help if revocation actually happens when agents are retired or repurposed.
The admitted tool list programs the agents; whoever writes it decides what every agent can be made to do.
The runtime's response is unauthenticated content, and only the application knows whether it is about to be rendered or executed.

capabilities.note: Use the platform's per-agent identities — distinct, revocable principals — instead of collapsing every agent onto one service principal.
Establish the user's identity here and propagate it to the tool call, so authorization stays per-user.
The standard permission gate between harness and tools: per-tool, per-agent grants enforced at the gateway, not a standing credential shared by everything.
Admit and inventory agent definitions like deployable code, because that is what they are.
Verify guardrail coverage on the custom-code path explicitly — declarative agents get it free, the escape hatch does not.
Set memory scope per session or per user as a reviewed decision; treat cross-user scope as a design exception.
Author the platform's per-invocation policy through governed intake and configuration — the customer's half of the shared-responsibility shape, enforced by the provider inside the loop.
Traces of steps, tool calls and decisions are the only window into an unreadable loop; turn all of it on.
Export the trail — a trace that lives only in the provider's console cannot be correlated with anything else.
Gate every definition change behind adversarial evaluation before it reaches a production alias.
Keep code execution and browsing on the provider's isolated path — and assure the isolation claim the way any critical vendor control is assured, because it cannot be tested from your side.

scenarios.title: A user's request becomes a tool call

steps.note: The user's identity is established at the customer's own surface.
The invocation carries two identities — the application's and the user's.
The loop plans; the tool call leaves under the agent's own principal, scoped per tool.
The action lands on customer systems under the grant the customer issued.
Whatever was read returns as context nothing has authenticated.
The response comes back; output handling is still the application's job.

scenarios.title: A team takes the code escape hatch

steps.note: The declarative definition is replaced with custom loop code after hitting a limitation.
Tool brokering now happens only if the code calls the gateway — nothing routes it there automatically.
The guardrails and scoping the declarative harness applied for free now apply only where the code asks. Nobody notices which controls stopped.

scenarios.title: Memory scope crosses users

steps.note: User A's turn runs, and the agent writes what it learned.
The write lands in a store whose scope flag was left at a shared default.
User B's turn reads it back as context — one user's content shaping another's session, looking like a feature.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the architecture where the agent writes: a request arrives, a decision happens, and an effect lands on a system of record in seconds with nobody between them. The organisation's requirements therefore centre on reversibility rather than accuracy — the review question for every design is not "how often is it right" but "what happens when it is wrong, and who can undo it, and how fast."

The requirements below assume the multi-agent workflow's guidance as a sibling: each subagent there is this pattern one level down, and everything here applies inside every one of them. What this pattern adds is the concentrated question of a single fast path — the action catalogue, the approval threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight a human carries in the chat pattern and durability machinery carries in the workflow pattern.

items.title: Make the action catalogue the policy surface — no arbitrary calls
body: Require a deterministic catalogue: named, parameter-validated actions, each declaring its blast radius and its compensating transaction. An agent that can compose arbitrary API calls has no policy surface at all — reject that design in review, whatever the framework makes convenient. Enforcement is per invocation, outside the loop: this action, this record, this value, now — evaluated by a policy engine the agent cannot edit, not a session-time grant. Evidence: the catalogue definition, and a denied-call log showing the bounds actually fire.

items.title: Tie approval to consequence, and reversal to everything else
body: The approval threshold is keyed to irreversibility and value, never to model confidence — and it must be rare enough that a human actually reads what fires. Below the threshold, the control is the compensating transaction: an action with no reversal path does not belong in the catalogue below the gate. Assessment probe: list the catalogue's actions and demand the compensating transaction for each; any blank cell below the threshold fails the review.

items.title: Give the agent an identity, and broker every credential
body: A distinct, revocable workload identity per agent — actions taken as a shared service account are neither attributable nor separately revocable, and turn every incident response into a full-service outage. The agent tier holds no standing keys: model and tool credentials are brokered at the gateway per call, short-lived and scoped. Assessment probe: revoke the agent's identity and confirm the loop stops without touching any other service.

items.title: Scope what the loop reads, because the requester is the attacker
body: The request text is authored by the party who benefits from the outcome, and record content written months earlier re-enters as context — both are injection paths with a short path to money. Classify inbound text before the loop, scope retrieval to the account under discussion rather than to what the service can reach, and keep case memory hard-scoped to one case. Assessment probe: a request against account A that attempts to retrieve account B's records into context.

items.title: Bound the spend, the destinations, and the time to stop
body: Rate and budget ceilings sit at the gateway, sized for a loop that retries in seconds; the write path reaches named destinations only, because unbounded egress is the exfiltration channel a steered agent looks for. The decision audit records action, reasoning, inputs and identity where the agent can append and cannot amend — the basis for reversal and dispute. And the stop must halt the agent and revoke its identity without a deploy, because the loop acts faster than a pipeline ships.

AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens — bounded autonomy and human oversight
CoSAI Shared Responsibility Framework V1.0 — autonomy levels and intervention tiers

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the pattern most organisations mean by "hosting agents": a durable orchestration loop with subagents, calling tools across business data connectors, running on infrastructure you operate. Because it is built rather than bought, the organisation's controls are architectural requirements — properties the design must have before it ships, enforced in review and in the platform the workload runs on.

The neighbouring archetype matters for scoping: the single agent workflow — one agent on one fast path, reading a request, deciding and writing to systems of record in seconds, with no supervisor, journal or replay — is not a contrast to this pattern but a nesting: each subagent here is that diagram one level down. The requirements below are the durability-and-supervision layer this pattern adds; the single-agent pattern's own controls (the action catalogue, reversibility thresholds, compensating transactions) still apply inside every subagent and get their own guidance.

items.title: Route every tool call through one governed gateway
body: Require a single choke point between agents and tools: one gateway that owns the tool catalogue, scopes each agent to the least set of tools its job needs, and is the only path — a subagent with its own side-channel to a connector is the design smell to reject in review. The registry behind the gateway is the inventory of record: which agents exist, which tools each may call, and who approved the pairing.

items.title: Give agents their own identity and short-lived credentials
body: Each agent and subagent acts as a non-human identity of its own — never a shared service account, and never a borrowed human session. Connector access is granted to that identity, scoped and revocable in the directory; credentials are issued ephemerally at call time from a secrets service rather than living in the agent's environment or prompt. The test worth applying in review: when this agent is compromised, what standing access does the attacker hold? The right answer is close to none.

items.title: Authorize actions at runtime, keep humans on the escalation path, and meter it
body: The model's plan is a proposal; a policy layer outside the model decides. Require runtime authorization on tool calls (policy on the action, its arguments and its target, not just on tool identity), human approval on the classes of action the organisation names as irreversible or sensitive, and rate, quota and spend limits per agent — an agent loop that can retry is a denial-of-wallet incident waiting for a bug.

items.title: Treat retrieved content as input, and inspect what leaves
body: Everything the connectors return — documents, records, messages — enters the context window as unauthenticated content that can steer the loop. Require injection screening on retrieved content and on inter-agent messages, and data-loss inspection on what flows out through responses and tool calls, at the gateway where both directions already pass.

items.title: Log for reconstruction, and build the stop before you need it
body: The audit requirement is reconstruction: from any effect on a business system, walk back through the tool call, the agent, the triggering context and the originating request. Structured, tamper-resistant logs at the gateway make that a query rather than an investigation. Pair it with a stop path that is designed, not improvised — quarantine one agent, revoke its identity and credentials, drain or halt its queued work — and exercise it before the first incident does.

CoSAI secure-ai-tooling (risk and control taxonomy this catalogue builds on)

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: A chat agent's security posture rests on one fact: the human reads every reply before the next action. Every requirement below either protects that gate (proposals worth reading, prompts rare enough to read), respects the delegated authority model (the tools act as the conversing user, never as the service), or bounds the conversation itself — which is a persistence surface where one poisoned tool result steers every later turn.

The bright line to police in review: remove the human from the turns — a scheduled run, an auto-approve setting, a background continuation — and the deployment has silently become the single agent workflow and must meet that pattern's requirements instead. The most common governance failure in this archetype is not a missing control; it is a chat agent that stopped being one without anybody re-reviewing it.

items.title: Keep the in-thread approval worth reading
body: The approval is only a control if the proposal is specific — "OK to proceed?" approves nothing in particular. Require action proposals that name the operation, the target and the consequence, and keep them rare: a gate that fires on every step trains the user to accept, which is this architecture's version of no gate at all. Assessment probe: read a week of approval prompts and count how many a reviewer could distinguish.

items.title: Every tool call carries the user's grant, not the service's reach
body: Authority is on-behalf-of: a delegated grant scoped to the session and the user, evaluated per call, ending when the session ends. The agent tier keeps its own workload identity — distinct from the users it serves — and holds no standing keys; the gateway brokers user-scoped credentials per call. Assessment probe: a user who cannot read a record directly asks the agent for it; the tool call must fail with the user's entitlement, not succeed with the service's.

items.title: Treat the conversation as a persistence surface
body: Context accumulates — retrievals, tool results, uploads — and all of it stands beside the system instruction on every later call. Scope memory to the conversation and the user with no cross-session reads; classify returned content before it re-enters the thread; and redact what a session may accumulate, because a late question can surface records the current topic never needed. Assessment probe: plant an instruction in a record the agent will retrieve, and verify classification catches it before the next model call.

items.title: Render output as content, and bound where it can go
body: The thread renders model output in a browser: sanitise markup and links before display, because a rendered image URL exfiltrates the conversation without a click. On the action side, tools reach named destinations only — the documented exfiltration chains in this archetype end at an attacker's collection endpoint that an egress allowlist would have refused.

items.title: Meter the edge, audit off the thread, and be able to stop
body: Session and per-user ceilings sit at the entry point, because per-token inference behind a public chat surface is a spend problem before it is anything else. The audit trail — proposal, approval, action — is recorded off the agent's write path; the thread the user sees is not the audit record. The stop ends live sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

CoSAI Shared Responsibility Framework V1.0 — autonomy levels and intervention tiers

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Protocol claims follow the 2026-07-28 MCP revision and its stable extensions; pattern-level by design.
overview: A published MCP server is an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models: conventional multi-tenant service engineering, plus a small set of inversions that follow from the caller being a model. The tool descriptions you publish execute as instruction inside somebody else's agent; the arguments you receive were composed by a model that may have been steered; and the user who consented is not present at call time. Every requirement below is either ordinary service discipline applied with unusual force, or a direct consequence of one of those three facts.

The deployment shape to require is boring on purpose: a service edge in front, identity federated to the enterprise IdP, one stateless application, a secrets manager behind it, and a governance plane that owns scopes, tool text, registry listing, audit and revocation. Teams should not be designing novel session schemes or token flows — the protocol deleted sessions and specifies the auth model; the review question is whether the build matches it.

items.title: Front the endpoint and federate identity — before any tool code is written
body: Require a gateway tier in front of the service: WAF, per-client and per-tenant rate limits sized for machine callers, and routing on the protocol's method and tool-name headers so metering never needs to parse bodies. Require identity to be federated, not invented: users consent at the enterprise IdP, the assertion is exchanged for an audience-bound token (the enterprise-managed authorization profile), and clients are pre-registered or use client-ID metadata documents — dynamic client registration is deprecated and should fail review. Evidence: the gateway config, the IdP federation record, and a token from a test client showing audience, expiry and scopes.

Tokens are validated on every request — client, user, scopes, audience, expiry — and audience validation is the server's own obligation even when the gateway pre-checks. A server that accepts a token issued for any other audience fails the assessment.

items.title: Build stateless; a state handle is a name, not a capability
body: The current protocol has no sessions: every request is self-contained, which is what makes the tier horizontally scalable. Where tools need cross-call state, the server mints opaque handles — high-entropy, bound to the token's subject, expiring, and re-authorized against the presenting token on every request. Possession of a handle must prove nothing. Reject designs that carry trust in the handle, vary tool listings per connection, or reimplement session affinity. Require Origin validation and TLS termination evidence at the edge. Assessment probe: present a valid handle with a different subject's token and confirm the request fails.

items.title: The caller's token never travels upstream
body: Most servers wrap existing systems, and the one rule with no exceptions is at that boundary: handlers call upstream as this service, on credentials a secrets manager issues, scopes and rotates — never by forwarding the inbound token. Token passthrough is the confused deputy the protocol forbids by name, and it is also the finding most often discovered in production. Bound egress to named upstream destinations; unbounded outbound reach from a tool server is the exfiltration path a steered agent is looking for.

On the data path, require the dual check on every operation — the scope permits it, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record — enforced in a shared layer rather than re-implemented per handler. Assessment probe: a valid token for tenant A requesting tenant B's record by identifier, on a read as well as a write.

items.title: Ship tool text like code, and list the server like a dependency
body: Descriptions, schemas and error text execute inside the caller's model, so they ship through the same pipeline as code: versioned, reviewed as a security artifact, adversarially read for what a model will do with the words, and published with provenance. Publish to the registry or private subregistry consuming clients admit from, with versions pinned, so a definition that changes after approval is detectable by the people trusting it. Mark consequential tools with confirmation semantics — declaration is the only lever the server holds — and keep results bounded in size, because output lands in someone else's context window.

items.title: Audit per call, and design revocation before launch
body: The audit record is per tool call — client, user, tenant, tool, arguments, result, with trace context propagated — because it is both the incident trail and the answer to a customer asking what their agent did. Scope design is where a hijacked agent's blast radius is decided: a catalogue of narrow scopes owned outside the service, no omnibus scope, and step-up challenges rather than over-asking at consent. Revocation must work at three grains without a deploy: a user (at the IdP), a client (at the authorization server), and a tool (at the definition layer). Assessment probe: revoke a test client and confirm its next call fails within the token lifetime.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; serving products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: Self-hosting open weights trades a data-disclosure risk for a supply-chain, availability and safety risk: no provider applies content policy, absorbs spikes, or patches the serving stack. The requirements below are the provider role, written down — and the two facts that shape them are that the serving stacks assume a trusted network (auth is partial, auxiliary endpoints and distributed control planes ship open by design), and that multi-tenancy inside the runtime is a set of configuration flags with data-protection consequences.

The review posture: treat serving configuration as security configuration. Continuous batching, cache sharing, tenancy scoping and network binding are tuning knobs to the platform team and controls to the security team; the gap between those two readings is where the incidents in this archetype live.

items.title: Nothing reaches the runtime except through the gateway
body: The serving stack is not safe as an exposed edge service and its own API keys guard only part of the surface — so the gateway in front is mandatory, not optional: one governed door carrying workload identity per calling tenant, per-tenant quotas sized for finite capacity, and admission control that sheds load at the front rather than at the accelerator. The distributed control plane behind it — job APIs, inter-node channels — ships unauthenticated by design; network isolation is the control there, not a version bump. Assessment probe: enumerate every listening endpoint on the serving tier and demand the auth story for each.

items.title: A blocking promotion gate, and digest verification at load
body: Weights reach the runtime only through the promotion pipeline: format policy and scanning as a blocking gate, per-version evaluation because a new checkpoint is a new model, and a digest verified at load so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly. Weights at rest get encryption, access control and integrity digests — the artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy.

items.title: Tenancy is a configuration review, not a default
body: Continuous batching mixes tenants in one forward pass; the KV and prefix caches hold their live context. Require tenant-scoped cache keys — published attacks reconstruct other tenants' prompts from cache-hit timing alone, so cross-tenant prefix sharing is off unless a review explicitly accepts it. For the highest-sensitivity tenants, hardware-backed isolation on the accelerators is the answer where shared silicon is not acceptable. Assessment probe: read the serving configuration and name which flags a tenant boundary depends on; anyone who cannot has not reviewed it.

items.title: Own the patch stream and the posture, including the gateway's
body: The serving stack is fast-moving third-party code with a live CVE stream, and nobody upstream patches it on your behalf — track it like any other exposed tier, and treat the gateway itself as supply chain: it is third-party code holding every tenant's credentials, an incident class with recent precedent. Posture management watches serving configuration for drift — versions, cache flags, bindings — and the guardrail checks a provider would have run are deployed at the gateway on both legs, because the output side is the half most often omitted.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; research findings are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: Treat the pipeline as a build system and hold it to build-system controls: reproducible runs, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks — the artifact cannot be diffed or read for backdoors — the substitutes are the two things that can be examined: what went into the training set, and how the result behaves. Every requirement below serves one of those two.

Scale the paranoia correctly: published results show a near-constant few hundred poisoned documents backdoor models regardless of size, backdoors in a base model survive tuning and the benchmarks that do not know their trigger, and fine-tuning on entirely benign data measurably erodes safety alignment. None of that is exotic; all of it is priced into the gates below.

items.title: Curate in front, with provenance captured at ingestion
body: Curation is the last point where a poisoned or improperly sourced example is a deletion rather than a retraining decision — filtering happens before the corpus, and per-example source and licence are recorded at ingestion because they cannot be reconstructed later. Lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset version is what makes a poisoning discovered months later scopeable at all. Include the labelling workforce in scope: labels steer behaviour directly and typically get no scrutiny relative to that influence.

items.title: Gate corpus access, and scope every job to its approved dataset
body: Corpus read access is the union of everything the organisation decided a model should learn, and it defaults to a broad platform role — gate reads and writes separately, and scope each training job to the dataset version approved for that run so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs. Restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was; decide who may read the corpus with that in mind.

items.title: Evaluation blocks promotion — and tests for what tuning broke
body: The gate is blocking or it is not a gate: capability and safety benchmarks with regression against the previous version, adversarial probing for triggers and behavioural anomalies, and extraction plus membership-inference testing before promotion. Require the safety evaluation even when the tuning data was benign — alignment erosion from ordinary instruction tuning is well replicated, so the post-tune eval is re-establishing a property the tuning degraded, not checking for sabotage alone. And treat a clean pass as necessary, never sufficient: a targeted backdoor passes every benchmark that does not know its trigger, which is why the input-side controls exist.

items.title: Sign outside the build, promote with separated duties
body: Whoever runs training cannot promote unilaterally, and the signing key lives outside the training environment so a compromised job cannot sign its own output — the default configuration usually violates both, so check rather than assume. Sign with the standardised model-signing tooling at promotion, verify at load, and keep the registry's own platform in scope: the common self-hosted trackers ship without authentication and have been exploited in the wild. The lineage record — dataset version, code, base model, run — is maintained for every artifact in the registry.

items.title: Scan what comes in from upstream, and roll out what goes downstream
body: Base checkpoints and training frameworks arrive from outside and execute with access to the corpus and the artifact: scan them before use, prefer formats that cannot execute on load, and treat scanner output as advisory next to format policy, because scanner bypasses are documented. Downstream, promotion is gradual — traffic split, signature verified at load, rollback target retained — because the last clean checkpoint is the incident response.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Vendor and product facts are confined to the dated tool entries and their cited documentation, verified at authoring time.
overview: Nobody builds their own Claude Code — this archetype is consumed, so the organisation's leverage is the policy tier each vendor ships. Every major coding agent now has one: a managed configuration channel that outranks whatever the developer sets locally, deliverable through MDM, an OS policy store, or the vendor's own admin console. Governing the archetype means using that tier deliberately, and holding one posture across four or five different products rather than five postures.

The guidance below is organised by control, not by product; the dated tool entries under each item carry the product-specific mechanics. Where vendors differ in strength — a console-delivered setting one vendor calls a client-side control versus an OS-enforced sandbox — the difference is called out, because it changes what the control is worth.

items.title: Deploy policy through the managed tier, not through documentation
body: Each vendor's managed tier can pin permission rules, approval behaviour and feature availability so the local user cannot loosen them: managed settings for Claude Code, an enforced requirements file for Codex, dashboard-plus-MDM policies for Cursor, and enterprise policies for Copilot. Treat a written standard with no managed-tier enforcement as not yet deployed.

Two properties are worth demanding everywhere: the auto-approval escape hatch is removable (the mode where the agent stops asking), and the policy channel fails closed — both Claude Code and Codex can refuse to start when the managed policy cannot be fetched, which turns a lost policy server into a stop rather than an unmanaged fleet.

Watch the conflict semantics per vendor: Copilot resolves a user's multiple organisations to the least restrictive setting within an enterprise, so a lockdown only holds when set at the enterprise level.

items.title: Constrain the tool plane with allowlists backed by a registry
body: The configuration file that admits tool servers arrives with the repository clone, which is why the allowlist has to be enforced outside it. Every one of the four vendors now supports centrally-managed MCP server allowlists; the shared semantics to get right are the empty-list case (for Claude Code and Codex an empty managed list is a full MCP lockdown, which is the correct starting state) and the matching strength — prefer the mechanisms that match on executable, URL or command rather than display name, since name-only matching is bypassable by design.

The allowlist is the enforcement point; the registry behind it is the decision record. Admit a server after a supply-chain review of its source, and keep the approved set somewhere reviewable rather than in a dashboard nobody diffs.

items.title: Sandbox execution and default-deny the network
body: The strongest available posture is OS-enforced sandboxing with the network off by default and a domain-filtered proxy where egress is genuinely needed — Codex ships exactly this shape, and its managed tier can forbid the profiles that escape it. Where a product's controls are weaker, the vendor's own documentation often says so: Cursor labels its terminal allowlist best-effort rather than a security boundary. Read those admissions as design guidance — pair weak in-product controls with endpoint-level egress filtering rather than treating them as equivalent.

Protect the paths that hold standing credentials from the agent regardless of sandbox: enforced deny-read patterns for key material and dotfiles are available in the managed tier (Codex's filesystem rules; Claude Code permission deny rules) and cost nothing to deploy fleet-wide.

items.title: Bind sessions to the organisation and export the audit trail
body: Force organisational login so every session maps to a directory identity — Claude Code and the Codex clients can both pin the login method and organisation, and block ambient personal API keys — and broker model credentials through managed helpers rather than long-lived keys in the environment.

Know what each audit surface actually captures before relying on it: Claude Code's managed OpenTelemetry emits per-session tool-decision events fleet-wide; Codex local usage exports through the workspace Compliance API; Cursor's Enterprise audit log records admin and account events but explicitly not agent output; Copilot's org audit log covers policy and licensing changes and the cloud agent's actions, not IDE prompts. The gaps define what endpoint or gateway logging still has to cover.

items.title: Deploy the desktop apps managed and govern connectors at the organisation, not the user
body: The desktop-shaped shells of this archetype reach the enterprise through the same door as any desktop software — someone installs one — but they connect to mail, files, calendars and internal services through per-user connector grants that no one sums. Both major desktop assistants now ship enterprise installers and honour device-level policy (MDM configuration profiles and policy registries), and both have org-level admission controls for what the assistant may connect to — allowlists for desktop extensions and role-scoped app and plugin enablement. The defaults differ in a way that matters: one vendor's extension allowlist ships disabled (everything available until an admin turns it on) while the other disables plugins by default on enterprise workspaces. Check the default, don't assume it.

Where managed connector authorization through the IdP is available, prefer it over per-user OAuth grants: it makes the connector's scope an administered decision and keeps revocation in the directory rather than in each employee's settings.

items.title: Contain what the desktop shells can reach from the device
body: Device policies can turn off the highest-risk local surfaces — local MCP server connections, computer-use and record modes, unmanaged workspace folders — and pin updates to managed channels. What the policies cannot see is content leaving through sanctioned chat, which is why this archetype pairs the vendor controls with interaction-level data loss prevention and network egress telemetry; the compliance export APIs both vendors ship are the hook for that monitoring, with source retention short enough that continuous export is part of the deployment, not an afterthought.

items.title: Discover what you did not deploy, and assume the repo is hostile input
body: The managed tier only governs the clients you deployed; developers can install others, and IDE forks and extensions ship agent capability by default now. Discovery — endpoint software inventory, extension allowlists, egress telemetry to known vendor endpoints — is what makes the sanctioned-tools list a fact rather than an aspiration.

Prompt injection for this archetype arrives with the working tree: source files, manifests, issue text and tool output all enter the context window without being the developer's instruction. That is an argument for keeping approval gates meaningful (a gate that fires on everything trains reflexive acceptance) and for treating repo-supplied configuration — hooks, tool manifests, agent instruction files — as untrusted until reviewed, which is what the managed hook and sideload restrictions in the vendor policy tiers exist to enforce.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; runtime products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: A local model runtime is a network service one person installs in an afternoon: it binds a port, speaks an OpenAI-compatible API, and in the flagship implementations ships without authentication by design — the vendors point at VPNs and reverse proxies rather than shipping auth. Everything a hosted API supplied — guardrails, rate limits, abuse monitoring, patching — is absent unless the device owner adds it, and the organisation's problem starts with not knowing the runtime exists.

Two facts should anchor the policy. Exposure is real and growing: internet scans keep finding these runtimes by the tens of thousands, bound to routable interfaces by users who never made that decision consciously. And the model files themselves are attack surface: formats that execute code on load, native parsers whose memory bugs are a code-execution class, and embedded templates that execute at inference time.

items.title: Publish a sanctioned runtime posture, and enforce it from the device
body: Take a position: whether local inference may run at all, on which runtimes, bound to loopback only, with authentication in front of the port — a reverse proxy or token-authenticated wrapper where the runtime itself refuses to ship auth. Locality is not authorization: a browser tab is local too, and a permissive cross-origin policy lets any visited page drive the runtime. Device management is the enforcement point, because there is no server side to enforce from.

items.title: Put format policy and scanning in front of the fetch
body: The runtime is usually the thing doing the fetching, so the control must sit in front of it: safe-by-construction tensor formats required, executable formats refused, and scanning before load — a scan after the runtime opens the file has documented an incident, not prevented one. Treat "safe" formats as reduced surface rather than no surface: their native parsers carry their own code-execution bug class. Protect the artifacts on disk with restrictive permissions and integrity checks, so a swapped file is detectable.

items.title: Replace the provider floor the callers assume is there
body: Local applications call the local API the way they would a hosted one, assuming a safety floor that is not there. Where local inference is sanctioned for real use, require the missing pieces on the request path: input and output classification, a per-caller rate bound on the shared unmetered port, and an evaluation of what the weights actually do before other software builds on them — there is no provider evaluation to inherit, and refusal behaviour is removable by fine-tune.

items.title: Inventory what is running, and find what never registered
body: Every response to a bad model release, a parser CVE or an exposure report presumes the organisation knows which machines run which runtimes serving which models from which sources. Build that inventory from the device — process, port and model-file telemetry — rather than from self-reporting, because this archetype spreads one install at a time and appears in no procurement record.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; harness products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: An open-source coding harness is the vendored product with the vendor column deleted: the same loop and tool surface, with pasted long-lived keys instead of session credentials, community registries instead of a signed channel, configuration files instead of a control plane, and — increasingly — serve modes, relay tunnels and chat bridges instead of an owner-bound remote relay. Nothing here can be governed from a vendor console, which puts every control on the organisation's side.

Two facts anchor the policy. The supply chain includes the agent itself: the category's landmark incident was a compromised harness release published through a community channel, whose payload installed further agents. And the remote surfaces ship weak: auth on the serve ports ranges from a mandatory shared secret down to none, and chat bridges put messaging-platform identity in front of a loop that runs with the developer's credentials.

items.title: Sanction specific harnesses, and pin their supply chain
body: Take a position on which harnesses are acceptable, and mirror them: harness releases, extensions and skills reviewed, version-pinned and served from the organisation's registry, with public marketplaces blocked on managed machines. An update is a decision — the update channel is the category's proven attack path. Pair the position with discovery built from package-manager and process telemetry, because these harnesses arrive one developer at a time and appear in no procurement record.

items.title: Vault the keys and route the calls through your gateway
body: The common state is a provider key in plaintext configuration, readable by the agent, its tools, and any repository script they run. The sanctioned state brokers credentials at the organisation's AI gateway — keychain-backed locally where the harness supports it, vaulted behind the gateway where it does not — with deny-by-default egress naming providers, registries and remote tool servers, and spend ceilings at the crossing, because the only native meter is the provider's invoice. Assessment probe: grep a sanctioned install's configuration for key material; anything found fails.

items.title: Lock the remote surfaces or turn them off
body: Serve modes, web UIs, relay tunnels and chat bridges are admission decisions, not conveniences: off by default on managed machines, and where a team has a stated need, admitted deliberately — mandatory shared secret, pinned transport, loopback or VPN binding, and a named allowlist for any chat bridge, because platform identity is the personal agent's admission model wearing a developer tool's clothes. Keep the local approval gate real at the same time: dangerous-command detection on and auto-approve flags banned on managed machines — it is the only gate there is.

items.title: The engine disciplines still apply — nobody else will apply them
body: Everything the vendored guidance requires of the engine holds here with no managed tier to enforce it: per-tool permission scoping configured outside the repository the agent works on; sandboxed execution treated as a harness-selection criterion, because the category default is bare-host; SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profiles kept outside the agent's reach; memory and rules files treated as untrusted input, with a repo-committed rules change reviewed like a code change; and repository content treated as instruction-bearing input, because it is.
