guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Vendor and product facts are confined to the dated tool entries and their cited documentation, verified at authoring time.
overview: An always-on personal agent is a daemon a person runs with their own credentials, taking ambient instructions from messaging channels and acting without a human in the loop. The organisation rarely operates it — someone installs it because it is useful — so governing this archetype means publishing a sanctioned way to run it that is safer than the default, and making the unsanctioned way visibly out of policy.

The archetype's exposure is concentrated in two places: the runtime (what the agent can execute, read and reach) and the control plane (the gateway that admits instructions and holds the operator's authority). Both have hardened configurations that exist today; the controls below are about making those configurations the required path.

items.title: Sanction a hardened runtime, or people will pick their own
body: Take a position on which runtimes are acceptable and publish it. A bare-host install — the agent executing shell commands directly on the operating system with the user's full profile — is not an acceptable posture for a daemon that takes instructions from inbound messages. The sanctioned configurations are the containerised ones: an OpenClaw-class agent with its sandbox backend enabled (tool execution isolated in a container with no network, a read-only root and dropped capabilities) or run inside a purpose-built sandbox product that adds an egress proxy; or a Hermes-class runtime whose execution goes through per-command approval and one of its isolated terminal backends.

The configurations differ in what they contain. An agent-native sandbox backend isolates tool execution only — the daemon, its memory and its credentials stay on the host. The microVM wrap contains the harness whole, keeps secrets host-side behind an injecting proxy, and shares only named workspace folders in; it is the only configuration under which the products' approval-free default is defensible. Sanction the whole-harness wrap where it is available, and in enterprise deployments require clone-mode (read-only) workspace sharing so agent edits return by git rather than landing on the host as they happen.

Pair the runtime position with a tool-policy floor: high-risk tools (arbitrary shell, browser control, unrestricted fetch) disabled unless the deployment has a stated need, and per-agent tool policies rather than one permissive default.

items.title: Lock down the control plane and keep credentials out of the agent
body: The gateway is the operator's authority; treat its exposure as the incident. Require loopback-only binding with token authentication, and set a version floor at the release that closed the control-plane token-exfiltration CVE — the exposed-instance scans that followed it are the case for making this a hard requirement rather than a recommendation.

Keep provider keys and account credentials out of the agent's own environment where the tooling allows it: sandbox egress through a proxy that injects API keys on the way out, so a compromised agent process has nothing durable to leak, and default-deny network egress from the execution sandbox with an explicit allowlist for what the agent legitimately needs to reach.

items.title: Keep a human between the agent and anything hard to undo
body: Unattended operation is the archetype's point, so the approval budget has to be spent precisely: dangerous-command detection with a blocking approval step, pairing codes or allowlists before an unknown sender can instruct the agent at all, and mention-gating in group channels. These are runtime-enforced policies in the current tooling, not etiquette.

Decide the quarantine path before the first incident: who can stop a personal agent, what stopping means (revoking the gateway token, killing the daemon, expiring its channel pairings), and how a compromised agent's standing access is enumerated afterwards.

items.title: Govern what the agent loads and what it remembers
body: Personal agents grow by acquiring skills, tools and server connections from public registries, and they keep long-lived memory. Both are injection surfaces: a fetched skill is unreviewed code admitted into the operator's session, and ambient-message instructions can write durable state into memory that outlives the message. Require vetting before third-party skills or tool servers are admitted, and treat memory as contaminated-by-default when the agent ingests content from senders who are not the operator.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; incidents are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: The organisation's exposure here is a sum nobody computes by default: thousands of individually reasonable connector grants, a file-upload path no connector governance sees, and a consumer version of the same product one session cookie away. The controls split cleanly into two halves — the vendor tenant you configure, and the edge and browser telemetry you own — and the second half matters more, because it covers the two paths the vendor's console cannot see.

One material change to re-review against: these products are agents now. The same standing grants that powered retrieval also carry write actions — mail sent, files changed, tickets moved — through vendor-side agent modes, scheduled tasks and code execution. The documented incident class is zero-click: content in a connected mailbox or drive steers the assistant into exfiltrating without the user clicking anything.

items.title: Restrict the tenant at the edge, or the enterprise terms are optional
body: Everything the enterprise agreement promises — retention, training opt-out, audit export — applies only to traffic that reaches the managed tenant. Tenant restriction enforced at the secure edge is what stops the consumer product being an alternative; without it, the crossing simply succeeds and corporate data leaves under consumer terms, invisibly. Identity establishes who is licensed and which tenant they may reach; the edge blocks or logs everything else.

items.title: Inspect the upload path, because nothing else can
body: A pasted document crosses the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record — every control that watches connectors misses it entirely. Inline inspection of prompts and uploads at the edge, plus in-browser visibility of which tenant a session is in and what is being pasted, are the only records this path will ever produce. Weight them accordingly: they carry more of the archetype's real control than the vendor's admin surface does.

items.title: Gate the agent modes and write-capable connectors deliberately
body: Own tenant configuration as living policy, re-reviewed every time the vendor ships a connector or an agent capability — the default for new ones is rarely off. Write actions get the strictest treatment the vendor offers: admin-gated per app and per action, with confirmation required on writes; the vendor ships the toggles, and leaving them at default is the decision not to use them. Treat connector-retrieved content as untrusted in policy and user guidance — the vendor's guardrails are the only inline control, and the zero-click incident record says they are not sufficient alone.

items.title: Treat grants as identities, and classify before connecting
body: Standing OAuth grants are non-human identities: inventoried, expiring, revoked when the employee or project goes — the broker keeps calling on grants issued for projects that ended. Govern by classification which systems may be connected at all, so individual consent cannot outrun policy, and know what sensitive data sits inside connector reach before the grants aggregate it — an assistant makes pre-existing oversharing instantly discoverable.

items.title: Fuse the vendor's audit with your own, and hunt the shadow traffic
body: The vendor's export covers the managed tenant; your edge and browser telemetry cover the uploads and the consumer product it will never see — only the fused record answers what actually left. Run discovery for personal-account and competitor traffic independently of the vendor: it is usually the larger flow, and it is the population the sanctioned tenant exists to absorb.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; incidents are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: The unit of risk in this archetype is the population, not the agent: hundreds of near-identical agents, each simple, each holding connector grants, many authored by people who have left. There is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data unless the platform's gates are turned on — and several of the platform defaults (sharing scope, agent-to-agent discovery, soft-enabled policy) are set for adoption, not governance.

The decisive technical question when evaluating or configuring any platform in this class: does a published agent execute on its author's credentials or its invoker's? Author-credential execution turns publishing into a privilege grant — a user who could not read a table reads it through an agent someone else built — and no amount of population management compensates for getting this one wrong.

items.title: Build the inventory first; everything else depends on it
body: Every agent, its author, its connector set, its audience, its sharing mode and its last use — the platforms now report this, and the vendors sell fleet-level control planes over it. Pair the inventory with run history per agent and per consumer: it is the basis for retiring what nobody uses, investigating what someone did, and noticing the agents shared to "anyone with the link" on the vendor's own domain, where exposure research keeps finding them by the thousands.

items.title: Decide who may build, and demand invoker-credential execution
body: Restricting who may build is the bluntest and often most effective population control — by default, creating an agent requires the same permission as opening a document. Require per-invoker authorisation so the organisation's existing access model survives publication, and use the platforms' per-agent identities: a directory principal per agent is the hook that lets conditional access, policy and revocation attach to one agent instead of the whole population, and the handle for transferring ownership when authors leave.

items.title: Author connector policy centrally, and gate publication
body: Blocking a connector pairing scales where reviewing agents does not: a source of confidential data plus a path that sends mail is the pairing worth banning outright. Check the enforcement default on whatever platform is in use — some enforce centrally out of the box, others ship policy soft-enabled where makers never feel it. Turn on the publication gate so review stands between an author and an audience; it is the nearest available thing to code review, and it is frequently off.

items.title: Treat grounding sources as instruction channels
body: A shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to — an instruction channel wearing a grounding label, where one planted document steers the agent for every user. Restrict attachable locations to ones with governed write access, govern by classification what connectors may reach at all, and know what sensitive data sits inside connector reach before hundreds of agents find it. Assume agent-to-agent discovery is on by default and decide deliberately whether it should be: one steered agent recruiting a teammate's stronger connectors is the documented second-order path.

items.title: Run it as a programme, and assure what you cannot test
body: Maker governance is ongoing: environments and licensing, lifecycle and ownership transfer, retirement as somebody's actual job — the population grows by default and shrinks only on purpose. The platform's execution, isolation and guardrail claims cannot be tested from your side; assure them the way any critical vendor control is assured, and revisit when the vendor ships the features that change the answer.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; platforms are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: Every provider converged on the same decomposition — runtime, memory, tool gateway, identity, sandbox, observability, evaluation, policy — which means the governance plane most self-built agent architectures never get is exactly what these platforms sell. The organisation's job splits accordingly: require teams to actually use the supplied controls (the platform makes them available, not mandatory), and configure the customer-owned half deliberately rather than accepting defaults.

The consequential engineering choice is between the declarative harness and the code escape hatch. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams start declarative, hit a limitation, move to code, and do not notice which controls stopped applying — make that transition a review event, because the platform will not.

items.title: Use the per-agent identities the platform mints, and carry the user's
body: The platforms supply first-class, revocable principals per agent — and teams routinely collapse everything back onto one shared service principal, which undoes attribution and per-agent revocation in one stroke. Require the distinct principal per agent, and require the user's identity to travel from the front end to the tool call: dropping it on the way is the confused-deputy failure this architecture makes easy to avoid and easy to commit. Assessment probe: revoke one agent's principal and confirm exactly one agent stops.

items.title: The escape hatch is a review event, and gateway coverage is the checklist
body: Tool brokering, scoping, logging and guardrails reach a declarative agent automatically and reach custom code only where it calls the gateway. Where enforcement sits is the platform-evaluation question: the strongest platforms enforce default-deny policy and guardrails at the tool gateway, outside agent code, with floor settings a builder cannot lower — on others the same controls are code the builder must remember to call. Require an explicit coverage check whenever a team takes the code path: which calls route through the gateway, which guardrails still apply, and who verified it.

items.title: Memory scope is a reviewed decision, never a default
body: Managed memory's scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence: cross-user scope means one user's content shapes another's turn, and it looks like a feature. Session or per-user scope is the default posture; cross-user scope is a design exception with a named owner and a written justification.

items.title: Admit definitions like code, and evaluate before every alias move
body: An agent definition — instructions, tool bindings, or loop code — is a deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do; it gets the same review, inventory and provenance as application code, and the population inventory matters because a managed runtime makes agents cheap enough to sprawl. No definition change reaches a production alias without adversarial evaluation, because the definition is the attack surface prompt injection negotiates with.

items.title: Turn on everything observable, export it, and assure the rest
body: The loop is not inspectable; traces are the only window, so all of it is on — steps, tool calls, decisions — and exported out of the provider's console, where it can be correlated with everything else and retained on your schedule. Policy and guardrail configuration is authored through governed intake, not console edits. What remains — the sandbox isolation claim, the runtime's own supply chain — cannot be tested from your side: assure it like any critical vendor dependency, and note the direction of travel toward sandboxes and compute in the customer's own perimeter where the claim is not acceptable.

guidanceTools.name: Claude Code
summary: Two admin channels share one top-precedence managed tier: endpoint-managed settings delivered as files or OS policies via MDM/GPO, and server-managed settings configured in the claude.ai admin console (Teams/Enterprise, Owner roles) and fetched by clients at login with hourly polling. Managed settings outrank command-line flags and all user and project files.

items.title: Managed settings via MDM, GPO or the admin console
body: Endpoint paths: macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json (plus a managed-settings.d/ drop-in directory), Linux and WSL /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json — the legacy ProgramData path is no longer supported as of v2.1.75. OS-policy channels: the macOS managed-preference domain com.anthropic.claudecode and the Windows registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode.

Server-managed settings cover the same keys from the console, with a caveat the docs state plainly: it is a client-side control, not a security boundary, and it is unavailable when routing through Bedrock, Vertex or a custom base URL. Endpoint management via MDM is the stronger channel; forceRemoteSettingsRefresh makes the server channel fail closed at startup.

links.title: Claude Code settings reference (precedence, paths, keys)

items.title: Permission, MCP and hook lockdown
body: Pin permission rules with permissions.allow / deny / ask, and set allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly to block user- and project-level rules entirely. disableAutoMode removes the auto-approval mode from the mode cycle (the settings reference's current name; older pages still show disableBypassPermissionsMode).

MCP admission: allowedMcpServers is the allowlist — undefined means unrestricted and an empty array is a full lockdown — with deniedMcpServers winning on conflict, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, and a managed-mcp.json file for exclusive control of MCP configuration. Hooks and sideloading close the remaining gaps: allowManagedHooksOnly, disableAllHooks, allowedHttpHookUrls, and disableSideloadFlags to reject --plugin-dir and --mcp-config at the command line.

items.title: Forced login, credentials and audit telemetry
body: forceLoginMethod and forceLoginOrgUUID pin sessions to the organisation; forceLoginOrgUUID also blocks startup on ambient API-key credentials (v2.1.146+). apiKeyHelper substitutes a managed credential script for stored keys.

Fleet-wide audit: set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and the OTEL_* exporter variables in the managed env block; when the exporter endpoint comes from managed settings, conflicting developer-set OTel variables are removed at startup (v2.1.217+). Sessions then emit per-tool decision events, prompt and API events (text redacted by default) and usage metrics to the organisation's collector.

guidanceTools.name: Cursor
summary: Enterprise governance spans SAML SSO with SCIM, MDM device policies, org-enforced Privacy Mode, model and MCP access control, agent run-mode policies, Enterprise-only audit logs with SIEM streaming, and a Basic-auth Admin API. Most controls are labelled Enterprise-tier in the documentation.

items.title: Identity and device management
body: SAML 2.0 SSO (password auth can be blocked), SCIM provisioning with group sync, and three dashboard roles. MDM policies for macOS and Windows cover Allowed Team IDs (blocks personal-account login on corporate devices), an Allowed Extensions allowlist (Cursor 2.1+) and Workspace Trust enforcement.

links.title: Cursor enterprise identity and access management

items.title: Privacy, model and MCP control
body: Privacy Mode is default-on for Enterprise teams and admins can enforce it so members cannot disable it; model access is set per team and per organisation group, and BYOK API keys can be blocked. MCP servers are governed by a dashboard allowlist with wildcard matching, per-server tool restrictions and per-server network policies, distributable to endpoints as ~/.cursor/permissions.json via MDM — admin settings take precedence over the local file and editor settings.

items.title: Agent run-mode policies and audit
body: Enterprise Run Mode policies (Cursor 3.6+) set the terminal posture — Auto-review, Allowlist, or Run Everything — and the docs are candid that the allowlist is best-effort, not a security boundary; hooks can scan prompts, block commands and redact secrets, and .cursorignore is likewise documented as not a boundary. Enterprise audit logs record admin and account events (explicitly not agent responses or generated code), stream to SIEM, and the Admin API exposes members, usage, spend, repo blocklists and model access.

guidanceTools.name: GitHub Copilot
summary: Governance runs through the enterprise AI-controls tab and organisation Copilot settings: Feature, Privacy and Models policies set enterprise-first (enable, disable, or let organisations decide), with content exclusion and MCP governance layered on for Business and Enterprise plans.

items.title: Enterprise and organisation policy framework
body: Policies gate which Copilot features, agents and models users can access — named policies include MCP servers in Copilot, restricting MCP to registry servers, allowed models, custom models, web search, Copilot Memory and suggestions-matching-public-code (blocked by default for Business seats). Conflict rules matter for design: within one enterprise the least restrictive setting wins across a user's organisations, so a lockdown must be set at the enterprise level to be a lockdown.

items.title: MCP governance and content exclusion
body: The MCP policy gates whether MCP servers run at all across Copilot clients; server allowlisting comes in two strengths — a GitHub-hosted Managed Settings File (GA, matched on name, URL and stdio command, not user-bypassable) and a Custom MCP Registry (preview, name matching only, bypassable by editing local config). Content exclusion (Business and Enterprise) applies at repository, organisation and enterprise scope with fnmatch patterns, but is not honoured by Copilot CLI or by agent and edit modes of Chat — scope guidance accordingly.

items.title: Audit surface and network posture
body: The organisation audit log records Copilot licensing, settings and policy changes (action:copilot) and the cloud agent's website activity (actor:Copilot) with 180-day retention — it does not capture client-side prompts, so IDE-level telemetry needs its own answer. Proxy and firewall allowlists are documented per-plan, with a /meta API endpoint for the current domain set.

guidanceTools.name: Codex
summary: One agent across the CLI, the IDE extension and the ChatGPT desktop app, configured through TOML with a documented precedence chain and a genuine enterprise enforcement layer: an admin-authored requirements.toml that constrains approval policies, sandbox profiles, network, MCP servers and feature flags, and that users cannot override.

items.title: Admin-enforced requirements.toml
body: Requirements arrive by system file (/etc/codex/requirements.toml on Unix, %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml on Windows), as a cloud-managed policy bundle assigned from chatgpt.com and delivered at sign-in, or via macOS MDM under com.openai.codex (base64-encoded TOML; the highest-precedence channel). If the cloud policy fetch fails with no valid cache, the client refuses to start unmanaged rather than failing open.

Enforceable keys cover the surfaces that matter: allowed_approval_policies and allowed_permission_profiles with default_permissions (e.g. pin ":workspace" and allow only read-only and workspace profiles), filesystem deny_read patterns for secrets paths, prefix command rules, managed hooks with allow_managed_hooks_only, experimental network domain allow/deny lists, and feature pins that disable computer use and browser surfaces org-wide.

items.title: Sandbox, approvals and network posture
body: Sandboxing is OS-enforced (Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox) with permission profiles from read-only through workspace-write to an explicit danger-full-access escape hatch. The agent runs with network access off by default; enabling it can route through a domain-filtering proxy, and .git, .codex and .agents stay read-only inside writable roots. Codex cloud blocks internet access during the agent phase by default, with per-environment allowlists and method restrictions.

items.title: Workspace gating and compliance export
body: Workspace admins gate Codex Local (desktop app, CLI and IDE extension together) and Codex cloud separately, assign access by role with SCIM-synced groups, and set starting model defaults — enforced requirements still win. Codex usage, including the local clients, exports through the Compliance API and the immutable Compliance Logs Platform alongside workspace audit and authentication logs.

guidanceTools.name: ChatGPT desktop app
summary: The current desktop app bundles Chat, Work and Codex, and is governed by the same managed-configuration system as Codex — requirements.toml cloud policies and the com.openai.codex MDM domain — plus workspace admin controls for plugins, apps, memory and identity from the ChatGPT admin panel.

items.title: Managed deployment and update control
body: Windows ships only as a Store-signed MSIX (no MSI or standalone EXE), deployable via Intune, MECM or winget with offline packages available; macOS deploys from the enterprise DMG, with device management arriving through the com.openai.codex MDM payload rather than a dedicated packaging guide. The built-in updater is disabled with an enforced requirements.toml feature pin, targeted by group, user or platform from the managed-configs console.

items.title: Workspace controls over connectors, apps and memory
body: On Enterprise and Edu workspaces, plugins and their underlying apps are disabled by default and enabled per role, with per-app configuration for real-time access, actions, approvals and domain restrictions — one control set that applies across web, mobile, desktop and Codex. Memory and record mode are workspace-level toggles (record off by default), and the Compliance Logs Platform exports immutable audit, authentication and usage events with 30-day source retention, so longer retention requires continuous export.

guidanceTools.name: Claude Desktop
summary: Enterprise installers (macOS PKG, Windows per-user MSIX) deploy via Jamf, Kandji, Intune, SCCM or GPO, with device-level policies covering extensions, local MCP, auto-updates and forced org login, plus an in-console desktop-extension allowlist and org-wide managed connector authorization for Team and Enterprise plans.

items.title: Managed deployment and device policies
body: Device policies live in the macOS configuration-profile domain com.anthropic.claudefordesktop and the Windows HKLM policy registry. The keys that matter for control: isDesktopExtensionEnabled and isDesktopExtensionDirectoryEnabled (kill switches for extensions and the directory), isLocalDevMcpEnabled (local MCP server connections), isClaudeCodeForDesktopEnabled, forceLoginOrgUUID, allowedWorkspaceFolders and auto-update enforcement. Device-level policy overrides the in-app allowlist.

items.title: Extension allowlist and managed connector authorization
body: Team and Enterprise Owners can turn on the desktop extension allowlist (Organization settings → Connectors → Desktop). It ships disabled — every extension is available until it is enabled — and enabling it force-deletes existing non-allowlisted installs; custom org-scoped extensions upload in .mcpb format. Managed authorization (beta) lets admins authorize MCP connectors org-wide through the IdP, assign them by role and scope their permissions.

guidanceTools.name: OpenClaw
summary: A self-hosted personal agent whose gateway is the control plane — channels, tool policy and auth under an explicit single-trusted-operator model. Official hardening is real and specific: loopback-plus-token gateway auth, DM pairing, high-risk tools disabled or sandboxed, and a container sandbox whose defaults are no network, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped.

items.title: Gateway lockdown and the version floor
body: The gateway defaults to loopback binding; the docs say plainly never to expose it unauthenticated on 0.0.0.0, and token auth is the recommended mode. DM hardening is dmPolicy pairing (time-limited codes for unknown senders), contact allowlists and requireMention in groups; `openclaw security audit` checks a deployment and can apply safe fixes. Enforce a version floor of 2026.1.29: earlier Control UI builds auto-connected to an attacker-supplied gatewayUrl and sent the operator token (CVE-2026-25253, CVSS 8.8), and internet scans found thousands of exposed instances.

items.title: Sandbox defaults and proxy-injected credentials
body: With the Docker sandbox backend enabled, tool execution runs in a container whose defaults are network none, readOnlyRoot true, all capabilities dropped and a non-root user, with the workspace mounted read-only or read-write by policy; per-agent sandbox and tool-policy overrides layer on top, and the docs warn never to mount the Docker socket into a sandbox. Docker's own Sandboxes product wraps the same agent with a configurable egress proxy that denies arbitrary hosts and injects provider API keys at the proxy, so the agent process never holds them.

guidanceTools.name: Hermes Agent
summary: An open-source (MIT) personal agent runtime — a competing product to OpenClaw, not a variant of it, with a one-command migration from it. Its posture centres on per-command approval with dangerous-command detection, DM pairing, fully isolated per-profile state, and sandboxed execution across multiple terminal backends.

items.title: Approval-first execution and isolated state
body: Execution goes through command approval with dangerous-command detection — blocked actions return a tool error naming the denied command rather than silently proceeding — and the first DM claims exclusive access to a deployment. Profiles are fully isolated (own memory store, session database and skills directory), subagents run isolated, and sandboxed execution spans local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona and Vercel Sandbox backends with container hardening and namespace isolation.

The governance trade-off to weigh: Hermes is a self-improving agent that writes its own skills from experience, which is also the feature demanding the most trust — an organisation sanctioning it should decide whether self-modification is acceptable and pin the approval policy accordingly.
